CVE-2026-98432 is a use-after-free vulnerability, or UAF for short.

Here’s what it means.

Think of memory as a space where programs temporarily keep the information they need. When they’re done with that information, they release the space so it can be used for something else.

That’s perfectly normal.

The problem occurs when a program tries to use that same memory after it has already been released. It shouldn’t happen, but sometimes it does. This is known as a use-after-free vulnerability.

Now, let’s bring that back to Linux.

The kernel manages socket options when it’s handling incoming IPv4 TCP connections. With this vulnerability, it can release the memory holding those options while another operation is still trying to use them.

That’s the problem in a nutshell.

CVE-2026-98432 has a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8, which puts it in the Critical category. An attacker doesn’t need to authenticate or have access to the system to try exploiting it. They can send specially crafted IPv4 TCP packets containing IP options to an affected system.

There’s another important detail here. Researchers demonstrated remote code execution against systems with a Multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener.

AWS also reported that it had no evidence of the vulnerability being exploited in the wild at the time of its advisory.

But how does the kernel end up releasing memory that’s still being used?

A Terrain-Based, Risk-Informed Approach to Track Key Vulnerabilities
  • Track Key Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs)
  • Visibility to Risk: Prioritizing CVEs
  • Terrain-Aware Defense
Download Whitepaper
So, How Does the Vulnerability Work?

Let’s start with something familiar: a device trying to connect to a Linux server.

When that connection request reaches the server, the Linux kernel has to process it and keep track of the information needed to establish the connection. Some of that information is stored in socket options.

Normally, this process should happen without any problems.

However, in this instance, the kernel moves those socket settings to a newly created child socket from a request socket. Instead of creating a separate copy, it transfers ownership of the existing memory.

Another operation might still be using those same socket options. For example, one CPU could be handling a new connection while another is processing a retransmitted SYN request for that connection.

Now imagine the child socket gets freed while that second operation is still running.

The memory is gone, but the other operation hasn’t finished using it. When it tries to access that memory again, the kernel runs into a use-after-free condition.

Here’s the sequence in simpler terms:

  • An attacker sends specially crafted IPv4 TCP packets to a system that's listening for connections.
  • The kernel processes the connection and transfers the socket options to a child socket.
  • At the same time, another CPU may be handling a retransmitted SYN request and trying to access those same options.
  • The child socket gets freed before the other operation finishes.
  • The second operation tries to access the memory even though it has already been released.

And that’s how the problem occurs.

This is what’s known as a race condition. Two operations are happening at the same time, and the kernel isn’t handling the memory release safely.

There’s another way to run into a similar problem, too.

It’s called request socket migration. Basically, the kernel moves a connection request from one socket to another. During this process, the original and cloned request sockets can share the same socket options.

That creates another opportunity for one operation to release the memory while another is still using it.

So, the real issue here is timing. The kernel needs to wait until other operations are finished using the memory before releasing it. In this case, it doesn’t always do that.

What Can Actually Happen If Someone Exploits It?

Okay, so we know what’s going wrong inside the kernel. But what does this mean for an organization running Linux systems?

Unfortunately, the impact can be quite serious.

Depending on the conditions, an attacker could potentially trigger:

  • System crashes: If the kernel tries to access invalid memory, it could crash the system and interrupt the services running on it.
  • Memory corruption: The kernel could end up accessing memory that's already been released, potentially affecting other operations.
  • Memory disclosure: Under certain conditions, information stored in kernel memory could be exposed.
  • Remote code execution: Researchers demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution against systems with an MPTCP listener.

The remote attack aspect is particularly important.

An attacker doesn’t need an account, special permissions, or someone to interact with a malicious file or link. They can attempt to trigger the vulnerable code remotely by sending specially crafted network packets.

For organizations running Linux servers that accept incoming TCP connections, that’s definitely something to pay attention to.

How Do You Know If Your Linux Systems Are Affected?

If you’re responsible for a Linux environment, this is probably the next thing on your mind.

CVE-2026-98432 affects Linux kernel versions 4.4 and later. But that doesn’t automatically mean every system running one of these versions is vulnerable.

Additionally, it depends on the Linux distribution, the kernel branch, and whether or not the necessary security patches have been installed.

Several vendors, including Amazon Linux, Red Hat, SUSE, and Debian, have published advisories and fixes.

Here’s something else to watch out for: Linux distributions often backport security fixes to older kernel versions.

In other words, a system might already have the fix even if its kernel version looks older. So, don’t rely on the version number alone when checking for vulnerable systems.

If you’re reviewing your environment, start with these questions:

  • Are any of your Linux servers running potentially affected kernel builds?
  • Have you installed the security updates recommended by your Linux distribution?
  • Are these systems accepting incoming IPv4 TCP connections?
  • Are you using Multipath TCP or request socket migration?
  • Have you rebooted the affected systems after installing the kernel update?

And don’t stop with your physical servers. Check your cloud-based Linux instances, too. They can easily get overlooked when organizations are reviewing their infrastructure.

How Can It Be Fixed?

Now for the important part: fixing the issue.

The good news is that vendors have released security updates. So, if you have an affected system, getting the fixed kernel installed should be your first step.

The upstream fix changes how the kernel releases socket options. It uses kfree_rcu() to make sure memory isn’t released until active readers have finished accessing it.

So, what should you do next?

1. Install the available kernel update

First, check the security advisory for your Linux distribution.

Find the fixed kernel package recommended for your version and install it. The package you need may differ depending on the distribution and release you’re running, so follow the vendor’s instructions.

2. Reboot the affected systems

Don’t skip this step.

Installing a kernel update doesn’t necessarily mean your system is already running the updated kernel. You need to make sure the new kernel has actually been loaded.

AWS specifically notes that affected self-managed EC2 instances must be rebooted after installing the update.

3. Can't patch everything immediately? Use temporary mitigations

We know that updating every system in a large environment isn’t always something you can do overnight.

If you need more time to roll out the patches, AWS recommends a few temporary measures to reduce exposure.

For example, you can disable Multipath TCP using net.mptcp.enabled=0. Applications built with Go 1.24 or later can also use GODEBUG=multipathtcp=0 to disable MPTCP support.

Another option is to block incoming IPv4 packets containing IP options using firewall rules. AWS provides an iptables rule for this, along with guidance for configuring AWS Network Firewall.

Just remember that these measures are workarounds, not permanent fixes. They can help reduce exposure while you’re working on the updates, but they don’t address the underlying vulnerability.

4. Double-check that everything is updated

Once the updates are installed and the systems have been rebooted, check that they’re actually running the fixed kernel.

It’s also worth keeping a simple record of which systems have been updated, which kernel packages they’re running, and when they were last rebooted.

This helps you avoid missing systems during the patching process.

Is Patching Enough? What About Network Monitoring?

Getting the security updates installed should obviously come first. But there’s another thing organizations need to think about.

What about the time between discovering the vulnerability and getting every affected system patched?

You still need to know what’s happening across your network during that period.

Since CVE-2026-98432 involves incoming IPv4 TCP traffic, monitoring network activity can help security teams spot unusual patterns and investigate anything that looks suspicious.

For example, repeated SYN retransmissions, sudden bursts of TCP connection requests, or unexpected IPv4 packets containing IP options might be worth investigating.

To be clear, these aren’t confirmed signs of an attempt to exploit CVE-2026-98432. But they can give security teams additional context when looking into unusual network activity.

This is where network detection and response (NDR) comes in.

Fidelis Network® uses Deep Session Inspection® (DSI) to inspect traffic across ports and protocols. This helps security teams get a closer look at network communications, examine traffic details, and investigate suspicious activity.

It also offers capabilities such as Network DLP, sandboxing, and threat intelligence. These can help teams examine suspicious files and communications, investigate potential data movement, and understand what’s happening across their network.

Of course, network monitoring won’t fix the kernel vulnerability. It doesn’t replace patching, either.

But it gives security teams another way to keep an eye on their environment, investigate unusual activity, and get a better understanding of what’s happening while potentially vulnerable systems are still being updated.

Fidelis DSI - Advanced Data inspection and Threat Detection Capabilities
  • Content Inspection
  • Content Identification
  • Full Session Reassembly
Download the Datasheet
So, What Should You Take Away from This?

CVE-2026-98432 is a good example of how something as basic as memory management can turn into a serious security problem.

The Linux kernel can end up accessing memory that’s already been released because two operations are trying to use the same socket options at the same time. Additionally, this may result in system crashes, memory corruption, or even remote code execution, depending on the situation.

Don’t wait to find out if you are impacted if your company uses Linux.

Review your systems, install the recommended kernel updates, and reboot where required. If you need more time to patch everything, look at the temporary mitigations recommended by your Linux vendor.

And while you’re doing all that, keep an eye on your network, too. Knowing what’s happening across your environment can help security teams spot unusual activity and investigate potential threats before they turn into bigger problems.

The post Linux Kernel Use-After-Free Vulnerability: What’s Happening and Why It Matters appeared first on Fidelis Security.

items.title: How Clone-Proof Is Your Game? 4 Signs to Check
items.summary: In my last blog post I explained how I think most developers don’t need to worry as much about AI cloning. For the most part the first game to release a demo will smother out the fast-follow clones. Steam is very winner take all. In my last blog post I showed that the first quality game to market is more likely to get all the attention and sales: Based on this, I still think the marketing strategy hasn’t changed: get your Steam page up early , 6 months minimum on Steam, release a demo, do Steam Next Fest, get into Steam’s Personal Calendar, release with as many wishlists as possible. However there are some games that are more susceptible to getting cloned and beat to market. In that case I wouldn’t change much in the marketing of your game except that you should be ready to react and launch a demo if clones start appearing. Disclaimer: Many people have misinterpreted the advice I am about to give as “blaming the victim” or “gatekeeping what games to make.” Valve’s Tom Giardino caught stray criticism by giving advice similar to what I am about to say. I am not saying you shouldn’t make these games that are “likely victims of cloning”. You can make whatever you want. I will cheer you on. Please don’t stop making your game! I don’t blame you! All I am saying is if you are making a game that falls into one of these categories, stay quiet and don’t start marketing until you have a backup plan if cloners arrive. Your best protection is to have a demo locked and loaded (but not fired) so you can react if an AI cloner catches you in a standoff. I firmly believe that the first game to get a QUALITY demo out will be the winner and all other games will be called “clones.” So if your game MIGHT fall under one of these conditions, play it quiet and get that demo ready before you say anything. 4 Types of games that are more likely to be vulnerable to AI cloning #1 The game is built upon a high concept player fantasy with a bit of humor or horror aka “Gimmick” In my previous blog I called this a “gimmick.” Basically a Gimmick is a single clever mechanic that sells people on your game. It might even make them laugh. However, one downside is once they experience that “gimmick” they are satisfied and they don’t have to buy your game and that gimmick can be quickly recreated by an AI cloner pretty easily. It is like a magic trick or a joke. You see it or hear it once and you know what it is so you are satisfied. The best example I can think of a “gimmick-first” game is Don’t Scream which was made by Twitter genius Indie Game Joe . The “Gimmick” is you hook up a microphone while you play and if you scream in real life, you die in the game. Funny. Great idea. But once experienced, there isn’t much variation on that one mechanic. Wisely, Indie Game Joe knew this game was built on a gimmick and released the game without a demo. Because, rightfully, players would be satisfied if they could play a free version of it. So his marketing plan was: put out a viral trailer , spend just 2 weeks marketing the game, release. That is the right call for this type of game (and this was years before AI cloning.) BUT DON’T CONFUSE GIMMICKS AND HOOKS. A “gimmick” is different than a “hook.” Very few games are built on gimmicks. Most successful games don’t have “gimmicks”, they have hooks. For instance The King is Watching is a successful game where the hook is “a city-builder-tower-defense strategy game where the city’s buildings only work when the king is “looking” at them.” It is a deep, fun game. The hook is a neat idea. But it isn’t one of those WOW viral ideas that will make you go viral on TikTok based on the premise. A “hook” is more complex than a simple gimmick. Gimmicks are like sugary-drinks that please at first taste and hooks are a complex wine that unfolds as you slowly taste it. The hook only comes into full view after you spend hours exploring the complex interplay of various gameplay mechanics. The King is Watching did amazingly well. A game can be successful without a gimmick. A game like The King is Watching could survive getting cloned and by releasing a demo because there are so many systems that aren’t apparent just from the screenshots or the hook. If this is your first game it is probably hard to distinguish between a “hook” and a “gimmick” but like wine appreciation, it takes time to develop your palate to be able to distinguish them. Study more games, release more games. Examples of fun “gimmicks” that would be in danger of clones today: Squirrel With A Gun Choo Choo Charles, Lunch Lady (most character based horror) Goat Simulator Don’t Scream Untitled Goose Game (although I think there were so many jokes deep in this game that it could survive clones) #2 The art is not a differentiating feature It’s easier to clone a game when the visual identity is “neutral.” I am not criticizing the art of any games mentioned here. For example: the simulation genre is notorious for having pretty basic art direction but great sales. For the typical simulation game on Steam, the in-game NPCs look like mannequins. It is “realistic.” Nothing is really stylized. The art is not the star of the show for these types of games, the actions you take are. For instance here is a typical Playway Simulation game: The cleanup genre is also vulnerable to AI-cloners because often the art style slots into a defined genre. Librarian: Tidy Up the Arcane Library is one such game. The game looks great. But a well trod, fantasy gothic art style can easily be cloned. It just looks “realistic.” Contrast this with Drunken Goddess Reflux . This game features a unique stylistic mix of 2D cel-shaded anime, 3D backgrounds, bold color palettes, and expressive characters. Drunken Goddess Reflux got free publicity by boldly canceling the release of their Demo for fear of AI Cloners. I don’t think they should worry about being cloned because their art direction is so unique and bold. A cloner can’t pass off something this unique looking as a “coincidence.” Some games that were once stylized become the default art style. The best example of this is Friendslop. At one point Peak’s characters were a signature look of the game. But subsequent games in the genre have established colorful but flat shaded, googly-eyed, muppets as the genre convention. Look at these examples from Friendslop games Dear Passengers and Gamble with Your Friends which have picked up and expanded upon the typical friendslop identity. This is not a criticism. I think it is a wise marketing move to lean into genre conventions so shoppers can identify the genre at a glance. #3 Design is well within a well established genre (This is not a criticism) If a game follows genre conventions, players know what to expect from it. In fact they find comfort in it. For instance, if you see an idle game you know that there will probably be a 2x, 3x, 4x damage and earnings multiplier, magnet with an expanding sphere of attraction, chain lightning, prestige system, and numbers are going to get huge by the end. Needle in a Haystack Simulator falls into the 3D incremental + simulation genre + “tidy up”. I think A Game About Digging a Hole was the first I saw in this genre. If you scroll down into the comments of the original Haystack tweet fans instantly knew what genre the game is and how it would play. They aren’t criticizing; they were actually excited about it. The developer confirmed their suspicions were very accurate: Well worn genres are easier to clone because you are mixing and matching setting and existing known gameplay pieces. Players love that, but it does make you vulnerable to cloners. #4 The content is “systematic” not hand crafted I recommend indies to focus on “crafty-buildy-simulational-strategy” games because the content players experience emerges from the systems not from hand-created content that is expensive for small indie teams to make. Crafty-buildy is in opposition to linear, narrative, experiences that are more popular in AAA games like Assassin’s Creed, Marvel’s Wolverine, and Ico. But a game like Needle In A Haystack Simulator has a clear systematic end state like “use tools and you win when you get the needle” it is more vulnerable to cloners. Crafty-buildy games are more likely to get cloned than linear narrative games. But don’t interpret this as “don’t make crafty-buildy games anymore.” I still think they are the types of games that Steam players like and can be made by small teams. However, crafty-buildy games do make it easier to clone since the “content” is usually the numbers in the meta layer arranged in various ways. Back to Drunken Goddess Reflux. Another strength of this game that makes it more clone-immune is that one of the hooks is “The drunker you get, the wilder the game.” Weird and unexpected things make your game clone-immune. This is a crafty buildy deck builder game but emergent weirdness is baked into the design and that rests on the shoulders of the creative game designers. A cloner can’t clone what can’t be experienced until you play the game. This is different from games that live in existing genre tropes. Similarly, the most-buildy-crafty game ever made is Dwarf Fortress . The fun is driven by a deep simulation of a fictional world. This game would be impossible to clone from just screenshots and a description of the hook because there are very creative decisions made deep within the game systems like the cats that get drunk licking their feet after walking through puddles of beer . So just because a game is systems-driven doesn’t mean that it will be easily cloned. But if the simulation is simplistic and only skin deep a clone can replicate it more easily. Maybe Needle In A Haystack Simulator needs to add an emergent, hidden, eldritch horror angle that blindsides players who thought they knew what they were getting since Find The Needle launched before them. Free idea. Please, don’t make bad marketing decisions because you are scared In the weeks since the Haystack clone debacle I get emails every day from developers who are shadow dropping, hiding their game, canceling their demo, and quitting game dev because they are scared. Don’t do that. Remember Banana ? In January 2024 the internet went nuts because a game where you click a BANANA took over Steam. Indie devs freaked out about the banana game (partly because it also stood in for NFT and web 3.0 debate.) There was a whole hype cycle where we talked about this simple free game. One of these videos said it “broke Steam.” After the success of BANANA, cloners started doing a fast follow with Egg, Burger, and Dollar. None of them succeeded. Nobody is making one-word food games anymore because that panic stopped. Every year or two something so stupid but so genius takes off. It is the simplest idea with the simplest concept. And every year indies freak out. Please don’t freak out.
items.summary_html:
In my last blog post I explained how I think most developers don’t need to worry as much about AI cloning. For the most part the first game to release a demo will smother out the fast-follow clones. Steam is very winner take all. In my last blog post I showed that the first quality game to market is more likely to get all the attention and sales:

Based on this, I still think the marketing strategy hasn’t changed: get your Steam page up early, 6 months minimum on Steam, release a demo, do Steam Next Fest, get into Steam’s Personal Calendar, release with as many wishlists as possible. 

However there are some games that are more susceptible to getting cloned and beat to market. In that case I wouldn’t change much in the marketing of your game except that you should be ready to react and launch a demo if clones start appearing. 

Disclaimer: Many people have misinterpreted the advice I am about to give as “blaming the victim” or “gatekeeping what games to make.” Valve’s Tom Giardino caught stray criticism by giving advice similar to what I am about to say.

I am not saying you shouldn’t make these games that are “likely victims of cloning”. You can make whatever you want. I will cheer you on. Please don’t stop making your game! I don’t blame you! All I am saying is if you are making a game that falls into one of these categories, stay quiet and don’t start marketing until you have a backup plan if cloners arrive. Your best protection is to have a demo locked and loaded (but not fired) so you can react if an AI cloner catches you in a standoff. 

I firmly believe that the first game to get a QUALITY demo out will be the winner and all other games will be called “clones.”

So if your game MIGHT fall under one of these conditions, play it quiet and get that demo ready before you say anything. 

4 Types of games that are more likely to be vulnerable to AI cloning #1 The game is built upon a high concept player fantasy with a bit of humor or horror aka “Gimmick”

In my previous blog I called this a “gimmick.” Basically a Gimmick is a single clever mechanic that sells people on your game. It might even make them laugh. However, one downside is once they experience that “gimmick” they are satisfied and they don’t have to buy your game and that gimmick can be quickly recreated by an AI cloner pretty easily. It is like a magic trick or a joke. You see it or hear it once and you know what it is so you are satisfied.

The best example I can think of a “gimmick-first” game is Don’t Scream which was made by Twitter genius Indie Game Joe. The “Gimmick” is you hook up a microphone while you play and if you scream in real life, you die in the game. Funny. Great idea. But once experienced, there isn’t much variation on that one mechanic. 

Wisely, Indie Game Joe knew this game was built on a gimmick and released the game without a demo. Because, rightfully, players would be satisfied if they could play a free version of it. So his marketing plan was: put out a viral trailer, spend just 2 weeks marketing the game, release. That is the right call for this type of game (and this was years before AI cloning.)

BUT DON’T CONFUSE GIMMICKS AND HOOKS.

A “gimmick” is different than a “hook.” Very few games are built on gimmicks. Most successful games don’t have “gimmicks”, they have hooks. For instance The King is Watching is a successful game where the hook is “a city-builder-tower-defense strategy game where the city’s buildings only work when the king is “looking” at them.”

It is a deep, fun game. The hook is a neat idea. But it isn’t one of those WOW viral ideas that will make you go viral on TikTok based on the premise. A “hook” is more complex than a simple gimmick. Gimmicks are like sugary-drinks that please at first taste and hooks are a complex wine that unfolds as you slowly taste it. The hook only comes into full view after you spend hours exploring the complex interplay of various gameplay mechanics. 

The King is Watching did amazingly well. A game can be successful without a gimmick. A game like The King is Watching could survive getting cloned and by releasing a demo because there are so many systems that aren’t apparent just from the screenshots or the hook.

If this is your first game it is probably hard to distinguish between a “hook” and a “gimmick” but like wine appreciation, it takes time to develop your palate to be able to distinguish them. Study more games, release more games. 

Examples of fun “gimmicks” that would be in danger of clones today: 

  • Squirrel With A Gun
  • Choo Choo Charles, Lunch Lady (most character based horror)
  • Goat Simulator
  • Don’t Scream
  • Untitled Goose Game (although I think there were so many jokes deep in this game that it could survive clones)
#2 The art is not a differentiating feature

It’s easier to clone a game when the visual identity is “neutral.” I am not criticizing the art of any games mentioned here. For example: the simulation genre is notorious for having pretty basic art direction but great sales. For the typical simulation game on Steam, the in-game NPCs look like mannequins. It is “realistic.” Nothing is really stylized. The art is not the star of the show for these types of games, the actions you take are. For instance here is a typical Playway Simulation game: 

The cleanup genre is also vulnerable to AI-cloners because often the art style slots into a defined genre. Librarian: Tidy Up the Arcane Library is one such game. The game looks great. But a well trod, fantasy gothic art style can easily be cloned. It just looks “realistic.”

Contrast this with Drunken Goddess Reflux. This game features a unique stylistic mix of 2D cel-shaded anime, 3D backgrounds, bold color palettes, and expressive characters. 

Drunken Goddess Reflux got free publicity by boldly canceling the release of their Demo for fear of AI Cloners. I don’t think they should worry about being cloned because their art direction is so unique and bold. A cloner can’t pass off something this unique looking as a “coincidence.” 

Some games that were once stylized become the default art style. The best example of this is Friendslop. At one point Peak’s characters were a signature look of the game. But subsequent games in the genre have established colorful but flat shaded, googly-eyed, muppets as the genre convention. 

Look at these examples from Friendslop games Dear Passengers and Gamble with Your Friends which have picked up and expanded upon the typical friendslop identity. This is not a criticism. I think it is a wise marketing move to lean into genre conventions so shoppers can identify the genre at a glance. 

#3 Design is well within a well established genre 

(This is not a criticism) If a game follows genre conventions, players know what to expect from it. In fact they find comfort in it. For instance, if you see an idle game you know that there will probably be a 2x, 3x, 4x damage and earnings multiplier, magnet with an expanding sphere of attraction, chain lightning, prestige system, and numbers are going to get huge by the end.

Needle in a Haystack Simulator falls into the 3D incremental + simulation genre + “tidy up”. I think A Game About Digging a Hole was the first I saw in this genre. If you scroll down into the comments of the original Haystack tweet fans instantly knew what genre the game is and how it would play. They aren’t criticizing; they were actually excited about it. The developer confirmed their suspicions were very accurate: 

Well worn genres are easier to clone because you are mixing and matching setting and existing known gameplay pieces. Players love that, but it does make you vulnerable to cloners. 

#4 The content is “systematic” not hand crafted

I recommend indies to focus on “crafty-buildy-simulational-strategy” games because the content players experience emerges from the systems not from hand-created content that is expensive for small indie teams to make. Crafty-buildy is in opposition to linear, narrative, experiences that are more popular in AAA games like Assassin’s Creed, Marvel’s Wolverine, and Ico. 

But a game like Needle In A Haystack Simulator has a clear systematic end state like “use tools and you win when you get the needle” it is more vulnerable to cloners. 

Crafty-buildy games are more likely to get cloned than linear narrative games. But don’t interpret this as “don’t make crafty-buildy games anymore.” I still think they are the types of games that Steam players like and can be made by small teams. However, crafty-buildy games do make it easier to clone since the “content” is usually the numbers in the meta layer arranged in various ways. 

Back to Drunken Goddess Reflux. Another strength of this game that makes it more clone-immune is that  one of the hooks is “The drunker you get, the wilder the game.” 

Weird and unexpected things make your game clone-immune. This is a crafty buildy deck builder game but emergent weirdness is baked into the design and that rests on the shoulders of the creative game designers. A cloner can’t clone what can’t be experienced until you play the game. This is different from games that live in existing genre tropes. 

Similarly, the most-buildy-crafty game ever made is Dwarf Fortress. The fun is driven by a deep simulation of a fictional world.

This game would be impossible to clone from just screenshots and a description of the hook because there are very creative decisions made deep within the game systems like the cats that get drunk licking their feet after walking through puddles of beer. So just because a game is systems-driven doesn’t mean that it will be easily cloned. But if the simulation is simplistic and only skin deep a clone can replicate it more easily. 

Maybe Needle In A Haystack Simulator needs to add an emergent, hidden, eldritch horror angle that blindsides players who thought they knew what they were getting since Find The Needle launched before them. Free idea. 

Please, don’t make bad marketing decisions because you are scared

In the weeks since the Haystack clone debacle I get emails every day from developers who are shadow dropping, hiding their game, canceling their demo, and quitting game dev because they are scared. Don’t do that. 

Remember Banana? 

In January 2024 the internet went nuts because a game where you click a BANANA took over Steam. Indie devs freaked out about the banana game (partly because it also stood in for NFT and web 3.0 debate.)

There was a whole hype cycle where we talked about this simple free game. One of these videos said it “broke Steam.”

After the success of BANANA, cloners started doing a fast follow with Egg, Burger, and Dollar. None of them succeeded. 

Nobody is making one-word food games anymore because that panic stopped.

Every year or two something so stupid but so genius takes off. It is the simplest idea with the simplest concept. And every year indies freak out. 

Please don’t freak out.

items.title: Ubuntu 26.10 Adds New Security Protection to curl, Blocking Revoked SSL Certificates
items.summary: Ubuntu 26.10 Stonking Stingray adds certificate revocation checks to curl, helping the command-line tool reject HTTPS connections that use revoked certificates. Announced on November 10, the change brings upki support into Ubuntu’s curl package. It marks an initial step toward browser-grade certificate checks across the operating system. The protection closes a gap in how applications check website certificates. Curl uses OpenSSL to verify certificate chains , but that process does not check revocation by default in the setup described by Ubuntu. A certificate could therefore pass those checks even after its issuer had withdrawn it. According to Ubuntu’s announcement, curl now uses upki-openssl to check server certificates against locally stored revocation data. The system builds on Mozilla’s CRLite technology, which Firefox also uses to identify revoked certificates. Because the check uses local data, curl does not need an extra network request during each connection. This keeps checks fast and avoids sending a separate revocation query when users visit a site. items.title: Hackers Could Abuse Microsoft Entra AI Agents to Hijack Enterprise Accounts Without Stealing Passwords
items.summary: Researchers have shown that attackers can take over parts of a Microsoft 365 environment by tricking one person into approving a fake AI agent. No password is stolen and no login screen is faked. The technique is called BluePhishing. It targets Microsoft Entra Agent ID, the system that gives AI agents their own identities inside a company’s cloud tenant. The method builds on a trick security teams already know, OAuth consent phishing. In that trick, a victim clicks “Accept” on a permission screen for a harmful app. BluePhishing moves the same idea into the new world of AI agents, where fewer people know what to look out for and fewer controls exist. Microsoft is also about to widen the door. A Microsoft 365 Message Center notice, MC1506733, says regular Entra users will be able to create agent blueprints by default starting in November 2026. That raises the number of places where a bad consent request could slip in. Analysts at Proofpoint identified and described the BluePhishing technique in a report published on November 9, 2026, and noted that they have not yet seen it used in real attacks. Proofpoint says it is a research-based proof of concept. It also told Microsoft about the problem before sharing the details. Hackers Could Abuse Microsoft Entra AI Agents Entra Agent ID works much like the older app model. An agent blueprint is the template, similar to an app registration. A blueprint principal is its local copy inside a company tenant. An agent identity is a working agent created from that blueprint, and one blueprint can create up to 250 of them. The attacker first builds a blueprint in a tenant they control and adds a client secret. They set the sign-in audience to allow other organizations, which the Entra portal does not show but PowerShell or Microsoft Graph can do. They also add broad permissions that agents will inherit. This is similar to earlier cases of OAuth apps in Entra being used to keep long-term access, where the app acts as a quiet entry point even after passwords are reset. BluePhishing attack (Source – ProofPoint) Next, the attacker sends the victim a consent link. When the victim approves it, a blueprint principal appears in the victim’s tenant. It automatically gets a permission named AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager, which Proofpoint says cannot be revoked. With that permission, the attacker can request a Graph token and create agent identities inside the victim’s tenant. The attacker only needs a few details: the blueprint ID and secret, which they make themselves, plus the victim’s tenant ID and a user to act as the “sponsor.” Proofpoint notes these are not treated as secret, and the tenant ID can be found through public sign-in lookups. Researchers showed that a created agent holding User.Read.All and Group.Read.All could be loaded into the GraphRunner tool to run Graph requests. Admin consent is stronger because one click can grant tenant-wide application permissions. User consent only grants delegated rights tied to that person. Why Defenders May Miss It and What to Do Agents are expected to act on their own, so their activity looks normal. A suspicious app that works in the background may raise questions, but a busy agent does not. Proofpoint also points out that consent controls for agents are less mature than those for apps. Inherited permissions do not show up in the Entra portal or in Microsoft Graph, so they appear only inside tokens at runtime. Example of arbitrary graph requests with agent identity token (Source – ProofPoint) A past case with Entra Agent ID logs showed that tracing agent actions takes careful work across several log sources. The blast radius is larger too. An app registration maps to one service principal per tenant, while one blueprint can create 250 agent identities. Earlier flaws, such as the Agent ID Administrator role problem found by Silverfort, show that this young identity system is still being tested. Proofpoint suggests these steps:- Teach staff to be careful when a third-party agent asks for permissions. Apply the same user consent limits to agent blueprints and agent identities. Use permission classifications. Microsoft already blocks risky Graph permissions such as User.ReadWrite.All for agents. Use least privilege, Conditional Access policies for agents, and Entra ID Protection for agents. Watch the audit log. “Add application” shows a blueprint being created, and “Add service principal” shows an agent identity being created. Similar lures have already worked with AI themes. The CoPhish Copilot Studio technique used a trusted-looking agent on a Microsoft domain to collect OAuth consent. BluePhishing could prove even more convincing because the agent is the identity itself. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Indicator Meaning Permission AgentIdentity.CreateAsManager Implicit permission on the blueprint principal that lets agent identities be created Property signInAudience = AzureADMultipleOrgs Setting that allows a third-party blueprint to receive consent Test name BluePhish (app_displayname) Name used in the researchers’ sample token Audit event Add application A new agent blueprint was created Audit event Add service principal A new agent identity was created Detection key Agent blueprint ID The same ID appears in every tenant that consents, so it can be used to find and remove known bad agents Permissions seen User.Read.All, Group.Read.All Application permissions held by the test agent identity Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. items.title: AI Hacking Frameworks Like ARTEX, PentAGI, and Agent Zero Found Running on Internet-Accessible Servers
items.summary: AI-powered hacking and penetration-testing frameworks are running on internet-accessible servers, with some management consoles left open without authentication. A November 7, 2026, Shodan snapshot recorded 1,428 services matching the ARTEX family, 419 matching PentAGI, and 173 matching Agent Zero, showing how widely these tools have spread. These platforms connect language models to security tools, allowing agents to run commands, examine results, and decide what to do next. They can support authorized testing, but attackers can use the same features to automate reconnaissance, exploitation, and credential theft. Public visibility alone, however, does not prove that a server supports criminal activity. Researchers from GitGuardian identified the exposed deployments in a technical investigation published November 9. Their findings concern dual-use frameworks and insecure deployments, not a newly discovered malware family. The team examined roughly 45 open-source projects and assessed 41 for fingerprints that defenders could use to locate internet-facing installations. AI Hacking Frameworks GitGuardian cataloged 32 frameworks across five groups: network attack automation, web application and API testing, command-and-control integration, wrappers around coding agents, and research prototypes. Other projects were forks or variants. Across the 41 assessed frameworks, 11 served web interfaces by default, 18 exposed services only in certain configurations or lacked distinctive root pages, and 12 had no network listener. PentAGI coordinates agents using tools such as Nmap, Metasploit, and sqlmap. As explained in earlier coverage of PentAGI penetration testing automation , this design helps agents move between discovery, testing, and reporting. GitGuardian counted 419 matching services, including 233 with the default certificate, while separate title and certificate searches returned different totals. These measurements should not be combined into a unique-server count. Agent Zero showed a clearer authentication gap. Of 173 matching services, 134 displayed a login page and 39 were open. GitGuardian described Agent Zero as a general-purpose agent without authentication by default, rather than a dedicated hacking tool. Its inclusion reflects reported attacker experimentation and the risks created when powerful agents become publicly reachable. ARTEX remained the largest visible family. GitGuardian reported that its creator removed the original project on October 8 following reports of abuse, but 102 forks and similarly named repositories appeared during that week. Earlier reporting on ARTEX GitHub credential theft documented how attackers used exposed application secrets to reach cloud resources, including Azure Key Vault. The code review also separated built-in functions from tasks an agent could assemble itself. Only Pojun, Cybermes, Xalgorix, and AIRecon shipped a secret scanner connected to the agent. None contained a GitHub fetcher. Several other projects supplied instructions without working scanner integration, while reviewed tools including PentAGI had no identified secret-hunting capability. That limitation does not eliminate the risk. Almost every framework supplied shell and web access, allowing a model to obtain missing tools or build a workflow at runtime. Coverage of AI agent credential exposure also explains how ordinary agent activity can move secrets into logs, transcripts, or model context, even without malware. For defenders, the distinction matters: an exposed console is an access-control concern, while a fingerprint match is only a discovery lead. GitGuardian published detection descriptions rather than a target list so organizations could identify their own deployments. Different queries produced different counts, making validation essential before treating a result as an exposed installation or evidence of compromise. Microsoft Ignite 2026: New Sentinel Connectors Announcement
items.summary: Microsoft Sentinel helps organizations detect, investigate, and respond to threats across increasingly complex environments. As AI transforms security operations, bringing together the right data and context is more important than ever, giving human defenders and AI agents a more complete view of the environment to reason over and act on. These integrations bring signals from Microsoft and third-party technologies together across the security environment, unlocking richer context for investigations and helping power the new Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender , where human defenders and AI agents can reason across the environment with shared context. The connector ecosystem isn’t the only area seeing rapid growth. Microsoft Sentinel continues to add new capabilities, including Nested API support, Azure Blob support, and multi-account support, while AI-powered tools like the connector builder agent are making it easier than ever for developers to build integrations and bring more of their security data into Sentinel. At the same time, Unified Data Management , now in public preview, makes it easier for customers to manage their Microsoft Sentinel data, connectors, tables, and ingestion health in one place. For Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re excited to showcase recent additions to this growing ecosystem and the partners making them possible. These new and enhanced connectors continue to broaden the security data available to customers, helping human defenders and AI agents gain the context they need across the technology estate. Airlock Digital for Microsoft Sentinel Airlock Digital helps prevent malware, ransomware, and unauthorized software with deny by default application control, allowing only trusted applications, scripts, and processes to run. Its Microsoft Sentinel push integration ingests execution history, browser extension control events, server administrative activity, and policy changes for monitoring and investigation. Included parsers map execution and audit events to Microsoft’s ASIM for analysis alongside other security signals. A customizable workbook supports investigation and monitoring, and teams can create analytics rules using the ingested data. NC Protect Data Connector for Microsoft Sentinel NC Protect Data Connector for Microsoft Sentin el from archTIS brings user activity and protection logs from NC Protect into Sentinel for centralized security analysis. The connector captures user activities and access-related events, while built-in workbooks support investigation and visualization of user behavior. By correlating NC Protect audit data with other security telemetry, the integration helps teams identify suspicious user activity, trigger alerts and response workflows, strengthen auditing, and monitor guest activity across SharePoint and Teams. blacklens.io for Microsoft Sentinel blacklens.io for Microsoft Sentinel brings external and internal attack-surface data, risk-prioritized vulnerabilities, darknet intelligence, and supply-chain risks into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector ingests exposed assets, compromised identities, stolen credentials and session cookies, typosquatting domains, and supplier activity on ransomware leak sites. The solution includes a data connector and analytics rule for creating Sentinel incidents, with configurable notification rules for alert severity and type. Findings are available in Log Analytics for correlation with existing Sentinel signals and can support custom analytics rules, workbooks, automation, and threat investigations. BloodHound Enterprise BloodHound Enterprise (BHE) helps organizations protect critical assets across modern hybrid environments by continuously uncovering identity attack paths and providing actionable remediation guidance. By integrating with Microsoft Sentinel, BHE delivers attack path data and identity security posture insights directly into Sentinel workflows. This helps security teams prioritize remediation efforts based on exposure to critical assets while enriching investigations into identity-based threats, including lateral movement and privilege escalation. Together, BHE and Microsoft Sentinel help security teams connect threat detection to underlying identity risk, speed investigations, and reduce opportunities for attackers. BlueVoyant Anthropic Claude Compliance BlueVoyant Anthropic Claude Compliance brings compliance activity from the Anthropic Claude Compliance API into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector ingests Claude compliance events into Sentinel, giving security, risk, and audit teams centralized visibility into AI usage and related activity. By correlating these compliance signals with identity, endpoint, and other security telemetry, the integration supports threat hunting, investigation of policy violations and anomalous behavior, compliance monitoring, and repeatable audit workflows. Cato Networks for Microsoft Sentinel Cato Networks for Microsoft Sentinel brings security and network events from the Cato SASE Platform into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF) Push pattern. The connector pushes events into a dedicated Log Analytics table, making Cato activity available alongside other Sentinel data. By centralizing this telemetry in Sentinel, the integration enables security teams to incorporate Cato events into threat hunting, detection, and visualization workflows alongside broader security signals. Check Point EM ThreatCloud Intelligence Feed Connector for Microsoft Sentinel The Check Point EM ThreatCloud Intelligence Feed Connector brings threat intelligence from Check Point Exposure Management into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector ingests indicators of compromise (IoCs), including malicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, enriched with threat context such as confidence, severity, kill-chain stage, and campaign associations. An included playbook further enriches incident IoCs through ThreatCloud, helping security teams correlate intelligence with existing telemetry, accelerate triage and investigation, and reduce the manual effort required to maintain threat intelligence. Check Point Exposure Management Threat Intelligence IoC for Microsoft Sentinel Check Point Exposure Management Threat Intelligence IoC for Microsoft Sentinel brings threat intelligence from Check Point Infinity External Risk Management into Sentinel. The connector ingests malicious IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, enriched with context such as severity, confidence, and detected activity. By correlating these indicators of compromise (IoCs) with existing logs through analytics rules, hunting queries, and watchlists, the integration helps security teams reduce manual intelligence management, identify matches with external threats, and accelerate threat detection and investigation. Citrix SPA Sentinel App Citrix SPA Sentinel App brings Citrix Secure Private Access and Device Posture service events into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector imports critical logs, policy outcomes, and user activity data, giving security teams greater visibility into application access and device posture activity. An included workbook supports visualization and analysis of Citrix data, helping SOC teams correlate activity with broader security telemetry, investigate security risks, support compliance monitoring, and strengthen threat hunting across their environment. ContraForce Events for Microsoft Sentinel ContraForce Events for Microsoft Sentinel brings security delivery and administrative activity from ContraForce workspaces into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). ContraForce is an Agentic Security Delivery Platform for service providers and security teams running triage, investigation, and response across Microsoft Defender XDR and Sentinel. The connector ingests incidents, privileged access changes, service account credential activity, and high-impact workspace actions. Three included analytics rules detect privileged access, credential, and high-impact workspace activity, helping teams monitor and investigate the platform supporting their security operations. Corelight for Microsoft Sentinel By transforming all network traffic into rich, comprehensive evidence, Corelight gives security teams using Microsoft Sentinel the visibility to understand exactly what is happening across their enterprise networks. In addition to native integration with Microsoft Sentinel, Corelight integrates with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Defender Vulnerability Management, and Entra ID to streamline investigations, accelerate responses, and remediate incidents quickly and easily. The Corelight App for Microsoft Sentinel includes intuitive dashboards, pre-defined workbooks , sample queries, and analytics rules that help make SOC teams more efficient and effective. CTM360 CTM360 brings external threat visibility into Microsoft Sentinel. The integration connects the CTM360 HackerView and CyberBlindspot platforms to Sentinel through REST APIs, so external attack surface and digital risk events flow straight into security operations workflows. HackerView surfaces externally exposed assets and security issues across your attack surface. CyberBlindspot adds organization-specific threat intelligence from surface, deep, and dark web monitoring. With these signals centralized in Sentinel, security teams can analyze external exposures alongside their broader telemetry and speed up detection, investigation, and response. Cyren CrowdStrike IOC Automation Cyren CrowdStrike IOC Automation connects Cyren IP reputation threat intelligence with Microsoft Sentinel and CrowdStrike Falcon to operationalize malicious IP indicators. An included Logic App playbook automatically retrieves known malicious IP addresses from Cyren and submits them to CrowdStrike Falcon as custom indicators of compromise (IOCs) for blocking and detection. Scheduled execution keeps the intelligence updated and automates the flow of Cyren IP reputation data into CrowdStrike Falcon for blocking and detection. Vaikora AI Agent Signals for Microsoft Sentinel Vaikora AI Agent Signals for Microsoft Sentinel brings behavioral security signals from AI agents into Sentinel for centralized monitoring and response. The connector ingests risk scores, anomaly and threat classifications, policy enforcement decisions, and audit data, including signals for prompt injection attempts and suspicious tool usage. Included analytics rules and a workbook help security teams detect behavioral anomalies, investigate policy violations, and incorporate AI agent risks into existing Sentinel incident workflows. Vaikora AI Agent Signals for SentinelOne Vaikora AI Agent Signals for SentinelOne brings high-risk behavioral security signals from Vaikora into SentinelOne as threat intelligence indicators of compromise (IOCs). The integration filters high-severity and anomalous AI agent activity and maps Vaikora risk scores to SentinelOne severity levels. The resulting IOCs are submitted to SentinelOne and expire after 90 days, enabling Vaikora security signals to be incorporated into SentinelOne endpoint protection workflows. DataBahn Agentic Data Control Plane for Microsoft Sentinel DataBahn’s agentic data control plane integrates with Microsoft Sentinel to provide our shared customers an AI-native data pipeline and orchestration platform that allows them to accelerate enterprise deployments. DataBahn’s pipeline standardizes onboarding and shaping across all data sources while providing operational visibility into data flow and health. items.summary_html:
Microsoft Sentinel helps organizations detect, investigate, and respond to threats across increasingly complex environments. As AI transforms security operations, bringing together the right data and context is more important than ever, giving human defenders and AI agents a more complete view of the environment to reason over and act on. 

These integrations bring signals from Microsoft and third-party technologies together across the security environment, unlocking richer context for investigations and helping power the new Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) in Microsoft Defender, where human defenders and AI agents can reason across the environment with shared context. 

The connector ecosystem isn’t the only area seeing rapid growth. Microsoft Sentinel continues to add new capabilities, including Nested API support, Azure Blob support, and multi-account support, while AI-powered tools like the connector builder agent are making it easier than ever for developers to build integrations and bring more of their security data into Sentinel. At the same time, Unified Data Management, now in public preview, makes it easier for customers to manage their Microsoft Sentinel data, connectors, tables, and ingestion health in one place. 

For Microsoft Ignite 2026, we’re excited to showcase recent additions to this growing ecosystem and the partners making them possible. These new and enhanced connectors continue to broaden the security data available to customers, helping human defenders and AI agents gain the context they need across the technology estate. 

 

 

Airlock Digital for Microsoft Sentinel 

Airlock Digital helps prevent malware, ransomware, and unauthorized software with deny by default application control, allowing only trusted applications, scripts, and processes to run. Its Microsoft Sentinel push integration ingests execution history, browser extension control events, server administrative activity, and policy changes for monitoring and investigation. Included parsers map execution and audit events to Microsoft’s ASIM for analysis alongside other security signals. A customizable workbook supports investigation and monitoring, and teams can create analytics rules using the ingested data.

NC Protect Data Connector for Microsoft Sentinel

NC Protect Data Connector for Microsoft Sentinel from archTIS brings user activity and protection logs from NC Protect into Sentinel for centralized security analysis. The connector captures user activities and access-related events, while built-in workbooks support investigation and visualization of user behavior. By correlating NC Protect audit data with other security telemetry, the integration helps teams identify suspicious user activity, trigger alerts and response workflows, strengthen auditing, and monitor guest activity across SharePoint and Teams.

 

blacklens.io for Microsoft Sentinel

blacklens.io for Microsoft Sentinel brings external and internal attack-surface data, risk-prioritized vulnerabilities, darknet intelligence, and supply-chain risks into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector ingests exposed assets, compromised identities, stolen credentials and session cookies, typosquatting domains, and supplier activity on ransomware leak sites. The solution includes a data connector and analytics rule for creating Sentinel incidents, with configurable notification rules for alert severity and type. Findings are available in Log Analytics for correlation with existing Sentinel signals and can support custom analytics rules, workbooks, automation, and threat investigations.

BloodHound Enterprise

BloodHound Enterprise (BHE) helps organizations protect critical assets across modern hybrid environments by continuously uncovering identity attack paths and providing actionable remediation guidance. By integrating with Microsoft Sentinel, BHE delivers attack path data and identity security posture insights directly into Sentinel workflows. This helps security teams prioritize remediation efforts based on exposure to critical assets while enriching investigations into identity-based threats, including lateral movement and privilege escalation. Together, BHE and Microsoft Sentinel help security teams connect threat detection to underlying identity risk, speed investigations, and reduce opportunities for attackers.

BlueVoyant Anthropic Claude Compliance brings compliance activity from the Anthropic Claude Compliance API into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector ingests Claude compliance events into Sentinel, giving security, risk, and audit teams centralized visibility into AI usage and related activity. By correlating these compliance signals with identity, endpoint, and other security telemetry, the integration supports threat hunting, investigation of policy violations and anomalous behavior, compliance monitoring, and repeatable audit workflows.

The connector pushes events into a dedicated Log Analytics table, making Cato activity available alongside other Sentinel data. By centralizing this telemetry in Sentinel, the integration enables security teams to incorporate Cato events into threat hunting, detection, and visualization workflows alongside broader security signals.

An included playbook further enriches incident IoCs through ThreatCloud, helping security teams correlate intelligence with existing telemetry, accelerate triage and investigation, and reduce the manual effort required to maintain threat intelligence.

Together, these integrations extend the NetApp Platform’s ability to help security teams triage and respond to ransomware attacks, limit data loss, protect recovery points, and coordinate response across storage and security teams. 

 

NordStellar for Microsoft Sentinel

NordLayer Intelligence by NordStellar for Microsoft Sentinel brings external threat and exposure findings into Sentinel through the Azure Monitor Logs Ingestion API. The integration provides findings including leaked credentials, breach exposures, malware and info-stealer infections, dark web activity, domain impersonation risks, and external attack surface vulnerabilities. By correlating these findings with other security telemetry in Sentinel, the solution helps teams investigate external threats, identify exposures affecting their organization, and automate triage and response through analytics rules and SOAR playbooks.

 

Panorays for Microsoft Sentinel

Panorays for Microsoft Sentinel brings third-party security findings from the Panorays platform into Sentinel through the Panorays API. The connector provides security teams with visibility into the security posture of vendors and supply-chain organizations, making third-party risk and vulnerability findings available alongside other security telemetry. By incorporating Panorays findings into Sentinel workflows, the integration helps SOC teams centrally monitor and investigate third-party risks and correlate them with internal security signals.

 

USTA Account Takeover Prevention Sentinel Connector

USTA Account Takeover Prevention Sentinel Connector brings compromised credential intelligence from the PRODAFT USTA Threat Intelligence platform into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector ingests alerts for exposed corporate credentials, enabling security teams to investigate potential account takeover risks within existing Sentinel workflows. Included analytics can identify newly compromised credentials and successful Microsoft Entra ID sign-ins involving known-compromised accounts, helping SOC teams operationalize external credential intelligence and prioritize investigation and response.

 

USTA IoC Threat Stream for Sentinel

USTA IoC Threat Stream for Sentinel brings curated indicators of compromise (IoCs) from the PRODAFT USTA Threat Stream into Microsoft Sentinel Threat Intelligence. The integration provides indicators including malicious URLs, phishing sites, and malware hashes derived from PRODAFT investigations. By making these indicators available for correlation with existing telemetry, hunting queries, and detection rules, the solution helps security teams identify connections to malicious infrastructure, investigate phishing and malware activity, and incorporate external threat intelligence into existing triage and response workflows.

 

USTA Payment Card Fraud Intelligence Sentinel Connector

USTA Payment Card Fraud Intelligence Sentinel Connector brings compromised payment card intelligence from the PRODAFT USTA Threat Intelligence platform into Microsoft Sentinel. The connector retrieves alerts associated with an organization’s payment card BIN ranges and makes them available within Sentinel for investigation. Included analytics identify newly exposed and non-expired compromised cards, helping security teams centralize payment fraud intelligence, prioritize potentially actionable exposures, and incorporate them into existing investigation and response workflows.

 

Pulumi Cloud Audit Logs for Microsoft Sentinel 

Pulumi Cloud Audit Logs for Microsoft Sentinel brings audit logs from Pulumi, the infrastructure platform for humans and agents, into Microsoft Sentinel through the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector ingests authentication events, organization membership changes, stack lifecycle operations, policy changes, and access token usage. It also includes three analytics rules that detect failed login attempts, stack deletions, and organization membership changes. Your security team can see what a human or agent did, when, and where across infrastructure as code, secrets, configuration, and policies, which helps speed up security and governance investigations.  

 

QCrypton PQC Scanner for Microsoft Sentinel 

QCrypton PQC Scanner for Microsoft Sentinel brings post-quantum cryptography readiness findings from Azure environments into Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The connector provides visibility into cryptographic assets including Key Vault keys, TLS certificates and configurations, and Entra ID app registration certificates, with quantum posture ratings and risk scores. Included are six analytics rules, a workbook, and a notification playbook to help security teams identify vulnerable cryptographic assets and prioritize post-quantum migration planning. 

 

SailPoint for Microsoft Sentinel 

SailPoint for Microsoft Sentinel brings identity security telemetry from SailPoint Identity Security Cloud into Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). The solution streams audit and search events into Sentinel tables, where analysts can correlate identity activity with other security signals and query SailPoint APIs for additional identity and account context during incident triage. Automated playbooks can also remediate threats by revoking access or disabling compromised accounts, helping teams connect identity insight with investigation and response.

 

SAP LogServ (RISE), S/4HANA Cloud private edition

SAP LogServ (RISE), S/4HANA Cloud private edition extends Microsoft Sentinel security monitoring for SAP RISE environments with infrastructure, database, operating system, and network security logs managed by SAP Enterprise Cloud Services. Deployed alongside the Microsoft Sentinel Solution for SAP applications, it complements application-layer monitoring to provide visibility across the SAP stack and enable cross-layer threat detection and correlation. The solution supports near real-time log collection, built-in analytics and workbooks, ASIM-based security content, and correlation with signals from endpoints, Microsoft Entra ID, and other sources in Microsoft Sentinel.   

 

MailRisk data connector for Microsoft Sentinel

MailRisk data connector for Microsoft Sentinel brings suspicious email data analyzed by users through Secure Practice MailRisk into Sentinel. The connector ingests enriched email metadata and risk assessment updates from the Secure Practice API, providing potential indicators of compromise identified from reported emails. By incorporating MailRisk data alongside other security telemetry, the integration helps security teams correlate suspicious email activity, search and investigate potential threats, and incorporate user-reported email intelligence into alerting and incident response workflows. 

SecurityScorecard Ratings for Microsoft Sentinel 

SecurityScorecard Ratings for Microsoft Sentinel provides cybersecurity posture ratings based on continuously monitored risk factors and threat intelligence. SecurityScorecard evaluates organizations using an A-F rating, helping security teams identify and track cybersecurity risks. The solution supports use cases including enterprise cyber risk management, third-party risk monitoring, executive reporting, and cyber due diligence. 

 

SIGNL4 - Mobile Alerting & Response for Microsoft Sentinel and Defender for Cloud

SIGNL4 bridges the gap between security detection and human response with mobile-first alerting and incident management for Microsoft Sentinel and Defender for Cloud. Its two-way integrations allow security teams to acknowledge, escalate, and resolve incidents directly from their mobile devices, with updates automatically synchronized back to Sentinel. Critical Defender for Cloud findings trigger actionable response workflows, while persistent mobile notifications, automated escalations, and on-call scheduling ensure the right people are reached when it matters most. The result is faster incident response, clear accountability, and a fully auditable process - wherever responders are.


SOC Prime Audit CCP

SOC Prime Audit CCP brings SOC Prime Platform audit logs into Microsoft Sentinel for centralized security monitoring and analysis. The connector ingests platform activity including user actions, API calls, and administrative events, providing an audit trail across detection engineering processes. By correlating SOC Prime activity with other security signals in Sentinel, the integration helps security teams investigate platform activity, support compliance monitoring, and incorporate audit telemetry into broader threat detection and response workflows. 

 

SOCRadar Alerts Azure Sentinel Directional Solution

SOCRadar Threat Intelligence for Microsoft Sentinel enriches security operations by bringing prioritized, context-rich alerts directly into Microsoft Sentinel. Covering SOCRadar’s Extended Threat Intelligence capabilities, including Brand Protection, External Attack Surface Management (ASM), Third-Party Findings, and other security modules, the integration helps organizations monitor external threats and manage investigations within their existing SOC workflows. Bidirectional synchronization also helps keep incident status, severity, and comments aligned between Microsoft Sentinel and SOCRadar.

SpyCloud Enterprise Protection for Microsoft Sentinel  

SpyCloud Enterprise Protection for Microsoft Sentinel brings stolen identity data from infostealer malware, phishing attacks, and third-party breaches into Microsoft Sentinel, helping security teams uncover compromised identities, prioritize high-risk exposures, and accelerate remediation to prevent session hijacking and other targeted identity-based attacks. The solution includes a custom API connector, a Logic Apps playbook for ingesting data into Log Analytics, analytic rules that generate Sentinel incidents from breach and malware data, and additional Logic Apps playbooks for incident automation and enrichment. 

 

Tenable App for Microsoft Sentinel

Tenable App for Microsoft Sentinel brings asset and vulnerability data from Tenable One Vulnerability Management into Sentinel for centralized security analysis. The integration combines Tenable cyber exposure insights with Sentinel’s collection, detection, and investigation capabilities, making vulnerability context available alongside other security telemetry. By incorporating asset and vulnerability findings into Sentinel workflows, the solution helps security teams correlate exposure data with security signals, investigate risks affecting vulnerable assets, and better prioritize remediation efforts.

Uniqkey Security Events for Microsoft Sentinel

Uniqkey Security Events for Microsoft Sentinel brings authentication, credential access and management, sharing, administrative activity, and platform threat detections into Microsoft Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). Included analytics rules identify scenarios such as sign-ins from unfamiliar IP addresses, excessive credential access, data exports, and security policy or privilege changes. A workbook visualizes activity and threat detections, helping security teams monitor password-management activity, investigate potential credential risks, and correlate findings with broader security telemetry. 

 

Utimaco Enterprise Secure Key Manager

Utimaco Enterprise Secure Key Manager (ESKM) integrates with Microsoft Sentinel to provide centralized security monitoring and visibility into cryptographic key management activities through KMIP server logs. The solution enables organizations to monitor key operations, KMIP client activity, and authentication events, helping security teams identify suspicious behavior and investigate potential threats. Built-in analytics rules help detect brute-force authentication attempts, repeated permission-denied events, and key-destruction activity, while hunting queries and a dedicated workbook support deeper investigation of unusual users, source IPs, key retrieval patterns, and after-hours activity. 

 

valimail-sentinel-enforce

Valimail enables organizations to see who sends email using your domain, protects against domain impersonation, and displays a verified logo in inboxes to increase brand trust. Our Microsoft Sentinel Connector brings Valimail Enforce event data directly into Sentinel, allowing security teams to incorporate our telemetry into unified SIEM workflows, monitor authentication and enforcement trends in real time, and build custom alerts and visualizations based on DMARC events. Once configured, Sentinel continuously ingests Valimail event logs, enriching your broader security intelligence and helping to improve your ability to detect and respond to threats across your environment. 

Varonis for Sentinel Solutions

Varonis for Sentinel Solutions brings enriched, data-centric Varonis alerts into Microsoft Sentinel for triage, investigation, and remediation. Varonis insights are contextualized alongside other security events to provide a unified view of data risk. This allows security teams to view and close Varonis alerts directly within Sentinel, reducing the need to switch interfaces and supporting incident resolution with less manual effort

Whisper for Sentinel

Whisper for Sentinel enriches Microsoft Sentinel incidents and alerts with threat and infrastructure intelligence for IPs, domains, ASNs, and networks. The solution provides threat scores, supporting evidence, infrastructure relationships, and historical context directly within Sentinel. Included enrichment playbooks, analytics rules, hunting queries, and workbooks support investigation of threats including C2 communications, malicious infrastructure, suspicious domains, and BGP anomalies, while retained enrichment data can be queried and correlated with existing logs.

WhoisFreaks Threat Intelligence for Microsoft Sentinel  

The WhoisFreaks solution for Microsoft Sentinel brings domain threat intelligence and newly registered domain (NRD) data into Sentinel using the Codeless Connector Framework (CCF). Customers can connect malware, phishing, and spam threat feeds, along with gTLD and ccTLD NRD feeds with or without WHOIS data. Included analytics rule templates help identify high-confidence malicious domains, newly registered domains appearing in threat feeds, threat-listed parked domains, and unusual NRD volumes that may indicate bulk registration activity. 

Wiz for Microsoft Sentinel  

Wiz for Microsoft Sentinel brings Wiz Issues, Vulnerability Findings, and Audit logs into Microsoft Sentinel. Wiz identifies and prioritizes cloud security risks across areas including vulnerabilities, malware, internet exposure, identity, and data security in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, OCI, Alibaba, and Kubernetes environments. 

 

In addition to the solutions from our third-party partners, we are also excited to announce the following connectors published by the Microsoft Sentinel team: 

  • Agari Solution 
  • Akamai DDOS Protection 
  • Alibaba Cloud Networking 
  • Atlassian Organization Audit

Building a more connected foundation for security operations 

The strength of the connector ecosystem reflects the work of Microsoft and our technology partners to support our shared customers. Together, we are helping organizations connect the technologies they rely on and bring more of their security data into a unified operational experience. 

For customers 

If you are a Microsoft Sentinel or ISOC customer, or considering adopting it, we want you to have the security connectors and integrations you need to get value from the platform. If an integration with an independent software vendor (ISV) is not yet available, or you have an issue with an existing solution, we have a dedicated team that may be able to assist by working with ISVs to build new or update existing connectors. 

For software companies 

If you are a software development partner, the Microsoft Sentinel Codeless Connector Framework (CCF) provides a streamlined way to bring your product into the Microsoft Security ecosystem. Partners can also work directly with Microsoft for engineering guidance and support to build or improve a connector. 

Building a more connected foundation for security operations 

Our goal is simple: help customers protect their digital environments by giving human defenders and AI agents a more complete picture of risk. We’ll continue investing in connectors, partnerships, and integrated security experiences to help customers defend their organizations with greater visibility, context, and confidence.
