items.summary: In this article From scans to reports Selected findings Closing thoughts At Microsoft’s FORGE Lab , we used codename MDASH to scan a subset of Linux kernel subsystems from late May to mid-June 2026. One full-time researcher and one intern led this three-month effort, which has so far produced 59 public upstream reports and 33 assigned CVEs . We confirmed working root privilege-escalation exploits for eight of those CVEs, and fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into mainline. Finding the bugs was only part of the work. The initial scans produced 26,502 raw findings in about two weeks, but turning those results into reproducible bugs, upstream reports, and patches took months of expert investigation and collaboration with Linux maintainers. In this post, we look back at how we went from thousands of potential findings to validated vulnerabilities and upstream fixes, and what we learned about scaling vulnerability discovery with AI. From scans to reports We focused on several core kernel subsystems, such as networking, filesystems, and security modules. Our selection criteria were straightforward: we picked security-sensitive components with no obvious dependence on specialized hardware, making QEMU-based validation simple and unified. Code scanning mainly used Sonnet 4.6 (71.1% of code-scanning tokens), GPT-5.4 (20.1%), and GPT-5.5 (7.1%). The codename MDASH scans produced 26,502 raw scan findings in about two weeks on two servers (64 cores/256 GB RAM and 32 cores/128 GB RAM), but turning that output into patches and reports took months of expert work. We filtered out low-confidence claims using codename MDASH’s confidence levels and separate fast screening agents we built, reducing the pool to 11,769 candidates. PoC-generating agents then attempted reproduction in QEMU, mainly using GPT-5.5 (77.3% of reproduction tokens), Opus 4.6 (13.2%), and GPT-5.5-cyber (9.4%). Experts then reviewed the 621 cases with PoC evidence to identify root causes, merge duplicates, and prepare upstream submissions. Figure 1 . Scan-to-report workflow. 26,502 raw findings → 11,769 screened candidates → 621 PoC-backed cases → 59 upstream reports. Where the 621 cases went Roughly one public upstream report landed from every ten PoC-backed cases: 59 reports from 621 cases (9.5%). Across those cases, the main reasons for not filing a separate new report were: 266 (42.8%) shared a root cause with another case, so one patch could fix them together. 163 (26.2%) were not reported after review, mostly due to limited security impact. 133 (21.4%) were already reported or fixed upstream. Submission timing explains many of the 133 overlaps. Most of the 621 cases were new when the scans finished (though some may already have been in flight by others). Our first public report went out on June 27, 2026, more than five weeks after scanning started. By September 1, 55 of the 59 had been posted to the public lists; the other four were reported privately during the same window and routed to the public lists by mid-October. Getting fixes merged Upstream Linux typically requires vulnerability reports to come with a working patch. Agents helped draft initial fixes, but human validation, subsystem understanding, and iterating with maintainers during review remained essential. So far, fixes for 38 of our reports have been merged into upstream mainline—half on the first submission, and the rest after one to four revisions. Reaching a mainline release from the first public patch took a median of 41 days (up to 108 days), and we are still working with maintainers on the remaining reports. How old the bugs were Interestingly, most of the bugs we reported had been in the kernel for years. Across the 59 reports, the average bug was 8.1 years old when we first reported it publicly. One of the oldest, a cls_u32 shift-out-of-bounds bug (CVE-2026-74544) , had been there for at least 21 years. Figure 2 . Age of reported kernel bugs, measured from the bug-introducing commit (the fix’s Fixes tag) to our first public report. Average age 8.1 years across 59 reports; six were 15–19 years old and three were at least 20 years old. Selected findings Among the 33 CVEs assigned so far from this batch, 24 are rated High or above (CVSS v3.1 score of at least 7.0). Below are eight CVEs for which we confirmed local root privilege-escalation exploits in controlled laboratory environments, with some cases requiring non-default settings or disabled exploit mitigations: CVE-2026-… Module Summary 64554 net/ipv6 Use-after-free in bridged IPv6 fragmentation: a saved pointer into a packet was reused after the packet’s buffer was reallocated. 64563 lib/rhashtable Use-after-free in hash-table walks: a walk resumed after the table was resized reused a pointer to a possibly freed entry. 64580 net/ipv6 Refcount underflow in IPv6 IPsec routing: an error path dropped a device reference but kept the pointer, so cleanup dropped it again. 74561 net/ipv4 Use-after-free in next-hop replacement: the route-cache flush walked an IPv6 route list without its lock, racing with route deletion. 74562 net/ipv4 Use-after-free in next-hop replacement: route checks and notifications walked an IPv6 route list without its lock, racing with route deletion. 89789 drivers/net Use-after-free in the GTP tunnel driver: when device creation failed, its lookup tables were freed while incoming packets could still read them. 98222 security/keys Heap buffer overflow in encrypted-key updates: long key parameters overflowed a 16-bit length, so the kernel wrote past an undersized buffer. 98364 net/xfrm Use-after-free in IPsec routing: a network device was used without holding a reference, so deleting it at the same time could free it mid-use. A closer look at CVE-2026-64563 CVE-2026-64563 is a one-line state-reset bug in rhashtable, the Linux kernel’s shared resizable hash table. Because callers trust the object pointers returned by a table walk, this small library flaw enabled a stable local privilege escalation on Linux—and affected Android with SELinux enforcing—without requiring special kernel configurations or user namespaces. Many kernel subsystems store live objects, such as sockets , in rhashtable and walk the table when user space asks to list them. Because a large listing may be split across several replies, a walk can pause and resume. Its iterator saves where it stopped, including a pointer to the last visited entry (iter->p). While the walk is paused, however, the table can still change: entries can be removed and freed, and resizing can replace the underlying bucket table. The missed reset Before 2018, rhashtable_walk_stop() always cleared iter->p = NULL on pause. To improve walk stability across stop/start cycles, a 2018 commit (5d240a8936f6) kept iter->p across walk_stop() and moved the reset into rhashtable_walk_start_check() —but only on one of its two resume paths: Old table freed by a resize (iter->walker.tbl == NULL) : lines 877–882 switch to the new table, reset slot and skip, and return -EAGAIN early without clearing iter->p: Old table still present (iter->walker.tbl != NULL) : lines 884–919 scan the bucket chain for iter->p and reset iter->p = NULL if the entry was removed. if (!iter->walker.tbl) { iter->walker.tbl = rht_dereference_rcu(ht->tbl, ht); iter->slot = 0; iter->skip = 0; return -EAGAIN; } After that restart, the next call to rhashtable_walk_next() sees iter->p still set and follows iter->p->next instead of starting over at slot = 0. If that entry was freed while the walk was paused, dereferencing iter->p->next reads from freed memory. Why did this bug go unnoticed for eight years? Triggering it requires three conditions to line up in the same walk: the caller must pause and resume the same iterator across walk_stop() and walk_start(), a table resize must free the old bucket table during that pause, and the entry at iter->p must also be removed and freed before the walk resumes. Most rhashtable walkers finish in a single pass without ever resuming a stopped iterator, and even when a caller does pause and resume, those three events rarely coincide by accident in normal workloads. The upstream fix simply clears the stale pointer before returning: + iter->p = NULL; From a socket listing to a kernel write Because rhashtable is a shared library, its callers determine both whether this bug is reachable and how severe its security impact can be. Across the kernel, there are about two dozen files that use the rhashtable walker API, and most walk the table in a single pass and immediately exit. Among those callers, we found two that pause and resume an iterator across batches and can at least cause a crash: TIPC’s socket dump (tipc_nl_sk_walk()) and Netlink’s socket diagnostics (__netlink_diag_dump()). Of the two, __netlink_diag_dump() is the exploitable caller. It is reachable by unprivileged users on standard kernels, and user space controls the pause between dump replies (via recvmsg()). An attacker can hold a dump paused while resizing the table and freeing the socket at iter->p, then reallocate that memory to control iter->p->next—causing rhashtable_walk_next() to return a fake socket pointer sk. __netlink_diag_dump() then checks net_eq(sock_net(sk), net) and passes sk to sk_diag_fill() and sock_diag_save_cookie() , which initializes sk->sk_cookie if it is zero. That turns the fake sk pointer into a constrained 64-bit write (when the target 8 bytes are zero and sk->sk_net matches &init_net). Paired with other general exploitation techniques, this write is enough for local privilege escalation. We thank Yuan Tan of NebuSec, who also independently found this vulnerability. He promptly shared its real severity with us and the maintainers, which helped the upstream fix, and later provided us with his working exploits for both Linux and Android. We also thank Frank Wu of NebuSec, who identified a viable exploitation primitive and developed a working privilege-escalation exploit. Closing thoughts Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance. Two weeks of codename MDASH scanning produced the initial findings, which we narrowed to 621 PoC-backed cases. But it took over four person-months to report 59 of them—and five months later, 38 fixes have been merged. For complex infrastructure like the Linux kernel, keeping humans in the loop is still necessary, making human effort the bottleneck. Both bug hunters and maintainers can be overwhelmed by the volume of real findings, so focusing on genuinely high-severity issues is essential. More tokens may yield more bugs, but not a secure system. We scanned only a small fraction of the kernel, and further tuning and more tokens could uncover substantially more bugs. But even after fixing all of them, is the system secure? At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we’re using AI to expand the scope of vulnerability research, but our experience shows that discovery is only one part of the work. The more urgent problem is how to build practical security solutions that are operational, cumulative, and economically sensible. These lessons also extend beyond our research. Through close collaboration with the engineering teams building codename MDASH, we’re applying what we learn from real-world vulnerability discovery and validation to inform how these capabilities evolve. The goal is to bring advances in AI-powered security research into the hands of security teams, helping them identify and address critical vulnerabilities more effectively.

While the walk is paused, however, the table can still change: entries can be removed and freed, and resizing can replace the underlying bucket table.

The missed reset

Before 2018, rhashtable_walk_stop() always cleared iter->p = NULL on pause. To improve walk stability across stop/start cycles, a 2018 commit (5d240a8936f6) kept iter->p across walk_stop() and moved the reset into rhashtable_walk_start_check()—but only on one of its two resume paths:

Old table freed by a resize (iter->walker.tbl == NULL): lines 877–882 switch to the new table, reset slot and skip, and return -EAGAIN early without clearing iter->p:

Old table still present (iter->walker.tbl != NULL): lines 884–919 scan the bucket chain for iter->p and reset iter->p = NULL if the entry was removed.

if (!iter->walker.tbl) {
	iter->walker.tbl = rht_dereference_rcu(ht->tbl, ht);
	iter->slot = 0;
	iter->skip = 0;
	return -EAGAIN;
}

After that restart, the next call to rhashtable_walk_next() sees iter->p still set and follows iter->p->next instead of starting over at slot = 0. If that entry was freed while the walk was paused, dereferencing iter->p->next reads from freed memory.

Why did this bug go unnoticed for eight years? Triggering it requires three conditions to line up in the same walk: the caller must pause and resume the same iterator across walk_stop() and walk_start(), a table resize must free the old bucket table during that pause, and the entry at iter->p must also be removed and freed before the walk resumes. Most rhashtable walkers finish in a single pass without ever resuming a stopped iterator, and even when a caller does pause and resume, those three events rarely coincide by accident in normal workloads.

The upstream fix simply clears the stale pointer before returning:

+		iter->p = NULL;
From a socket listing to a kernel write

Because rhashtable is a shared library, its callers determine both whether this bug is reachable and how severe its security impact can be. Across the kernel, there are about two dozen files that use the rhashtable walker API, and most walk the table in a single pass and immediately exit. Among those callers, we found two that pause and resume an iterator across batches and can at least cause a crash: TIPC’s socket dump (tipc_nl_sk_walk()) and Netlink’s socket diagnostics (__netlink_diag_dump()).

Of the two, __netlink_diag_dump() is the exploitable caller. It is reachable by unprivileged users on standard kernels, and user space controls the pause between dump replies (via recvmsg()). An attacker can hold a dump paused while resizing the table and freeing the socket at iter->p, then reallocate that memory to control iter->p->next—causing rhashtable_walk_next() to return a fake socket pointer sk.

__netlink_diag_dump() then checks net_eq(sock_net(sk), net) and passes sk to sk_diag_fill() and sock_diag_save_cookie(), which initializes sk->sk_cookie if it is zero. That turns the fake sk pointer into a constrained 64-bit write (when the target 8 bytes are zero and sk->sk_net matches &init_net). Paired with other general exploitation techniques, this write is enough for local privilege escalation.

We thank Yuan Tan of NebuSec, who also independently found this vulnerability. He promptly shared its real severity with us and the maintainers, which helped the upstream fix, and later provided us with his working exploits for both Linux and Android. We also thank Frank Wu of NebuSec, who identified a viable exploitation primitive and developed a working privilege-escalation exploit.

Closing thoughts

Finding bugs and fixing them are drastically out of balance. Two weeks of codename MDASH scanning produced the initial findings, which we narrowed to 621 PoC-backed cases. But it took over four person-months to report 59 of them—and five months later, 38 fixes have been merged. For complex infrastructure like the Linux kernel, keeping humans in the loop is still necessary, making human effort the bottleneck. Both bug hunters and maintainers can be overwhelmed by the volume of real findings, so focusing on genuinely high-severity issues is essential.

More tokens may yield more bugs, but not a secure system. We scanned only a small fraction of the kernel, and further tuning and more tokens could uncover substantially more bugs. But even after fixing all of them, is the system secure? At Microsoft FORGE Lab, we’re using AI to expand the scope of vulnerability research, but our experience shows that discovery is only one part of the work. The more urgent problem is how to build practical security solutions that are operational, cumulative, and economically sensible.

These lessons also extend beyond our research. Through close collaboration with the engineering teams building codename MDASH, we’re applying what we learn from real-world vulnerability discovery and validation to inform how these capabilities evolve. The goal is to bring advances in AI-powered security research into the hands of security teams, helping them identify and address critical vulnerabilities more effectively.

The post Lessons from 59 Linux Kernel Bug Reports appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog.

items.title: Introducing CNCF User Groups: Long-lived homes for End User collaboration
items.summary: The CNCF End User Community is launching its User Group Program at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America. These are long-lived groups, each built around an industry vertical or problem domain, that serves the common need of the end user community, and reports directly to the CNCF Technical Advisory Board (TAB). Why user groups Cloud native adoption looks different in a telecom network, a research lab, a public agency and a platform team at a software company. Each has its own constraints, vocabulary and gaps in the tooling landscape. A CNCF User Group gives each of those communities a durable place to organize around its own needs, rather than relying on one-off efforts that fade after a single project or event. A User Group is the primary organizational unit of the program. It is aligned with an industry vertical, a problem domain, or a common need of the CNCF end user community, and it is long-lived by design: user groups perform standing functions for projects and the organizations that adopt them. Each group: Represents and serves the needs of end users in its domain Identifies gaps in the CNCF project portfolio and helps attract projects to fill them Educates users with unbiased, practical information scoped to cloud native Proposes community-sourced reference architectures, best practices and how-tos for publication Gives CNCF projects feedback on usability, reliability and performance User groups also come with accountability. Every group operates under a charter, is led by chairs approved by the TAB, holds at least one public monthly meeting that is recorded and posted to YouTube, and reports regularly on its health and work to the TAB. Groups are also expected to show up at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon, whether through talks, booths or ecosystem updates. Technical Community Groups and User Groups: what’s the difference? The program is designed as a path, not a single door. Technical Community Groups (TCGs) are the lightweight starting point: part of the broader CNCF Community Groups Program, they act as a rallying point where practitioners discuss a topic, share knowledge and coordinate possible future initiatives. User Groups are the long-lived, chartered layer on top. Technical Community Group User Group Purpose Discussion, knowledge sharing and a rallying point around a topic or domain Standing, long-term coverage of an industry vertical or problem domain Governance Minimal; follows the Community Groups process, plus TAB approval Charter required; reports directly to the TAB Leadership Organizers (2-year terms) Chairs approved by the TAB (2-year terms) Meetings One meet-up every 90 days At least one public monthly meeting, recorded and posted to YouTube Reporting Minimal Periodic health and initiative updates to the TAB; KubeCon presence expected Scope of work Free to propose initiatives with an explicit deliverable Standing functions, plus initiatives, white papers and reference architectures The governance model expects most future user groups to begin life as community groups. A TCG that wants to graduate must have completed numerous initiatives, cover a gap not already served by an existing group, and win TAB approval. The group then drafts a charter with defined scope, and the TAB votes on it. Once the vote passes, the user group is formed. Source: User Group Governance . One on-ramp, two destinations Community groups are a shared on-ramp across CNCF. Where a TCG lands depends on its focus. End user-driven domains such as an industry vertical go to the TAB and become User Groups. Project-focused domains go to the Technical Oversight Committee (TOC) and can become a Technical Advisory Group (TAG). The governance documents tell TCG organizers to talk to the TOC and TAB chairs early, so the group lands in the right place. The TAG path has the same shape as the User Group path. A TCG applying to become a TAG must have completed numerous initiatives, cover a gap in the currently defined groups, have a documented history of collaboration with its parent group, and be approved by the TOC. The group then drafts a charter, the TOC votes on it, and the TAG is formed once the vote passes. Source: Tech Group Governance . Platform Engineering: from TCG to User Group The Platform Engineering community shows how that path works in practice. It started life as a Working Group under the previous TAG App Delivery, became a Technical Community Group during the TAG restructuring last year, and is now transitioning to a User Group. Over time, the group moved from conversation to output, including the Platform Engineering Maturity Model and the Platforms White Paper . Becoming a User Group changes what the community can do. It now has a TAB-approved charter, a direct reporting line to the TAB, a standing public monthly meeting, and a formal role in representing platform engineering end users across the CNCF ecosystem. Its focus areas include internal developer platforms, golden paths, self-service capabilities, platform as a product, developer experience, and operational practices such as GitOps and policy as code. “Being recognized as a CNCF User Group is an exciting milestone for us. It validates years of dedication from our community members and provides the elevated visibility we need to bring in new ideas, attract fresh talent, and continue shaping the future of Platform Engineering together.” – Chris Plank aka Planko Four user groups, and room to grow The program launches with four groups, each serving a distinct end user community: Platform Engineering : Cloud native collaboration for platform engineering end users Public Sector : Cloud native collaboration for public-sector end users Research : Cloud native collaboration for research organizations and scientific workloads Telecom : Cloud native collaboration for telecom end users New groups are formed when there is a documented, outstanding gap in coverage of a technical domain within cloud native. If your community fits that description, the path starts with a conversation with the TAB. Community groups that have a track record of completed initiatives are the natural candidates. Meet the Platform Engineering User Group at KubeCon The best way to see what a user group does is to meet the people in it. Stop by the Platform Engineering User Group kiosk on Day 1, Tuesday, November 10, from 3:00 PM to 7:00 PM at P-16B . Talk with the group about your platform challenges, hear how the move from TCG to user group came together, and find out how to get involved. Can’t make it to the show floor? You can join the conversation any time: Learn about the program and every group at endusers.cncf.io/community/user-groups Find meeting details and initiatives at cloudnativeplatforms.com Join #platform-engineering on CNCF Slack Share a platform architecture or case study with the group Also at KubeCon: the Public Sector User Group Working in or alongside government or another regulated environment? The Public Sector User Group has two sessions this week, back to back: Public Sector User Group Meetup: Cloud Native in the Public Sector is an informal, social meetup with no slides or agenda. Meet the co-chairs and other members, swap stories about deploying cloud native technology in regulated environments, and learn how to get involved. Public Sector User Group BoF: Roadmap, White Papers, Our Group is a Birds of a Feather session led by co-chairs William Crum and Daniel Moch. It covers the group’s mission and roadmap, its white papers published and in progress, and how it works with the TAB. They will also ask for help with current work and open a discussion on the biggest adoption challenges in the public sector. Both ancillaries are aimed at government employees, contractors and service members. Can’t make it? The group meets biweekly on Wednesdays at 2:00 PM US/Eastern. Find the details on the Public Sector User Group page , the CNCF community page , or in #ug-public-sector on CNCF Slack .

items.title: Q&A: Why Cybersecurity Has to Move Beyond Technology
items.summary: Cybersecurity increasingly sits at the centre of how organisations operate, from protecting critical financial systems to managing identity across cloud environments. For Ben Hanson, the challenge has never been purely technical. Ben Hanson is Global Field CTO and Director of Field Engineering at Zenity, and a former Senior Security Strategist and Advisor at Microsoft. A 25-year industry veteran, Ben previously served as Senior Security Strategist and Advisor at Microsoft, working with security and transformation leaders across some of the world’s largest financial institutions. In an interview with the IT Security Guru, conducted by the Cyber Security Speakers Agency , Ben discusses why cybersecurity work carries such responsibility, what separates strong security practitioners from purely technical ones, and why identity has become one of the most important areas of modern cyber defence. Cybersecurity often operates behind the scenes. What makes the work so consequential, and why is it a meaningful career to pursue? Ben Hanson : “What we do in cybersecurity enables the whole of society to flourish. In this day and age, that is absolutely true. “Recently, I was working in a coffee shop in the village that I live in. It was early in the morning, and outside the window I could see mums and dads walking with their kids through the village square to school. I was working on my laptop with a very large bank, helping them through a particular security challenge they were having. “I remember thinking, as I looked outside at these folks walking across the square, what we’re doing matters to every one of those people, but none of them know it. “If you lose a global systemic financial institution, like a large systemic bank, it doesn’t just affect cities and nations. It affects the financial systems of entire continents, which undermines the fabric of society in a very tangible, practical way. “So this, for me, is both the great responsibility of working in cybersecurity, but also the privilege of working in cybersecurity. You can invest yourself in something that really matters. “If you have a North Star in your career and you want to invest yourself in work that’s meaningful and consequential, you can’t find an industry to work in that’s more consequential than this one. “That’s what I love about it the most.” For someone building a career in cybersecurity, what separates the strongest practitioners from those who remain too narrowly focused on technology? Ben Hanson : “I’d give two pieces of advice. “First of all, remember who you work for and why. Security and risk management are not ends in themselves. They both exist to enable your business, your organisation, to achieve and sustain its goals and objectives. “For a very long time, security organisations, and also IT organisations, have defined themselves as separate from their business. You’ll actually hear technology people and security folks refer to the rest of their organisation as “the business”, as though they were not a part of it. “So we’re over here in the security ivory tower doing what we do, and all the business people are over there doing whatever it is they do. “The problem with that is two things. Number one, that business signs our paycheques, which leads to number two: the only reason that anyone in security even has a job is because we work for growing, successful, innovative businesses. “If you can remember that security’s job is to enable your business to achieve and sustain its business goals and objectives, it will help you not to bias towards security controls that are overly or unnecessarily risk-averse. “It will help you to prioritise business enablement over stopping bad things happening, because those are two very different things. “So remember who you work for and why. “A second piece of advice I would give is to be careful about being overly technology-centric in security. That might sound like a weird thing to say, but security practitioners tend to have technology backgrounds. I include myself in this, networks and infrastructure. “That is a good thing, but it also has some consequences if you’re not careful. One of those is that we tend to look at problems through technology lenses, and we tend to see solutions through technology lenses. “This predisposes us to what I would call silver bullet syndrome, which is: technology is the answer, whatever the question. “That is not true. “Technology can enable transformation, but it cannot sustain it. All sustainable transformation is a transformation of culture. “So the three Bs: the beliefs, the biases, the behaviours of your organisation, and the way that you think about and approach security in your organisation. “If you don’t also transform the way that you think about and approach security, the non-technical dynamics, any success you make in the short term you can’t sustain. You will find yourself drawn backwards towards where you were. “Many of you will have experienced this. The status quo has an incredible gravitational pull associated with it, and it takes a lot of energy to escape that gravitational pull. “Organisations may make some progress by deploying new technology. We do this all the time in security. But inevitably, over time, the gravitational pull of that status quo, the culture as we’ve known it which did not evolve, pulls us back to the world that we’re trying to move on from. “Many people will be familiar with Peter Drucker’s famous quote that culture eats strategy for breakfast. I would just like to say that culture eats everything for breakfast, including that shiny new security toy that you just bought.” Why has identity become the new security perimeter, and how has the shift to cloud changed the way organisations need to defend themselves? Ben Hanson : “It’s the central role of identity in security. It’s the idea of identity as the modern perimeter. “Attackers are becoming more identity-centric. The industry is still trying to catch up with the implications of identity becoming essentially the central focus of what we have to protect. “If you go back to the early 1990s, this is when enterprise firewalls came to the fore. This was before widespread cloud adoption, so it was very easy for organisations to draw a very stark dividing line delineating their traditional network perimeter and what was inside versus outside, what was trusted versus untrusted, what was us versus them. “If you fast forward to the early 2000s, with widespread adoption of the internet and also adoption of cloud, you had organisations like the Jericho Forum talking about de-perimeterisation. “The traditional network perimeter was eroding and was now contracting around assets themselves. This is where we got the “endpoint is bastion” idea. This is what led us into very advanced endpoint protections and EDR platforms. “We’ve now taken another step towards the central role of identity in security. I think there are three reasons why this is happening. “First of all, if you look at modern access scenarios, often the user’s corporate identity is the only common factor across all of the various domains. “You have people using networks that you can’t control, at their house or at the coffee shop. You have people using endpoints, depending on your bring-your-own-device strategy, that you can’t control or control as well as you might like. “They’re accessing data on systems that you don’t control, accessing SaaS applications that are run by someone else. “Almost out of necessity, because it’s the only common unifying factor across all of those components, identity becomes the fulcrum around which all of these other pieces balance. “A second reason why this is happening is attacker behaviour. Attackers have always been identity-focused. “Effectively, every attack is an attack on identity. At some point around the middle of the attack chain, attackers try to get control of privileged identity so that they can get access to the data they want. “Even though that’s true, it’s shifted even further. “Very common attacks involve compromising cloud-native identities, moving to cloud-native applications, compromising application service principals, connecting via API to cloud-native services and extracting data out of those services. “Nothing about that attack sequence touches your endpoint. “So if you’re still focusing most of your attention on your devices, you’re going to miss a lot because those kinds of attacks don’t trigger any endpoint controls. And if they do, by that point it’ll be far too late.”

“We’ve now taken another step towards the central role of identity in security. I think there are three reasons why this is happening. 

“First of all, if you look at modern access scenarios, often the user’s corporate identity is the only common factor across all of the various domains. 

“You have people using networks that you can’t control, at their house or at the coffee shop. You have people using endpoints, depending on your bring-your-own-device strategy, that you can’t control or control as well as you might like. 

“They’re accessing data on systems that you don’t control, accessing SaaS applications that are run by someone else. 

“Almost out of necessity, because it’s the only common unifying factor across all of those components, identity becomes the fulcrum around which all of these other pieces balance. 

“A second reason why this is happening is attacker behaviour. Attackers have always been identity-focused. 

“Effectively, every attack is an attack on identity. At some point around the middle of the attack chain, attackers try to get control of privileged identity so that they can get access to the data they want. 

“Even though that’s true, it’s shifted even further. 

“Very common attacks involve compromising cloud-native identities, moving to cloud-native applications, compromising application service principals, connecting via API to cloud-native services and extracting data out of those services. 

“Nothing about that attack sequence touches your endpoint. 

“So if you’re still focusing most of your attention on your devices, you’re going to miss a lot because those kinds of attacks don’t trigger any endpoint controls. And if they do, by that point it’ll be far too late.”

items.title: Hackers Could Exploit MCP Server Supply Chain Weaknesses to Steal API Keys and Administrator Credentials
items.summary: Security teams that run AI coding assistants may be exposing their most powerful credentials without knowing it. A new study shows that Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers can quietly change their own code after they are set up. If an attacker poisons just one package in that chain, they could steal API keys and administrator logins. MCP servers let AI assistants talk to other tools, such as firewalls, SIEM platforms and cloud consoles. To do this work, they usually hold the keys of the person who installed them. Attackers already know this. A malicious MCP server found in the wild has shown how easily one trusted tool can leak data. Researchers at Corelight noted the weakness while checking an administrator’s workstation. They did not find malware there. They found AI assistants running MCP servers with privileged access, and they asked where the code in those servers came from and how it got updated. The answer is in Corelight’s research , published on November 10, 2026. Hackers Could Exploit MCP Server Supply Chain Weaknesses The assistants launched their MCP servers with a one-step tool called uvx. It downloads a Python package and runs it from a single line of settings. The settings looked safe, because they named an exact release, a version number or a Git commit. The catch is that pinning the main package does not pin the packages underneath it. One community server had pinned its seven direct dependencies and even published a hash-locked file. But the launcher ignored that file and fetched the roughly 60 other packages fresh from the Python Package Index (PyPI) whenever it rebuilt its environment. Over five weeks, that one server was rebuilt 19 times and produced 15 different sets of dependencies. Of its 69 packages, 23 changed versions, including the cryptography library and the MCP software kit itself. Nobody had touched the configuration. Corelight saw the same drift on every server launched this way. Every one of those packages runs inside the same process as the server. That means any of them can read the API tokens, the user’s files and the network paths the server can reach. A bad update does not even need to be called. Some malicious packages run the moment Python starts. The risk is not limited to Python. Some vendors tell users to start a local proxy with npx and a “latest” tag. That fetches the newest version at every start. It also echoes the critical mcp-remote flaw rated 9.6 on the CVSS scale, where fast updates helped, but a hijacked release would spread just as fast. Corelight stressed that this is not a flaw in MCP itself. Each case came from a setup choice. Of the 35 MCP servers it reviewed, 23 had a recommended install that would pull dependencies fresh from a public registry. Why Package Hijacks Make This Worse Attackers go after whichever dependency is easiest to take over. That might be a maintainer account with a reused password, a phished token or a weak release pipeline. The bad version then looks like a normal update. Corelight pointed to past cases such as xz Utils, Ultralytics and Nx, where stolen tokens and keys were the prize. The Shai-Hulud npm worm is a recent example. It used stolen npm tokens to publish infected versions of every package a victim maintained. A June 2026 variant reached PyPI and went after cloud credentials, GitHub tokens and API keys for AI coding tools. In one wave, six bad releases were live for under 30 minutes. A server that rebuilds every couple of days, and starts on its own, has more chances to land in a window like that. This pattern matches wider reports of how attackers poison trusted software updates to reach developer and cloud secrets. A managed update has a build you control and a version number you can see. A launcher that rebuilds at start-up offers neither, and the server’s own version number never changes. Corelight showed how to spot the problem. DNS and TLS logs list the hosts that contact GitHub, PyPI and npm. In its lab, that left four hosts. Endpoint data then showed that only the administrator’s workstation installed PyPI packages, and it did so whenever an AI assistant started its servers. Those servers made more than 1,600 connections in a week to 11 management systems. The fix is to freeze the environment. Teams should pin to a commit, install from a hash-pinned lock file, launch the server directly and turn off start-up update checks. Corelight froze five servers and started them 457 times over two weeks, and their package lists never changed. Each server should also get its own account with the least access it needs, and a named owner should review updates on a schedule. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Indicator Use Domain github.com Code download hunting Domain codeload.github.com Code download hunting Domain raw.githubusercontent.com Code download hunting Domain objects.githubusercontent.com Code download hunting Domain pypi.org Package registry contact Domain files.pythonhosted.org Package file downloads Domain registry.npmjs.org npm registry contact Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: CNCF Welcomes Adyen as Platinum End User Member to Advance Open Source Financial Infrastructure
items.summary: Operating over 100 Kubernetes clusters across €1.39T in volume, Adyen brings production-scale fintech expertise to CNCF governance and open source projects Key Highlights Adyen joins the CNCF as a Platinum End User Member, gaining seats on the CNCF Governing Board and End User Technical Advisory Board. Operating over 100 Kubernetes clusters with Cilium, Prometheus, and OpenTelemetry, Adyen brings production-scale operational expertise to the open source community. Adyen open sourced kubectl-rexec, a Kubernetes tool that supports auditable kubectl exec access for regulated cloud native environments. KUBECON + CLOUDNATIVECON NORTH AMERICA, SALT LAKE CITY – November 11, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, today announced that Adyen , the global financial technology platform, has joined the foundation as a Platinum End User. The move comes as 87% of financial organizations report clear business value from open source, according to the FINOS 2025 State of Open Source in Financial Services Report , reinforcing Adyen’s commitment to advancing the open source technologies that help power secure, scalable financial infrastructure. Processing billions of transactions each year and €1.39 trillion in volume in 2025, Adyen is investing at the Platinum level to help advance the secure, reliable cloud native infrastructure that financial services require. Its participation brings the operating perspective of a global fintech platform to the open, vendor-neutral community shaping the technologies on which modern finance depends. “End users are the operational backbone of the cloud native ecosystem, and Adyen represents the pinnacle of high-scale, zero-downtime engineering,” said Jonathan Bryce, executive director, CNCF. “Operating over 100 Kubernetes clusters at a global scale gives Adyen unique technical insights. We are thrilled to welcome them as a Platinum End User and look forward to their leadership on our Governing and Technical Advisory Boards.” Adyen’s membership provides the cloud native community with a direct feedback loop from an environment where platform availability, performance, and security carry immediate financial weight. Beyond leveraging Kubernetes , Cilium , Prometheus , and OpenTelemetry across its global infrastructure, Adyen actively contributes solutions designed for regulated engineering teams. This includes open sourcing kubectl-rexec, a tool that adds strict auditability to Kubernetes container-access workflows while preserving native developer velocity. “Investing in the CNCF helps us to maintain full control of our technology,” said Pedro Oliveira, VP of Infrastructure. “When you operate at our scale, vendor lock-in isn’t an option, and having a seat at the table matters. Bringing our real-world experience to the community lets us help shape the tools we rely on every day, making them more reliable for us and for the broader ecosystem.” As a Platinum End User Member, Adyen will hold a seat on the CNCF Governing Board , which provides business, marketing, and budget oversight for the foundation. The company will also appoint a representative to the End User Technical Advisory Board , which brings end-user needs and perspectives to CNCF community discussions. To learn more about becoming a CNCF member, visit https://www.cncf.io/about/join/ . The Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) hosts critical components of the global technology infrastructure, including Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy. CNCF brings together the industry’s top developers, end users, and vendors and runs the largest open source developer conferences in the world. Supported by nearly 800 members, including the world’s largest cloud computing and software companies, as well as over 200 innovative startups, CNCF is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation. items.title: Meta Wins CNCF End User Case Study Contest for Accelerating AI Infrastructure Deployments From Hours to Minutes
items.summary: Using Argo CD and Kargo, Meta is building a GitOps platform to streamline application delivery across 100 Kubernetes clusters supporting AI research and inference Key Highlights Meta’s Cloud Foundation team won the CNCF End User Case Study Contest for its GitOps platform, built with Argo CD and Kargo to streamline Kubernetes application delivery. The new platform cuts routine application deployment times from more than four hours to minutes, streamlining the small team’s workflow through a simplified application definition while adding more advanced features such as automated deployment configuration, independent release promotion, and health verification. By separating application delivery from infrastructure provisioning, Meta is enabling independent application rollouts while retaining Terraform for infrastructure management. SALT LAKE CITY – KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 – November 10, 2026 – The Cloud Native Computing Foundation ® (CNCF®), which builds sustainable ecosystems for cloud native software, announced Meta as the winner of the CNCF End User Case Study Contest for its adoption of cloud native technologies to accelerate application delivery across its AI infrastructure. Through a GitOps platform built on Argo CD and Kargo, Meta’s Cloud Foundation team is transforming how applications are deployed and managed across approximately 100 Kubernetes clusters supporting AI research and inference, reducing routine deployment times from more than four hours to minutes. “AI infrastructure is causing organizations to rethink how they manage applications across distributed environments,” said Chris Aniszczyk, CTO, CNCF. “Meta’s approach demonstrates how open source technologies like Argo can help teams automate their application delivery, reduce operational complexity and scale infrastructure without adding unnecessary overhead. It’s a powerful example of how cloud native technologies are supporting the operational demands of AI at scale.” Meta’s Cloud Foundation team, composed of more than 15 engineers, supports approximately 100 Kubernetes clusters across multiple cloud providers and accelerator families. Previously, Terraform was used for both infrastructure provisioning and Kubernetes application deployment, tying even routine application updates to a lengthy infrastructure release process. The shared deployment model meant stalled rollouts could delay unrelated releases and lacked automated health checks to verify application status. To address these challenges, Meta began building a GitOps platform that separates application delivery from infrastructure provisioning. Terraform continues to manage infrastructure, while Argo CD reconciles application deployments against configurations stored in Git. Kargo orchestrates release promotion across environments, enabling independent rollouts, automated health checks and versioned release records that improve deployment traceability and recovery. “GitOps and Argo CD give our small team a great foundation, shaped by years of community experience in Kubernetes delivery,” said Phong Nguyen, Production Engineer, Meta. “We focus on connecting it to Meta’s systems and aim to share our own lessons along the way.” Meta also simplified application delivery by allowing developers to specify deployment requirements through a short application definition. The platform automatically generates Argo CD and Kargo configurations, enabling independent release promotion, automated health verification and deployment consistency without requiring application teams to manage complex configurations. Meta plans to expand adoption of its GitOps platform and transition to a centrally managed Argo CD service to reduce maintenance overhead across its Kubernetes fleet. The team is also exploring upstream contributions to improve container registry authentication and Argo CD performance in large clusters. To learn more about Meta’s implementation and results, read the full GitOps at Meta: How We Went From Terraform on Cron to GitOps for AI Infra case study. items.title: OpenShell on Kubernetes: A guide for platform engineers
items.summary: What OpenShell is AI agents do more than call APIs. They run shells, install packages, read files, and open network connections. Often they act on text they pulled from the internet a minute earlier. So every agent is untrusted code that holds real credentials. OpenShell , started by NVIDIA and now a CNCF Sandbox project , is a runtime for running agents like this safely. OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox. A trusted supervisor outside the sandbox decides what the agent may reach. You declare four kinds of control in YAML: Filesystem : Landlock limits which paths the agent can read or write. In the demo, /usr, /etc, and a few other paths are read-only, and only /sandbox, /tmp, and /dev/null are writable. Process : before the agent starts, the sandbox runtime drops it to a non-root user with no capabilities and applies seccomp. Network : outbound traffic is denied by default. Rules can allow traffic per binary, host, port, and HTTP method. Credentials : the agent sees only a placeholder for each API key. The supervisor swaps in the real key, and only for endpoints the provider allows. For Kubernetes admins, a key point is that OpenShell does not bring its own scheduler. Its Kubernetes backend uses Agent Sandbox , the agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resource from SIG Apps. Agents show up as Pods, Services, PVCs, Secrets, and NetworkPolicies, which you already know how to run. OpenShell adds what Kubernetes can’t see: which agent is calling, which binary made the request, and whether a given POST may leave the cluster. A NetworkPolicy can say “this Pod may reach api.github.com on 443.” It cannot say “curl may read issues but not create them.” OpenShell can, and it can change that rule on a running sandbox without a restart. How a sandbox is created and run On Kubernetes, the OpenShell gateway owns every sandbox, and Agent Sandbox turns each one into Pods. The nirmata/demo-openshell repo runs the whole flow on a two-node kind cluster with Kubernetes 1.35, Cilium 1.20, Agent Sandbox v1.0.5, OpenShell 0.1.3, and Kyverno 1.18.2. Its openshell-sandbox-lifecycle.md file describes each step in detail. Note 1: Currently, OpenShell sandboxes can only be created by calling the Gateway API and not via the Kubernetes API. There is an open issue ( openshell/#1719 ) for a Kubernetes OpenShellSandbox CRD, and an operator. Note 2: a Supervisor Pod per agent provides strong isolation, but may not scale well in large environments. The roadmap includes flexible deployment options (see RFC 0018 ). OpenShell on Kubernetes · control path and data path The gateway creates the Kubernetes objects, and Agent Sandbox creates the agent Pod. The agent Pod has no outbound network access of its own. The supervisor opens the only connection to it, and every request the agent makes goes back over that connection for a policy check. Kyverno checks the Kubernetes objects at admission. Prepare the cluster. Install a CNI that enforces both ingress and egress NetworkPolicy. The demo replaces kindnet with Cilium. Then install the Agent Sandbox controller and CRDs, and then the OpenShell gateway Helm chart. Create a sandbox. openshell sandbox create –workspace demo –name policy-demo –from nicolaka/netshoot@sha256:… –no-auto-providers sends the request to the gateway over mTLS. Clients never talk to the Kubernetes API. A workspace, here demo, groups sandboxes, policy, and logs. The gateway checks and records the request. It authenticates the caller, resolves the image, policy, providers, and resources, and rejects unsafe settings. It then saves a sandbox record in the Provisioning phase. This record, not the Pod, is the source of truth. Network policies come first. The Kubernetes driver creates two NetworkPolicies in the namespace, or checks them if they already exist. One covers workload Pods: no outbound traffic at all, and inbound traffic only from supervisors on TCP 5500. The other covers supervisor Pods. Only then does the driver create the Sandbox resource, in a suspended state. Agent Sandbox creates the workload. The controller creates the workload Pod and a PVC for /sandbox. A scheduling gate holds the Pod back. OpenShell checks the admitted Pod. After admission, the driver reads the Pod back. It checks for a non-root UID and GID, no added capabilities, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no host namespaces, no ServiceAccount token, and the expected labels and volumes. If an admission webhook changed any of these, creation fails. The supervisor is created. The driver creates a supervisor Pod, a Service in front of the workload Pod’s port 5500, TLS and bootstrap Secrets for this sandbox, and a short-lived token for the supervisor. The workload never gets gateway credentials. Then the scheduling gates come off. The supervisor connects. The supervisor authenticates to the gateway with an identity tied to the namespace, the Sandbox UID, its own Pod UID, and the runtime generation. It receives the policy and connects to the workload through the Service. Inside the workload, the sandbox runtime applies the filesystem, process, socket, and DNS controls. The agent’s command does not start until these controls are confirmed. Run and update. Each outbound request from the agent goes to the supervisor, which checks the destination, port, calling binary, and HTTP request before it opens the upstream connection. Exec, SSH, logs, and file sync also go through the supervisor. openshell policy update loads a new policy version and waits for the sandbox to confirm it, without a restart. In the demo, curl starts out blocked. After the update it can be read from api.github.com, but a POST to /issues returns policy_denied. openshell logs policy-demo –source sandbox shows each allowed and denied request. Stop, start, and delete. Stopping suspends the Sandbox and removes the workload Pod, but keeps the PVC. Starting creates a new runtime generation and runs the Pod checks again. Deleting removes the Sandbox, and owner references clean up its Pods, Service, Secrets, and PVC. The two namespace NetworkPolicies stay. If creation fails partway, the driver rolls back. OpenShell checks only the Pod settings it needs to stay safe. What OpenShell is

AI agents do more than call APIs. They run shells, install packages, read files, and open network connections. Often they act on text they pulled from the internet a minute earlier. So every agent is untrusted code that holds real credentials. 

OpenShell, started by NVIDIA and now a CNCF Sandbox project, is a runtime for running agents like this safely. OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox. A trusted supervisor outside the sandbox decides what the agent may reach. You declare four kinds of control in YAML:

  • Filesystem: Landlock limits which paths the agent can read or write. In the demo, /usr, /etc, and a few other paths are read-only, and only /sandbox, /tmp, and /dev/null are writable.
  • Process: before the agent starts, the sandbox runtime drops it to a non-root user with no capabilities and applies seccomp.
  • Network: outbound traffic is denied by default. Rules can allow traffic per binary, host, port, and HTTP method.
  • Credentials: the agent sees only a placeholder for each API key. The supervisor swaps in the real key, and only for endpoints the provider allows.

For Kubernetes admins, a key point is that OpenShell does not bring its own scheduler. Its Kubernetes backend uses Agent Sandbox, the agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resource from SIG Apps. Agents show up as Pods, Services, PVCs, Secrets, and NetworkPolicies, which you already know how to run. OpenShell adds what Kubernetes can’t see: which agent is calling, which binary made the request, and whether a given POST may leave the cluster.

A NetworkPolicy can say “this Pod may reach api.github.com on 443.” It cannot say “curl may read issues but not create them.” OpenShell can, and it can change that rule on a running sandbox without a restart.

How a sandbox is created and run

On Kubernetes, the OpenShell gateway owns every sandbox, and Agent Sandbox turns each one into Pods. The nirmata/demo-openshell repo runs the whole flow on a two-node kind cluster with Kubernetes 1.35, Cilium 1.20, Agent Sandbox v1.0.5, OpenShell 0.1.3, and Kyverno 1.18.2. Its openshell-sandbox-lifecycle.md file describes each step in detail.

Note 1: Currently, OpenShell sandboxes can only be created by calling the Gateway API and not via the Kubernetes API. There is an open issue (openshell/#1719) for a Kubernetes OpenShellSandbox CRD, and an operator.

Note 2: a Supervisor Pod per agent provides strong isolation, but may not scale well in large environments. The roadmap includes flexible deployment options (see RFC 0018). 

OpenShell on Kubernetes · control path and data path

The gateway creates the Kubernetes objects, and Agent Sandbox creates the agent Pod. The agent Pod has no outbound network access of its own. The supervisor opens the only connection to it, and every request the agent makes goes back over that connection for a policy check. Kyverno checks the Kubernetes objects at admission.

  2. Create a sandbox. openshell sandbox create –workspace demo –name policy-demo –from nicolaka/netshoot@sha256:… –no-auto-providers sends the request to the gateway over mTLS. Clients never talk to the Kubernetes API. A workspace, here demo, groups sandboxes, policy, and logs.
  3. The gateway checks and records the request. It authenticates the caller, resolves the image, policy, providers, and resources, and rejects unsafe settings. It then saves a sandbox record in the Provisioning phase. This record, not the Pod, is the source of truth.
  4. Network policies come first. The Kubernetes driver creates two NetworkPolicies in the namespace, or checks them if they already exist. One covers workload Pods: no outbound traffic at all, and inbound traffic only from supervisors on TCP 5500. The other covers supervisor Pods. Only then does the driver create the Sandbox resource, in a suspended state.
  5. Agent Sandbox creates the workload. The controller creates the workload Pod and a PVC for /sandbox. A scheduling gate holds the Pod back.
  6. OpenShell checks the admitted Pod. After admission, the driver reads the Pod back. It checks for a non-root UID and GID, no added capabilities, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no host namespaces, no ServiceAccount token, and the expected labels and volumes. If an admission webhook changed any of these, creation fails.
  7. The supervisor is created. The driver creates a supervisor Pod, a Service in front of the workload Pod’s port 5500, TLS and bootstrap Secrets for this sandbox, and a short-lived token for the supervisor. The workload never gets gateway credentials. Then the scheduling gates come off.
  8. The supervisor connects. The supervisor authenticates to the gateway with an identity tied to the namespace, the Sandbox UID, its own Pod UID, and the runtime generation. It receives the policy and connects to the workload through the Service. Inside the workload, the sandbox runtime applies the filesystem, process, socket, and DNS controls. The agent’s command does not start until these controls are confirmed.
  9. Run and update. Each outbound request from the agent goes to the supervisor, which checks the destination, port, calling binary, and HTTP request before it opens the upstream connection. Exec, SSH, logs, and file sync also go through the supervisor. openshell policy update loads a new policy version and waits for the sandbox to confirm it, without a restart. In the demo, curl starts out blocked. After the update it can be read from api.github.com, but a POST to /issues returns policy_denied. openshell logs policy-demo –source sandbox shows each allowed and denied request.
  10. Stop, start, and delete. Stopping suspends the Sandbox and removes the workload Pod, but keeps the PVC. Starting creates a new runtime generation and runs the Pod checks again. items.title: How to Export Logs with Amazon Athena
items.summary: Athena doesn’t store logs itself. It queries log files in S3, such as CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, load balancer and WAF logs, through tables you define. Normal query results are saved as CSV in your results bucket. To get JSON instead, wrap the query in UNLOAD … WITH (format = ‘JSON’): Athena writes newline-delimited JSON to an S3 prefix, and you download it. Plenty of AWS teams keep months of logs in S3 and query them with Athena rather than shipping everything to a SIEM. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get a slice out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Permissions. You need to run Athena queries (athena:StartQueryExecution and related), read the table definitions in Glue, read the source bucket, and write to an export bucket. Add kms:Decrypt if the logs are encrypted with KMS. Know the table and its partitions. A CloudTrail table is usually partitioned by region and date, either with partition projection or with partitions you’ve added. Athena bills by data scanned, so filter on partitions every time. A query without them can scan years of logs. A workgroup. Athena runs queries in a workgroup with a results location. UNLOAD writes to its own target, but the workgroup still needs to be set up. Export with UNLOAD UNLOAD ( SELECT * FROM cloudtrail_logs WHERE region = 'eu-west-1' AND day = '2026/10/19' AND useridentity.arn LIKE '%suspicious-user%' ) TO 's3://my-athena-exports/ct-1019/' WITH (format = 'JSON', compression = 'NONE') Adapt the partition columns (region, day) to your table definition. The target prefix must be empty. items.summary_html:
Athena doesn’t store logs itself. It queries log files in S3, such as CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, load balancer and WAF logs, through tables you define. Normal query results are saved as CSV in your results bucket. To get JSON instead, wrap the query in UNLOAD … WITH (format = ‘JSON’): Athena writes newline-delimited JSON to an S3 prefix, and you download it.

Plenty of AWS teams keep months of logs in S3 and query them with Athena rather than shipping everything to a SIEM. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get a slice out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Permissions. You need to run Athena queries (athena:StartQueryExecution and related), read the table definitions in Glue, read the source bucket, and write to an export bucket. Add kms:Decrypt if the logs are encrypted with KMS.

Know the table and its partitions. A CloudTrail table is usually partitioned by region and date, either with partition projection or with partitions you’ve added. Athena bills by data scanned, so filter on partitions every time. A query without them can scan years of logs.

A workgroup. Athena runs queries in a workgroup with a results location. UNLOAD writes to its own target, but the workgroup still needs to be set up.

Export with UNLOAD 
UNLOAD (
  SELECT *
  FROM cloudtrail_logs
  WHERE region = 'eu-west-1'
    AND day = '2026/10/19'
    AND useridentity.arn LIKE '%suspicious-user%'
)
TO 's3://my-athena-exports/ct-1019/'
WITH (format = 'JSON', compression = 'NONE')

Adapt the partition columns (region, day) to your table definition. The target prefix must be empty.

From the command line:

QID=$(aws athena start-query-execution –work-group primary \
  –query-string “$(cat unload.sql)” \
  –query ‘QueryExecutionId’ –output text)

# wait until SUCCEEDED
until [ “$(aws athena get-query-execution –query-execution-id “$QID” \
  –query ‘QueryExecution.Status.State’ –output text)” = “SUCCEEDED” ]; do sleep 5; done

aws s3 cp s3://my-athena-exports/ct-1019/ ./ct-1019/ –recursive
zcat -f ./ct-1019/* > ct_1019.jsonl

zcat -f handles both compressed and uncompressed output, in case compression was left at the default. If the query fails, the wait loop never ends. Check for FAILED too if you script this regularly.

Why not get-query-results? It works, but it returns rows as lists of strings, 1,000 per page, which you then have to stitch back into objects. UNLOAD gives you clean JSON in one step.

Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. 
  2. Sanitize. 
  3. Review. 
When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFixQuery scans terabytesNo partition filterFilter on the partition columnsError about the output locationTarget prefix isn’t emptyUse a new prefixAccess DeniedMissing S3, Glue or KMS permissionCheck each one; KMS is the usual suspectZero rowsPartitions not loaded, or the wrong partition formatCheck partition projection or run MSCK REPAIR TABLEOutput files won’t open as textGZIP compressionUse zcat, or set compression = ‘NONE’
FAQ

Is this the same as Amazon Security Lake?

Security Lake uses Athena too, but with its own OCSF tables and Lake Formation permissions.

Can I export raw CloudTrail files instead?

Yes. If you only need whole days, copying the files from S3 is simpler. Athena earns its keep when you need to filter.

items.title: How to Export Snowflake Logs
items.summary: “Snowflake logs” means one of two things, and the export works the same for both. It can be security data your team stores in Snowflake tables. Or it can be Snowflake’s own audit trail, the SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE views such as LOGIN_HISTORY and QUERY_HISTORY. For small pulls, run the query in SnowSQL with JSON output. For anything bigger, unload with COPY INTO a stage using FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON), and download the files with GET. Snowflake’s own logs drew a lot of attention in 2024, when attackers used stolen credentials to log in to customer accounts that didn’t enforce MFA. Login and query history are now standard asks in an investigation. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get the data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Before you start Access to ACCOUNT_USAGE . By default, only ACCOUNTADMIN can read these views. Other roles need the IMPORTED PRIVILEGES grant on the SNOWFLAKE database, or one of its database roles. Latency and retention. ACCOUNT_USAGE views keep a year of history but lag behind by up to a couple of hours. For the last seven days with no lag, the INFORMATION_SCHEMA.LOGIN_HISTORY table function is an alternative. A warehouse. Queries and unloads need a running warehouse, and they consume credits. Filter by time. Option 1: SnowSQL with JSON output (small pulls) snowsql -q "SELECT * FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY WHERE EVENT_TIMESTAMP >= '2026-10-19' AND EVENT_TIMESTAMP < '2026-10-20'" \ -o output_format=json -o friendly=false -o timing=false > sf_logins_1019.json jq -c '.[]' sf_logins_1019.json > sf_logins_1019.jsonl Option 2: Unload to a stage (larger exports) COPY INTO @~/exports/login_history_1019/ FROM ( SELECT OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*) FROM SNOWFLAKE.ACCOUNT_USAGE.LOGIN_HISTORY WHERE EVENT_TIMESTAMP >= '2026-10-19' AND EVENT_TIMESTAMP < '2026-10-20' ) FILE_FORMAT = (TYPE = JSON COMPRESSION = NONE) OVERWRITE = TRUE; JSON unloads need a single column, which is why the query wraps each row in OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*). That function leaves out NULL fields. Then download from your user stage (@~): GET @~/exports/login_history_1019/ file:///tmp/sf_export/; and combine the files with cat /tmp/sf_export/* > sf_logins_1019.jsonl. The same pattern works for your own security tables. Swap in the table name and its timestamp column. What to look for in login history Look for failed logins (IS_SUCCESS = ‘NO’) in bursts, and password logins without a second factor (SECOND_AUTHENTICATION_FACTOR empty). Note logins from client IPs and client types you don’t recognize. Then follow those sessions into QUERY_HISTORY to see what was read. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Object does not exist or not authorized on ACCOUNT_USAGE Role lacks access to the SNOWFLAKE database Ask for IMPORTED PRIVILEGES or a database role Today’s logins missing ACCOUNT_USAGE latency Use INFORMATION_SCHEMA.LOGIN_HISTORY for recent events COPY INTO error about columns JSON unload needs one column Wrap rows in OBJECT_CONSTRUCT(*) Fields missing in the JSON OBJECT_CONSTRUCT drops NULL values Expected; absent means NULL GET fails Not run from SnowSQL or the Snowflake CLI GET runs from a client, not the web UI FAQ Can I do this in the web interface? Querying, yes. Downloads from the web interface aren’t JSON. The client route above gives you JSON lines. What about Snowflake event tables? Event tables hold logs and traces from your own functions and apps. Export them the same way as any table.

items.title: Criminal IP Launches New TI Feed App on Splunkbase for Automated Threat Detection
items.summary: Torrance, USA, November 11th, 2026, CyberNewswire Criminal IP , the AI-powered threat intelligence and attack surface management platform developed by AI SPERA, has launched the Criminal IP TI Feed app for Splunk. Available through Splunkbase , the app automatically correlates Criminal IP threat intelligence with firewall traffic logs collected in Splunk. The integration enables security teams to determine whether organizational assets communicated with malicious IP addresses and whether sessions were successfully established. It also expands Criminal IP’s existing Splunk ecosystem beyond individual IP lookups and fraud detection, helping SOC teams identify high-priority threats within their existing Splunk workflows. Connecting Threat Intelligence with Network Activity Security teams often receive large volumes of IP reputation alerts without enough context to determine whether a connection was attempted, blocked, unanswered, or successfully established. This can make it difficult to distinguish routine scanning from communications that require immediate investigation. The Criminal IP TI Feed app addresses this challenge by correlating inbound and outbound threat intelligence feeds with firewall traffic already indexed in Splunk. Network activity is classified according to observed session outcomes, including completed, unanswered, denied, neutral, and unknown connections. Severity is also determined using actual firewall activity. Detections without a completed session cannot exceed the watch tier, while critical detections indicate that a session with a malicious IP was successfully established. This helps analysts prioritize incidents with the greatest potential impact. Automated Correlation and Retrospective Detection The app downloads Criminal IP TI Feed data every three hours and runs correlation searches against firewall traffic every 10 minutes. Results are written to a dedicated summary index, allowing dashboards and alerts to operate without repeatedly searching large volumes of raw logs. A daily retrospective search compares the latest Criminal IP threat intelligence against the previous 30 days of firewall traffic. This helps identify historical communications with IP addresses that were not recognized as malicious when the activity originally occurred. Seven dashboards- Overview, Investigate, All Detections, IP Lookup, Trends, Alerts, and Health- provide visibility into affected assets, malicious IP addresses, traffic direction, session status, severity, detection history, and feed collection health. The app can also deliver consolidated Slack alerts grouped by malicious IP address and traffic direction. These alerts retain asset-level details, including session counts, timestamps, and transferred data, while throttling repeated notifications to reduce alert fatigue. Advancing Intelligence-Driven Security Operations By connecting external threat intelligence with actual network activity, the Criminal IP TI Feed app provides the context analysts need to identify which assets interacted with malicious infrastructure and which detections require immediate attention. Automating feed collection, log correlation, historical analysis, dashboards, and alerts reduces manual investigation and helps SOC teams respond to meaningful threats more efficiently. AI SPERA CEO Byungtak Kang stated, “Threat intelligence becomes significantly more actionable when connected to the network activity occurring inside an organization. The Criminal IP TI Feed app for Splunk helps security teams identify affected assets and prioritize incidents based on observed session behavior.” About Criminal IP Criminal IP is AI SPERA’s flagship cyber threat intelligence platform. Used in more than 150 countries, it provides comprehensive threat visibility through Criminal IP Search, Criminal IP ASM, Criminal IP FDS, and Criminal IP TI Feed. Criminal IP continues to expand its global security ecosystem through integrations and strategic partnerships. Its threat intelligence is also accessible through major cloud and data marketplaces, including Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, and Snowflake. Users can learn more and download the app from Splunkbase: Contact Michael Sena AI SPERA support@aispera.com

items.title: How to Export Databricks Logs
items.summary: As with Snowflake, “Databricks logs” can mean security data you keep in Delta tables, or Databricks’ own audit log in the system.access.audit system table. The simplest export for both is a notebook cell. Query with Spark SQL, write the result as JSON to a Unity Catalog volume, then download it with the Databricks CLI. Spark writes newline-delimited JSON, so the files are ready for upload. Databricks is increasingly used as a security data lake, and its audit log matters in its own right: who logged in, who created tokens, who changed permissions. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get the data out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Access. Reading system.access.audit needs the system schema enabled for your metastore and a SELECT grant from an account or metastore admin. For your own tables, you need the usual Unity Catalog grants. A volume to write to. You need a Unity Catalog volume you can write to, for example /Volumes/security/exports/logtotal, and the Databricks CLI configured on your machine. Compute. A notebook needs a cluster or serverless compute. Filter by date so you don’t scan more than you need. Export from a notebook (spark.sql(""" SELECT * FROM system.access.audit WHERE event_date = '2026-10-19' AND action_name IN ('login', 'tokenLogin', 'generateDbToken') """) .write.mode("overwrite") .json("/Volumes/security/exports/logtotal/audit_20261019")) Spark writes several part-*.json files plus marker files. Download and combine them: databricks fs cp -r dbfs:/Volumes/security/exports/logtotal/audit_20261019 ./audit_20261019 cat ./audit_20261019/part-*.json > databricks_audit_20261019.jsonl For your own security tables, change the query: select from your table and filter on its timestamp column. Without a notebook , the SQL Statement Execution API can run the same query on a SQL warehouse and return JSON. Rows come back as arrays, with the column names in a separate manifest, so you need an extra step to turn them into objects. For anything sizable, the notebook route is simpler. What to look for in the audit log Look at logins and token logins from unusual IP addresses, new personal access tokens, changes to permissions and group membership, and workspace or cluster configuration changes outside normal hours. Downloads of notebooks or results in bulk are worth a look too. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix system.access.audit not found System schema not enabled Ask an account admin to enable it Permission denied on the system table No SELECT grant Ask a metastore admin for the grant Can’t write to the volume Missing WRITE VOLUME Use a volume you can write to Download includes _SUCCESS and other files Spark marker files Combine only part-*.json Huge, slow query No date filter Filter on event_date FAQ Is the audit log also delivered to cloud storage? Workspaces can deliver audit logs to your own storage as well. If that’s set up, you can copy those files directly. Does this work on workspaces without Unity Catalog? The system tables need Unity Catalog. Older workspaces rely on audit log delivery to storage, and you write to DBFS paths instead of volumes.
