items.title: How to Export BigQuery Logs
items.summary: When security logs sit in BigQuery (from a Cloud Logging sink, a Google Workspace export or your own pipeline), export them with EXPORT DATA. It writes newline-delimited JSON to a Cloud Storage bucket, and you download that. For small results, bq query –format=json prints the rows directly. Either way, filter on the table’s time or partition column first, because BigQuery bills by data scanned. BigQuery is where many Google Cloud teams keep log history long after Cloud Logging’s default retention has passed. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get a slice out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal. Get Started For Free Before you start Permissions. You need to run jobs (BigQuery Job User), read the dataset (BigQuery Data Viewer), and write to the export bucket. Know the tables. A Cloud Logging sink to BigQuery creates tables named after the logs, for example cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity, often partitioned by timestamp. Workspace exports have their own schema. Check the cost first. Add –dry_run to a bq query to see how many bytes it would scan. If the number makes you wince, add a tighter time filter. Option 1: EXPORT DATA to Cloud Storage EXPORT DATA OPTIONS ( uri = 'gs://my-bq-exports/audit-20261019/*.json', format = 'JSON', overwrite = true ) AS SELECT * FROM `my-project.audit_logs.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity` WHERE timestamp >= TIMESTAMP('2026-10-19') AND timestamp < TIMESTAMP('2026-10-20'); The URI needs a wildcard (*), because BigQuery may write several files. Download and combine them: gcloud storage cp 'gs://my-bq-exports/audit-20261019/*' ./audit-20261019/ cat ./audit-20261019/*.json > bq_audit_20261019.jsonl Option 2: bq query for small results bq query --nouse_legacy_sql --format=json --max_rows=10000 \ 'SELECT * FROM `my-project.audit_logs.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity` WHERE timestamp >= TIMESTAMP("2026-10-19") AND timestamp < TIMESTAMP("2026-10-20")' \ > bq_audit_small.json jq -c '.[]' bq_audit_small.json > bq_audit_small.jsonl –format=json prints a JSON array, which jq flattens to one row per line. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. Sanitize. Review. When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Query scans the whole table No filter on the partition or time column Filter on timestamp (or _PARTITIONTIME) EXPORT DATA fails on the URI No wildcard in the URI Use …/*.json Permission denied writing to the bucket Missing Storage object create rights Grant write access on the bucket bq output cut at 100 rows Default –max_rows Set –max_rows, or use EXPORT DATA Nested fields look odd Repeated and nested columns keep their structure Expected; it’s still valid JSON FAQ Is this the same as exporting from Cloud Logging? No. Cloud Logging has its own export. This guide is for logs that already live in BigQuery tables. Can I export a whole table without a query Yes: bq extract –destination_format NEWLINE_DELIMITED_JSON copies a table or a partition to Cloud Storage. For investigations, a filtered query is usually better.

It writes newline-delimited JSON to a Cloud Storage bucket, and you download that. For small results, bq query –format=json prints the rows directly. Either way, filter on the table’s time or partition column first, because BigQuery bills by data scanned.

BigQuery is where many Google Cloud teams keep log history long after Cloud Logging’s default retention has passed. Prime Core has more than 24,000 unique detection rules, mapped to 676 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Below is how to get a slice out, sanitize it, and investigate it for free in LogTotal.

Get Started For Free

Before you start

Permissions. You need to run jobs (BigQuery Job User), read the dataset (BigQuery Data Viewer), and write to the export bucket.

Know the tables. A Cloud Logging sink to BigQuery creates tables named after the logs, for example cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity, often partitioned by timestamp. Workspace exports have their own schema.

Check the cost first. Add –dry_run to a bq query to see how many bytes it would scan. If the number makes you wince, add a tighter time filter.

Option 1: EXPORT DATA to Cloud Storage 
EXPORT DATA OPTIONS (
  uri = 'gs://my-bq-exports/audit-20261019/*.json',
  format = 'JSON',
  overwrite = true
) AS
SELECT *
FROM `my-project.audit_logs.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity`
WHERE timestamp >= TIMESTAMP('2026-10-19') AND timestamp < TIMESTAMP('2026-10-20');

The URI needs a wildcard (*), because BigQuery may write several files. Download and combine them:

gcloud storage cp 'gs://my-bq-exports/audit-20261019/*' ./audit-20261019/
cat ./audit-20261019/*.json > bq_audit_20261019.jsonl
Option 2: bq query for small results 
bq query --nouse_legacy_sql --format=json --max_rows=10000 \
  'SELECT * FROM `my-project.audit_logs.cloudaudit_googleapis_com_activity`
   WHERE timestamp >= TIMESTAMP("2026-10-19") AND timestamp < TIMESTAMP("2026-10-20")' \
  > bq_audit_small.json

jq -c '.[]' bq_audit_small.json > bq_audit_small.jsonl

–format=json prints a JSON array, which jq flattens to one row per line.

Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal
  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file.
  2. Sanitize. 
  3. Review. 
When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFixQuery scans the whole tableNo filter on the partition or time columnFilter on timestamp (or _PARTITIONTIME)EXPORT DATA fails on the URINo wildcard in the URIUse …/*.jsonPermission denied writing to the bucketMissing Storage object create rightsGrant write access on the bucketbq output cut at 100 rowsDefault –max_rowsSet –max_rows, or use EXPORT DATANested fields look oddRepeated and nested columns keep their structureExpected; it’s still valid JSON
FAQ

Is this the same as exporting from Cloud Logging?

No. Cloud Logging has its own export. This guide is for logs that already live in BigQuery tables.

Can I export a whole table without a query

Yes: bq extract –destination_format NEWLINE_DELIMITED_JSON copies a table or a partition to Cloud Storage. For investigations, a filtered query is usually better.

items.title: CVE-2026-124194: Microsoft Outlook Zero-Day Exploited to Steal NTLM Hashes
items.summary: Microsoft has patched CVE-2026-124194, an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability in Microsoft Outlook that can expose a user’s NTLMv2 authentication information when a specially crafted message file is opened. Microsoft classifies the issue as a spoofing vulnerability and rates it Moderate with a CVSS 3.1 score of 6.5. The vulnerability allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to send a malicious message file and convince a victim to open it in an affected Outlook version. Outlook can then connect to an attacker-controlled network location without displaying the external-content warning users would normally expect. During that connection, Windows may expose NTLMv2 authentication information that can potentially be abused to impersonate the victim. Contact Sales Microsoft confirmed that CVE-2026-124194 has already been exploited in attacks. However, the company has not disclosed the threat actors involved, the scale of the campaign, victim organizations, delivery infrastructure, or whether the stolen authentication material has been used for subsequent lateral movement or account compromise. The flaw was addressed as part of Microsoft’s November 2026 Patch Tuesday release on November 10. Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Microsoft Office LTSC 2021, and Microsoft Office LTSC 2024 on both 32-bit and x64 systems. CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 10, confirming evidence of active exploitation and establishing November 24, 2026 as the remediation deadline for applicable U.S. federal agencies. Security teams can use SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to operationalize threat intelligence, identify suspicious Outlook and NTLM activity, and accelerate detection engineering and threat hunting across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments. Detect CVE-2026-124194 by correlating Outlook activity with unexpected outbound SMB connections, NTLM authentication attempts to external systems, suspicious message-file execution, and subsequent credential or identity abuse. Detection content may not be available for every CVE. Check the SOC Prime Platform for current coverage. If relevant detections are not yet available, check again as new threat intelligence and detection content are continuously added. CVE-2026-124194 analysis CVE-2026-124194 affects Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise, Microsoft Office LTSC 2021, and Microsoft Office LTSC 2024. Microsoft assigns the flaw a CVSS 3.1 score of 6.5 with the vector AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N, reflecting remote accessibility, low attack complexity, no required attacker privileges, required user interaction, and high confidentiality impact. The vulnerability is classified under CWE-356, Product UI Does Not Warn User of Unsafe Actions. In practical terms, Outlook does not display the warning that should normally alert a user before the application accesses potentially dangerous external content. Exploitation begins with a specially crafted Outlook message file delivered to the target. The attacker does not need an account on the victim’s system or Microsoft 365 tenant, but the victim must open the malicious file. Microsoft specifically states that the Preview Pane is not an attack vector, meaning simply displaying the message in Outlook’s preview interface is not sufficient. Once the file is opened, Outlook can initiate a connection to a network location controlled by the attacker without presenting the usual external-content warning. This is significant because Windows environments can automatically attempt NTLM authentication when accessing remote resources. The resulting challenge-response exchange can expose the user’s NTLMv2 authentication hash to the remote server. An NTLMv2 hash is not the user’s plaintext password. However, possession of authentication material can create several follow-on risks depending on the environment and the attacker’s capabilities. BleepingComputer notes that captured hashes may be subjected to offline password cracking, while Microsoft’s advisory warns that the leaked authentication information can potentially be used to authenticate as the victim. This makes the vulnerability particularly relevant to enterprise environments that still rely heavily on NTLM for file shares, legacy applications, remote resources, or internal authentication workflows. The CVSS score of 6.5 may initially appear relatively modest for a zero-day under active exploitation. The score reflects the fact that exploitation requires user interaction and primarily affects confidentiality rather than directly delivering code execution, integrity loss, or service disruption. Operational risk is nevertheless considerably higher because Microsoft has already observed exploitation and CISA has independently added the flaw to KEV. Security teams should therefore prioritize exploitation status over CVSS alone when determining remediation urgency. The CVE record identifies the following affected and fixed versions: Product Affected versions Fixed version Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise Vulnerable releases before the applicable November security update Current Office Security Release Microsoft Office LTSC 2021 Earlier than 16.0.14334.21048 16.0.14334.21048 Microsoft Office LTSC 2024 Earlier than 16.0.17932.21140 16.0.17932.21140 Both 32-bit and x64 installations are affected. Organizations using Microsoft 365 Apps should rely on Microsoft’s Office Security Releases information because build numbers differ across servicing channels. Microsoft published CVE-2026-124194 on November 10, 2026 and released the corresponding security updates through Patch Tuesday. The vulnerability was not publicly disclosed before a fix became available. Microsoft credits a researcher using the moniker “nono” and security researcher Benoît Sevens with discovering or reporting the issue. SecurityWeek notes that Microsoft’s acknowledgment for Sevens references the use of Anthropic’s Claude AI model during the research. The available sources do not provide the exact date on which the vulnerability was privately discovered or initially reported to Microsoft. The CVE-2026-124194 PoC landscape remains less important than the confirmed exploitation status. Microsoft and the two supplied reports do not provide public exploit code or detailed reproduction instructions. Some third-party exploit aggregators have produced conflicting signals regarding newly published proof-of-concept material, so defenders should not rely on public PoC availability when assessing risk. Active exploitation has already been independently established through Microsoft and CISA. For CVE-2026-124194 detection, defenders should monitor endpoint and network activity together. One particularly valuable signal is OUTLOOK.EXE initiating SMB traffic toward an external or previously unseen destination shortly after a user opens an Outlook message file. Outbound TCP port 445 traffic deserves particular attention. Microsoft recommends blocking outbound SMB traffic to the internet as a general defense-in-depth control because it can prevent internal devices from sending SMB data directly to external hosts. Security teams can also review Microsoft’s NTLM Operational log under Applications and Services Logs/Microsoft/Windows/NTLM and audit outgoing NTLM authentication. Microsoft provides a policy specifically designed to audit or deny outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers. Useful behavioral hunting pivots include: Outlook initiating unexpected external SMB connections. NTLM authentication attempts toward internet destinations. Successful authentication to internal services shortly after suspicious Outlook activity. Message-file activity associated with unusual external network connections. Repeated authentication attempts involving the same compromised identity. New logons from systems or IP addresses inconsistent with the user’s normal activity. Defenders should avoid treating every outbound SMB or NTLM connection as proof of exploitation. Both technologies can still exist legitimately in enterprise environments. The strongest detections will correlate Outlook activity, destination reputation, user interaction, NTLM telemetry, and subsequent authentication behavior. Microsoft has not published campaign-specific CVE-2026-124194 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, attachment hashes, sender addresses, or filenames associated with the observed attacks. The identity of the attackers and their targeting remain undisclosed. This means organizations currently need to prioritize behavior-based hunting rather than static IOC matching. CVE-2026-124194 Mitigation The primary remediation is to install Microsoft’s November 2026 Office security updates immediately. Office LTSC 2021 installations should be updated to build 16.0.14334.21048 or later, while Office LTSC 2024 installations should run 16.0.17932.21140 or later. Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise users should verify that their servicing channel has received the corresponding current security release. Because exploitation is already occurring, organizations should verify successful deployment rather than assuming automated Office updates have reached every device. Administrators should take the following actions: Inventory Microsoft Outlook installations across managed endpoints. Identify Microsoft 365 Apps, Office LTSC 2021, and Office LTSC 2024 systems that have not received the November security update. Deploy the corrected builds immediately and verify installation. Review endpoints that remained vulnerable while exploitation was active. Block unnecessary outbound SMB traffic to the internet. Audit outgoing NTLM authentication and reduce NTLM usage wherever operationally possible. Investigate unusual Outlook-to-network activity and unexpected authentication attempts. Educate users not to open unsolicited Outlook message files or attachments from untrusted sources. Blocking outbound SMB on TCP port 445 provides an important additional protection layer. Microsoft explicitly recommends preventing SMB traffic from leaving the corporate network unless there is a specific operational requirement for internet-hosted SMB services. Organizations should also consider restricting NTLM. Windows provides the Network security: Restrict NTLM: Outgoing NTLM traffic to remote servers policy, which can first be configured in audit mode to identify dependencies before administrators begin blocking authentication. Abruptly disabling NTLM across an enterprise can break legacy applications and workflows. Organizations should therefore audit usage, identify legitimate dependencies, implement required exceptions, and progressively move authentication toward Kerberos or other stronger mechanisms. If suspicious exploitation is identified, merely installing the update is not sufficient to close the incident. Security teams should identify the affected identity and review authentication activity occurring after the suspected message file was opened. Look for unusual SMB connections, remote logons, lateral movement, access to file shares, VPN authentication, cloud sign-ins, and other services that accept the affected credentials. Where evidence suggests that authentication information was exposed or successfully abused, reset the relevant password and revoke active sessions according to the organization’s identity-response procedures. Additional privileged credentials accessible to the affected account should also be investigated. Endpoint, proxy, firewall, email, EDR, and identity logs should be preserved before remediation when compromise is suspected. Correlating these sources can help reconstruct the sequence from phishing delivery through NTLM disclosure and possible subsequent authentication. CISA added the vulnerability to KEV on November 10 and requires applicable federal agencies to remediate it by November 24, 2026. CISA lists known ransomware campaign use as unknown. FAQ What is CVE-2026-124194 and how does it work? CVE-2026-124194 is an actively exploited Microsoft Outlook spoofing vulnerability caused by Outlook failing to warn users before performing a potentially unsafe external-content action. An attacker can send a specially crafted message file and convince a user to open it. Outlook may then connect to an attacker-controlled network resource and expose the user’s NTLMv2 authentication information without displaying the expected warning. When was CVE-2026-124194 first discovered? Microsoft publicly disclosed and patched the vulnerability on November 10, 2026. The company credits researchers “nono” and Benoît Sevens, but the available public reports do not specify the precise date of the original private discovery. The vulnerability was not publicly known before Microsoft released the fix. What is the impact of CVE-2026-124194 on systems? Successful exploitation can disclose a user’s NTLMv2 authentication hash to an attacker-controlled server. Attackers may potentially use the captured authentication information to impersonate the victim, attempt offline password recovery, or gain unauthorized access to services that accept the compromised credentials. The vulnerability does not itself provide direct remote code execution. Can CVE-2026-124194 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Microsoft has confirmed active exploitation, and CISA added the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 10, 2026. Systems running vulnerable Outlook versions remain at risk until the corresponding Office security update is installed. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-124194? Install Microsoft’s November 2026 Office security updates immediately, verify that affected Outlook installations are running fixed builds, block unnecessary outbound SMB traffic, and audit or restrict outgoing NTLM authentication. Users should also avoid opening unsolicited Outlook message files from unknown sources. Security teams should continue monitoring Microsoft’s guidance for updated details for CVE-2026-124194 as additional information about the exploitation campaign becomes available.

items.title: Meet the Magnet Forensics Training Team: Grant Hazell
items.summary: Our Training team continues to grow. In our latest “Meet the Forensic Trainer” blog, meet Grant Hazell, based on Perth, Australia! Want a chance to learn from Grant in the classroom? Learn more about what courses are offered through our Training & Certification portal . 1. Tell us about your life before becoming a Trainer. After a long career within military and policing environments, a move into training with Magnet Forensics was something I was hoping to achieve. I served for six years with the UK Armed Forces, before joining Suffolk Police in the UK in 2001. After seven years, I moved to the other side of the world and continued my policing career with Western Australia Police for 18 years, working in frontline response, education and digital forensics environments. 2. What made you want to be a Trainer? I have always enjoyed classroom environments and explaining things in a way which people can understand and grasp. I thrive on helping students progress and use the material they’ve learned in a practical and meaningful way. Being a qualified counsellor, I’m also very keen on looking after students’ emotional welfare regarding the anxiety and stress of training, especially in the face of difficult content and the sometimes difficult dynamic of training when personal life issues arise. 3. What type of training have you taken part in personally? What is your favorite part of the role? I have previously trained police personnel in legal, law and policy matters, ensuring they were fully aware of the powers and policies which underpin the role they perform. Since being employed with Magnet Forensics, I have primarily trained students in mobile device forensics, notably the GK200 course. 4. What excites you the most about a new class? The opportunity to travel to new places and meet new people, getting a feel for their needs both in an operational and educational perspective. 5. Do you ever learn anything from the students? Being new to the role, I know the only way to improve is to be the classroom – responding to questions, researching, learning the manuals and making mistakes. Mistakes can be daunting as an instructor, but they are crucial to self-development and ongoing professionalism. 6. Is there a particular moment that stands out the most to you in your career in the classroom? I recently taught my first solo GK200 class in Parramatta, NSW. The class was very diverse regarding experience and the questions were challenging. I found the entire experience very rewarding and although uncomfortable at times, crucial for my confidence. 7. What do students get out of training in person that they can’t get on their own? Students get direct access to not only my knowledge and experience, but that of the entire organization. Teaching in person also provides a valuable ‘personal touch’ and the ability to assess all students to ensure they’re grasping concepts and haven’t been left behind. 8. How prepared do you feel students are to use Magnet Forensics products after taking the training course? Every day, I plan on ensuring that the students can learn at least one thing they didn’t know prior to the lesson commencing. If they can understand the settings of Magnet Graykey, configure it correctly for their desired output, and prevent one device from rebooting and losing access to data, I consider that a success. 9. What is most unique about Magnet Forensics’ approach to training? The personal touch. Not only do Magnet Forensics trainers have a wealth of professional and technical knowledge, but they’re also able to relate to students and content, using real-world examples and lived experience. 10. Why do you think certification is important to examiners? Certification proves to the courts and other interested parties that an operator has the proficiency to use the forensic tool/methodology. It demonstrates that a student has not only attended a course but has personally invested in their own development by subjecting themselves to testing. 11. How do you manage to keep up with the latest trends in digital forensics? Being involved in conversations with other trainers has always been one of the best sources of information. Speaking to previous law enforcement colleagues about frontline trends, ensuring our own qualifications are current and displaying an enthusiasm to learn new material is crucial to maintaining currency. 12. What trends do you see coming down the pipeline in digital forensics? The trends will vary widely across the practice of digital forensics. The challenges of certain specialized domains such as vehicle systems and IoT analysis will continue to grow exponentially.

I recently taught my first solo GK200 class in Parramatta, NSW. The class was very diverse regarding experience and the questions were challenging. I found the entire experience very rewarding and although uncomfortable at times, crucial for my confidence.

7. What do students get out of training in person that they can’t get on their own?

Students get direct access to not only my knowledge and experience, but that of the entire organization. Teaching in person also provides a valuable ‘personal touch’ and the ability to assess all students to ensure they’re grasping concepts and haven’t been left behind.

8. How prepared do you feel students are to use Magnet Forensics products after taking the training course?

Every day, I plan on ensuring that the students can learn at least one thing they didn’t know prior to the lesson commencing. If they can understand the settings of Magnet Graykey, configure it correctly for their desired output, and prevent one device from rebooting and losing access to data, I consider that a success.

9. What is most unique about Magnet Forensics’ approach to training?

The personal touch. Not only do Magnet Forensics trainers have a wealth of professional and technical knowledge, but they’re also able to relate to students and content, using real-world examples and lived experience.

10. Why do you think certification is important to examiners?

Certification proves to the courts and other interested parties that an operator has the proficiency to use the forensic tool/methodology. It demonstrates that a student has not only attended a course but has personally invested in their own development by subjecting themselves to testing.

11. How do you manage to keep up with the latest trends in digital forensics?

Being involved in conversations with other trainers has always been one of the best sources of information. Speaking to previous law enforcement colleagues about frontline trends, ensuring our own qualifications are current and displaying an enthusiasm to learn new material is crucial to maintaining currency.

12. What trends do you see coming down the pipeline in digital forensics?

The trends will vary widely across the practice of digital forensics. The challenges of certain specialized domains such as vehicle systems and IoT analysis will continue to grow exponentially.

As you probably know, the software can verify the integrity and authenticity of digital images and videos. Present video authentication findings with supporting evidence. Generate structured Amped Authenticate reports with relevant images, plots, and tables, and export batch analysis results when examining multiple files. How To: Generate Forensic Authentication Reports with Amped Authenticate Set up your case. Open Amped Authenticate, select Image or Video mode, and load the evidence you need to examine. Run the relevant analysis filters. Use Visual Inspection, file and metadata analysis, local forensic filters, or video compression analysis according to your case requirements. Open Project Properties to enter case and author information, and select the images, plots, and tables you want to include. Generate and supplement your report. Use Tools > Generate Report to produce your document, then export additional metadata logs or batch analysis tables where necessary. How to Structure an Authentication Report for Court Choosing the Authentication Report Format When conducting any forensic analysis case, I spend some time planning the analysis and the presentation format before I even start the analysis itself. I do this because I know that I may otherwise end up doing a lot of work before I realise that I have chosen an inadequate presentation method. Everything is dictated by the questions that are being asked of the multimedia evidence and the complexity of the case. This is a list of such considerations: Image or Video Authentication? The amount and type of reports you produce will depend on the type of multimedia evidence you are analysing. Does the case involve many clips? If so, you may want to consider outputting tables in Amped Authenticate as well as the conventional report. Are you comparing questioned images with reference images in your analysis? Consider using the reference image tab and outputting comparative tables in Amped Authenticate as well as the conventional report. Are you highlighting visual inconsistencies? Consider using the Annotate Bookmark function in the Project Panel. Choose the report output mode. My personal preference is the HTML format. This does require you to include a folder with the included images and plots, but it allows hyperlinking much better than other formats (you can link to specific paragraphs or sections of the Amped Authenticate report). What Should a Forensic Authentication Report Include? I will go through these in more detail, but when you produce an analytical report for court, it is imperative that it follows criminal justice guidelines and a set structure. I would expect an admissible report to have, at the very least, the following sections: An introductory page with exhibit and case references. A witness statement and/or an expert witness declaration , listing the expert’s duties and responsibilities to the court. An index of contents. A summary of the case circumstances, instructions and final conclusions for quick reference. A list of the exhibits received and integrity verification (copying, hash verification etc.) An explanation of the methodologies used for the analysis : this should be explained in lay terms as much as possible (use practical examples, if necessary). A chronology of the analysis conducted with reference to the instructions received. Consider different chapters to address each set of instructions. The significance of your findings and how much weight do they lend to your final conclusions. Your final conclusions , based on the objective and factual analysis that you have conducted and your expert opinion on how it answers the questions raised by the evidence. Annexes containing your full curriculum vitae, any publications relevant to your analysis and further explanations of complex technical aspects of the analysis. Authenticate’s report is great at explaining the processes and tests conducted on the evidence but obviously cannot contain all of the above sections in full. You can either produce an analytical report and create hyperlinks to relevant sections in the Authenticate report, or you may even export it to an editable format (such as docx) and manually add any extra analytical content. The choice is yours. Analysis and Report Generation Let’s look at a case in which a number of images showing a theft were sent to the Police by the suspect himself. The image shows a person going through an inventory of items in a metal warehouse before he proceeds to remove a number of steel brackets. The suspect claims he is not the person depicted in the image and that’s his alibi. This information is important to us because, like in most cases, it helps direct our image analysis and investigation in the right direction. Open Authenticate and load your clip into the viewer. Remember that you can analyze multiple images in your AAP project, so you can create one report that contains the analysis of as many images as you like. I’ve loaded one of the images that I have been asked to assess for any traditional or AI manipulation. I have more images to analyze, but I will do one at a time. Try and follow the workflow chronology set out in the filters panel. There is a good reason why filters are in the order they are listed in the program interface. Visual Analysis: Identify and Annotate Suspicious Image Details I’ve added the Visual Inspection filter to my Project panel (step 1 in the image above), which I usually do as standard. This will ensure the original image is digitally printed in full in the report . In this instance, by zooming in to several areas of the image (hovering over the image and using the scroll wheel of the mouse), I noticed a visual anomaly with the right eye of the subject. It really looks more like a shark eye to me than a human eye, so I annotated the bookmark by clicking the “Annotate bookmark” button (step 2 in the image above). I used a Magnify object to enlarge this suspicious area of the image and also used a yellow arrow to highlight the eye in question (step 3 in the image above). When I generate the report later, t he bookmark will be annotated inside the document . If you wish to add some notes or commentary to your bookmarks, you can do so by double-clicking and adding a bookmark description, as shown above. In this instance, I also changed the bookmark status to “warning” as this bookmark clearly shows some suspicious findings. This is now red color coded due to its gravity and will also be highlighted in red in the report . File and Metadata Analysis: Compare Questioned and Reference Images In this instance, I was also given a reference image to compare with the questioned images. Authenticate has some very powerful comparison tools, which can highlight expected and unexpected differences (highlighted in black and red, respectively) with pretty much every filter output. Below, you can see I have conducted a file analysis showing metadata for both the questioned and reference image and their differences in every field. I then added this filter as a bookmark, marked its status yellow (“To check”) and added a description, explaining the reference image contains a thumbnail, camera make and model and time/date of creation, which the questioned image does not contain. Local Forensic Analysis: Investigate Image Manipulation Indicators Filters from the Local Analysis group can provide some factual evidence of manipulated regions in the image as they rely on strong forensic principles to output their results. In this instance, I applied an ELA (Error Level Analysis) filter. It shows the local differences between pixels of the original image and pixels of the same image resaved at a different JPEG quality to reveal local traces of JPEG quality differences. Our initial suspicion about the strange appearance of the eye is now backed up by strong evidence of this region having been added to the original image. Just like before, I have magnified the relevant area of the filter output and added a bookmark description to feature in my report . My approach with Local Analysis filters is to try and back up every finding with several filters within the same group. One filter alone can reveal inconsistencies that may be accounted for by technical reasons, rather than actual deliberate manipulation. It is important to remain unbiased and collect as much evidence as possible to strengthen the weight of your suspicions. In this instance, I found the RAW Conversion Watermark filter also points to the same area of the subject as inconsistent (shown above). But this filter is considerably different than the ELA . It highlights areas of the image not containing the invisible Adobe watermark that is introduced in original images when converted from RAW to JPEG. The fact that it highlights the same area as the ELA can really not be a coincidence. Image Deepfake Detection Analysis Amped Authenticate also features two AI-based deepfake detection filters. One analyzes the entire image for signs of content generated by diffusion models, while the other examines facial regions for signs of content generated by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Both filters provide a confidence score to help assess whether the analyzed content may be AI-generated. In this instance, the diffusion model deepfake filter outputted a confidence score of 0.51 (where 0 indicates no confidence at all, and 1.0 maximum confidence). However, this could be accounted for by the size of the manipulated region, which is too small compared to the rest of the image. As we are unbiased, it is important to state that this could also equally mean that the image is not a deepfake at all. The GAN Deepfake Detection filter was also applied and this reveals maximum confidence that the face of the subject has not been generated by a GAN. Mind that this does not necessarily mean that the face of the subject is real, simply that it has not been generated by this model. It could have been generated by a different model (for instance, a diffusion model), OR, quite simply, it could be a real face. Remember also that the Deepfake Detection filters are quick and easy to use, but should not be your only analysis tool, as they essentially output a machine opinion. In this case, the face of the person has been changed from the original image and generated by a diffusion model. It is likely that the manipulated area was too small to be detected by the filter. Other filters, though, using a more solid forensic approach, correctly detected the manipulated area. Below, you can see the original image before manipulation. How to Generate an Image Authentication Report Once you have added all the relevant bookmarks with descriptions and status flags, you can go to the File menu and select the “Project Properties” option. Here, you can add case and author information as well as customize the size of your report illustrations. You can then go to the Tools menu and select the “Generate Report” option. Select your preferred output format (HTML in this case) and customize other options such as adding hash values and file information, as well as the agency logo. Below, you can admire the key areas of our report, with all the factual data gathered and our expert opinions on the significance of the findings. Preparing a Video Authentication Case Let’s switch to video authentication for a little while. If we want to work on a video case, we need to use the Amped Authenticate Video Mode. The analysis and report generation are similar to the Image mode. However, we obviously need to perform some tests that are relevant to digital video, such as the analysis of compression and continuity. When preparing the report, we can include selected frames from different analyses to illustrate our findings. We can start by clicking on the Visual Inspection filter and bookmarking the frames we want to illustrate in the report. In the example below, I note a suspicious rectangular outline surrounding the area of the visual timestamp. I have bookmarked a couple of frames where this outline is more visible and adjusted the levels to increase the contrast in that area. These frames will all be printed in the report later . Video Metadata Analysis: Examine File History and Export Logs File and metadata analysis in the Video Mode is done via the Advanced File Info utility at the top of the filter list. For those of you familiar with Amped FIVE, this is the same utility available in that application. Unlike the Image Mode, the output of the utility does not go into the report. However, the utility offers a number of different ways to export your data into a disclosable document. Let’s return to the video we previously examined using the Visual Inspection filter. In the MediaInfo tab of Advanced File Info, we noticed that the file’s creation date is October 17, 2026. However, the timestamp displayed in the video indicates that the original recording was made on September 3, 2026, as shown above. This discrepancy suggests that the video may not be the original recording and could have been re-saved or exported at a later date. We documented this observation by clicking the Save to Log File button. We have also saved the contents of the Exif log, as this contains numerous indications that the video has been edited with Adobe Premiere Pro, as shown below. It is all starting to look very suspicious! Video Compression Analysis: Investigate Continuity and Editing Indicators We then performed a compression analysis to investigate the video further. Our initial suspicions were supported by additional evidence, which we can present in the report in the form of plots and compelling illustrations . We clicked on the Motion Vectors filter and then on the “Generate Plot and Table” button in the filter settings. The plot showed very high motion vector activity at around frame 300. This is consistent with a visual “jump cut” on the subject with the green shirt, even though the timestamp at the top right corner is contiguous. We then added frame 307 as a bookmark, added a description explaining the anomaly and marked the status as “warning”. We ticked both the image and the plot options to ensure both are digitally printed in the report . And finally, we clicked on the Macroblocks filter and found a few frames with suspicious intra-block activity (shown in purple in the image below) on the superior aspect of the frame. This suggests the frames in question were originally I-frames. When re-encoded, they left traces behind in the area where the alleged manipulation had occurred. In this instance, I only included the image and the table as no plot is applicable to my analysis . Video Deepfake Detection Analysis We finally clicked on the Diffusion Model Deepfake filter and ran the analysis to check if any portions of the video may have been generated synthetically. The analysis came back negative for all the frames of the video. In this instance, we added any frame as a bookmark and simply selected the plot and table for the report (as shown below). How to Generate a Video Authentication Report Once the bookmarks were reviewed and checked in the Project panel, I simply clicked on the Project Properties button to add case information and then navigated to the Tools menu and selected the option “Generate Report” (as shown above). As you can see, the report is quite comprehensive and contains all the relevant illustrations, plots and tables relevant to my analysis. I also included the Advanced File Info data, which I printed to PDF from the log files generated by Amped Authenticate. This allowed me to provide factual evidence that, although the video was not manipulated by any form of AI image generation, it had been edited with Adobe Premiere Pro. The actual crime (theft by employee) was cut from the video and the visual timestamp in the top right corner was laid as a rectangular crop to make it look as if the video was contiguous. Exporting Batch Analysis Results and Tabular Data in Amped Authenticate As mentioned earlier, there may be instances where your analysis involves multiple files (images or videos). You may have been asked to separate images that have been possibly manipulated from camera originals. Or, you may have been asked to conduct a batch comparison of images or a mass deepfake detection analysis. Authenticate’s report already supports multiple images or videos, but you may also want to produce tables containing data in a more granular format. Authenticate supports this workflow wonderfully. Let’s take a look at a case where I have been asked to perform camera ballistics on a folder full of images. Batch Image Analysis: Export PRNU Camera Identification Results The best thing to do when working with multiple clips is to simply load one of them in the evidence tab. Various filters offer options to analyze or compare all images in a folder and where this is the case, there will be a button at the top of the viewer. The filter will then output the data in a table that can be exported as an HTML or Excel file simply by right-clicking on it and selecting the appropriate option. The image below comes from a folder seized from a suspect’s computer. We also have his digital camera which we used to capture some reference images. Our goal is to determine whether any of the recovered images were taken with that specific camera, as some contain child sexual abuse material (CSAM). We applied the PRNU Identification filter from the Camera Identification group, loaded the camera reference pattern from the file generated with the reference images and immediately found the loaded image as positive with a high PCE (peak correlation energy) value. We then used the arrow buttons in the evidence tab to navigate to the other questioned images contained in the same folder. We found a second image positive, whilst all the others came back as negative. We added a bookmark for each of the two positive images so that the PRNU data will be shown in the report for both. But, we then clicked on the “Analyze all Images in the Evidence Folder” button and this outputted a table containing the results for all the images in the folder. I then right-clicked on the table and selected the “export as HTML” option. This wrote an HTML standalone file which I then linked to my master report. Conclusions We come to the end of this article and of the whole Court Presentation series. We really hope that this series gave you some food for thought when it comes to presenting forensic multimedia evidence in court. Remember, you may have found compelling evidence that images have been tampered with or manipulated with AI image generation. However, if you can’t present the factual evidence supporting your conclusions, even the strongest findings may fail to stand up to scrutiny in court. Amped products are designed to help you present and report your findings clearly and effectively, demonstrating to the trier of fact how your expert opinions are supported by scientific evidence. Throughout this series, we’ve explored practical workflows to help you achieve exactly that. If you would like to practice firsthand on the many presentation workflows we have in Amped Authenticate, Amped FIVE and Amped Replay, make sure you check out our training page where a number of courses relevant to court presentation are on offer at an affordable price. Until the next time, my friends, stay safe and take care. FAQ: Reporting Image and Video Authentication Findings for Court What should a forensic image or video authentication report include? Your report should clearly document the evidence examined, its integrity, the forensic methods applied, your findings, and the reasoning behind your conclusions. Depending on the applicable legal requirements, you may also need to include case references, an expert witness declaration, and supporting documentation. Amped Authenticate helps you generate technical reports with analysis results, annotated images, plots, and tables that you can incorporate into your final expert report. How can I document suspected image manipulation in Amped Authenticate? You can use Visual Inspection to identify suspicious details, then apply relevant forensic filters to investigate potential inconsistencies. Use bookmarks, annotations, and descriptive notes to highlight important findings. Where appropriate, compare questioned images with reference images and use multiple analysis methods to support your conclusions. How can I present evidence of possible video editing or manipulation? You can combine visual inspection with metadata, compression, and continuity analysis to identify potential editing indicators. Amped Authenticate allows you to document suspicious frames, highlight anomalies, and include relevant plots and tables in your report. You should explain what each finding indicates and consider whether alternative explanations are possible. Can deepfake detection results alone prove that an image or video has been manipulated? No. AI-based deepfake detection filters provide indications based on the models and methods they use, but their results are not conclusive proof of authenticity or manipulation. A negative result does not necessarily exclude AI-generated content. You should interpret detection scores alongside other forensic findings and clearly explain their limitations in your report. How can I include video metadata analysis results in my forensic report? In Amped Authenticate’s Video mode, you can examine file information and metadata using the Advanced File Info utility. Since these results are not automatically included in the generated report, you can export the relevant information to log files and incorporate it into your supporting documentation. Can I export forensic analysis results for multiple images or videos? Yes. Amped Authenticate supports the analysis of multiple files and the generation of reports containing their findings. For supported filters, you can also perform batch analysis and export tabular results in HTML or Excel format. This is particularly useful when comparing numerous images, conducting camera identification analysis, or reviewing results across larger evidence collections. https://blog.ampedsoftware.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Evidence-prep-for-court-Ep.3-1.png

The fact that it highlights the same area as the ELA can really not be a coincidence.

Image Deepfake Detection Analysis

Amped Authenticate also features two AI-based deepfake detection filters. One analyzes the entire image for signs of content generated by diffusion models, while the other examines facial regions for signs of content generated by Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). Both filters provide a confidence score to help assess whether the analyzed content may be AI-generated.

In this instance, the diffusion model deepfake filter outputted a confidence score of 0.51 (where 0 indicates no confidence at all, and 1.0 maximum confidence). However, this could be accounted for by the size of the manipulated region, which is too small compared to the rest of the image. As we are unbiased, it is important to state that this could also equally mean that the image is not a deepfake at all.

The GAN Deepfake Detection filter was also applied and this reveals maximum confidence that the face of the subject has not been generated by a GAN. Mind that this does not necessarily mean that the face of the subject is real, simply that it has not been generated by this model. It could have been generated by a different model (for instance, a diffusion model), OR, quite simply, it could be a real face.

Remember also that the Deepfake Detection filters are quick and easy to use, but should not be your only analysis tool, as they essentially output a machine opinion. In this case, the face of the person has been changed from the original image and generated by a diffusion model. It is likely that the manipulated area was too small to be detected by the filter. Other filters, though, using a more solid forensic approach, correctly detected the manipulated area. Below, you can see the original image before manipulation.

How to Generate an Image Authentication Report

Once you have added all the relevant bookmarks with descriptions and status flags, you can go to the File menu and select the “Project Properties” option. Here, you can add case and author information as well as customize the size of your report illustrations.

You can then go to the Tools menu and select the “Generate Report” option. Select your preferred output format (HTML in this case) and customize other options such as adding hash values and file information, as well as the agency logo.

Below, you can admire the key areas of our report, with all the factual data gathered and our expert opinions on the significance of the findings.

Preparing a Video Authentication Case

Let’s switch to video authentication for a little while. If we want to work on a video case, we need to use the Amped Authenticate Video Mode. The analysis and report generation are similar to the Image mode. However, we obviously need to perform some tests that are relevant to digital video, such as the analysis of compression and continuity.

When preparing the report, we can include selected frames from different analyses to illustrate our findings. We can start by clicking on the Visual Inspection filter and bookmarking the frames we want to illustrate in the report.

In the example below, I note a suspicious rectangular outline surrounding the area of the visual timestamp.  I have bookmarked a couple of frames where this outline is more visible and adjusted the levels to increase the contrast in that area. These frames will all be printed in the report later.

Video Metadata Analysis: Examine File History and Export Logs

File and metadata analysis in the Video Mode is done via the Advanced File Info utility at the top of the filter list. For those of you familiar with Amped FIVE, this is the same utility available in that application. Unlike the Image Mode, the output of the utility does not go into the report. However, the utility offers a number of different ways to export your data into a disclosable document.

Let’s return to the video we previously examined using the Visual Inspection filter. In the MediaInfo tab of Advanced File Info, we noticed that the file’s creation date is October 17, 2026. However, the timestamp displayed in the video indicates that the original recording was made on September 3, 2026, as shown above.

This discrepancy suggests that the video may not be the original recording and could have been re-saved or exported at a later date. We documented this observation by clicking the Save to Log File button.

We have also saved the contents of the Exif log, as this contains numerous indications that the video has been edited with Adobe Premiere Pro, as shown below. It is all starting to look very suspicious!

Video Compression Analysis: Investigate Continuity and Editing Indicators

We then performed a compression analysis to investigate the video further. Our initial suspicions were supported by additional evidence, which we can present in the report in the form of plots and compelling illustrations.

We clicked on the Motion Vectors filter and then on the “Generate Plot and Table” button in the filter settings. The plot showed very high motion vector activity at around frame 300. This is consistent with a visual “jump cut” on the subject with the green shirt, even though the timestamp at the top right corner is contiguous.

We then added frame 307 as a bookmark, added a description explaining the anomaly and marked the status as “warning”. We ticked both the image and the plot options to ensure both are digitally printed in the report.

And finally, we clicked on the Macroblocks filter and found a few frames with suspicious intra-block activity (shown in purple in the image below) on the superior aspect of the frame. This suggests the frames in question were originally I-frames. When re-encoded, they left traces behind in the area where the alleged manipulation had occurred. In this instance, I only included the image and the table as no plot is applicable to my analysis.

Video Deepfake Detection Analysis

We finally clicked on the Diffusion Model Deepfake filter and ran the analysis to check if any portions of the video may have been generated synthetically. The analysis came back negative for all the frames of the video. In this instance, we added any frame as a bookmark and simply selected the plot and table for the report (as shown below).

How to Generate a Video Authentication Report

Once the bookmarks were reviewed and checked in the Project panel, I simply clicked on the Project Properties button to add case information and then navigated to the Tools menu and selected the option “Generate Report” (as shown above). As you can see, the report is quite comprehensive and contains all the relevant illustrations, plots and tables relevant to my analysis.

I also included the Advanced File Info data, which I printed to PDF from the log files generated by Amped Authenticate. This allowed me to provide factual evidence that, although the video was not manipulated by any form of AI image generation, it had been edited with Adobe Premiere Pro. The actual crime (theft by employee) was cut from the video and the visual timestamp in the top right corner was laid as a rectangular crop to make it look as if the video was contiguous.

Exporting Batch Analysis Results and Tabular Data in Amped Authenticate

As mentioned earlier, there may be instances where your analysis involves multiple files (images or videos). You may have been asked to separate images that have been possibly manipulated from camera originals. Or, you may have been asked to conduct a batch comparison of images or a mass deepfake detection analysis.

Authenticate’s report already supports multiple images or videos, but you may also want to produce tables containing data in a more granular format. Authenticate supports this workflow wonderfully. Let’s take a look at a case where I have been asked to perform camera ballistics on a folder full of images.

Batch Image Analysis: Export PRNU Camera Identification Results

The best thing to do when working with multiple clips is to simply load one of them in the evidence tab. Various filters offer options to analyze or compare all images in a folder and where this is the case, there will be a button at the top of the viewer. The filter will then output the data in a table that can be exported as an HTML or Excel file simply by right-clicking on it and selecting the appropriate option.

The image below comes from a folder seized from a suspect’s computer. We also have his digital camera which we used to capture some reference images. Our goal is to determine whether any of the recovered images were taken with that specific camera, as some contain child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

We applied the PRNU Identification filter from the Camera Identification group, loaded the camera reference pattern from the file generated with the reference images and immediately found the loaded image as positive with a high PCE (peak correlation energy) value. We then used the arrow buttons in the evidence tab to navigate to the other questioned images contained in the same folder.

We found a second image positive, whilst all the others came back as negative. We added a bookmark for each of the two positive images so that the PRNU data will be shown in the report for both. But, we then clicked on the “Analyze all Images in the Evidence Folder” button and this outputted a table containing the results for all the images in the folder.

I then right-clicked on the table and selected the “export as HTML” option. This wrote an HTML standalone file which I then linked to my master report.

Conclusions

We come to the end of this article and of the whole Court Presentation series. We really hope that this series gave you some food for thought when it comes to presenting forensic multimedia evidence in court.

Remember, you may have found compelling evidence that images have been tampered with or manipulated with AI image generation. However, if you can’t present the factual evidence supporting your conclusions, even the strongest findings may fail to stand up to scrutiny in court.

Amped products are designed to help you present and report your findings clearly and effectively, demonstrating to the trier of fact how your expert opinions are supported by scientific evidence. Throughout this series, we’ve explored practical workflows to help you achieve exactly that.

If you would like to practice firsthand on the many presentation workflows we have in Amped Authenticate, Amped FIVE and Amped Replay, make sure you check out our training page where a number of courses relevant to court presentation are on offer at an affordable price.

Until the next time, my friends, stay safe and take care.

FAQ: Reporting Image and Video Authentication Findings for Court

What should a forensic image or video authentication report include?

Your report should clearly document the evidence examined, its integrity, the forensic methods applied, your findings, and the reasoning behind your conclusions. Depending on the applicable legal requirements, you may also need to include case references, an expert witness declaration, and supporting documentation. Amped Authenticate helps you generate technical reports with analysis results, annotated images, plots, and tables that you can incorporate into your final expert report.

How can I document suspected image manipulation in Amped Authenticate?

You can use Visual Inspection to identify suspicious details, then apply relevant forensic filters to investigate potential inconsistencies. Use bookmarks, annotations, and descriptive notes to highlight important findings. Where appropriate, compare questioned images with reference images and use multiple analysis methods to support your conclusions.

How can I present evidence of possible video editing or manipulation?

You can combine visual inspection with metadata, compression, and continuity analysis to identify potential editing indicators. Amped Authenticate allows you to document suspicious frames, highlight anomalies, and include relevant plots and tables in your report. You should explain what each finding indicates and consider whether alternative explanations are possible.

Can deepfake detection results alone prove that an image or video has been manipulated?

No. AI-based deepfake detection filters provide indications based on the models and methods they use, but their results are not conclusive proof of authenticity or manipulation. A negative result does not necessarily exclude AI-generated content. You should interpret detection scores alongside other forensic findings and clearly explain their limitations in your report.

How can I include video metadata analysis results in my forensic report?

In Amped Authenticate’s Video mode, you can examine file information and metadata using the Advanced File Info utility. Since these results are not automatically included in the generated report, you can export the relevant information to log files and incorporate it into your supporting documentation.

Can I export forensic analysis results for multiple images or videos?

Yes. Amped Authenticate supports the analysis of multiple files and the generation of reports containing their findings. For supported filters, you can also perform batch analysis and export tabular results in HTML or Excel format. This is particularly useful when comparing numerous images, conducting camera identification analysis, or reviewing results across larger evidence collections.
