items.title: Open code isn’t the problem: experts on the “god-tier” flaws exposed across UK government repositories
items.summary: A security researcher has uncovered more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, including credentials that could have given an attacker read-write access across an entire public body’s Microsoft 365 estate. The findings, first reported by WIRED , have reignited a long-running Whitehall debate: should government keep publishing its code at all? ControlPlane researcher Chris Nesbitt-Smith examined 349 public-sector codebases belonging to 33 organisations and found serious weaknesses in roughly two-thirds of them. The problems were familiar ones – exposed credentials, missing access checks, overpowered service accounts and insecure defaults. What made the exercise notable was the toolkit: consumer versions of Anthropic’s Claude Opus and Sonnet models, run from a laptop. Nesbitt-Smith has stressed that many of the issues could have been caught by a routine IT health check. All of the issues highlighted have since been disclosed to the organisations involved and addressed. For Olly Maxwell, principal security operations analyst at Huntress , the story is depressingly recognisable. “Having transitioned from Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office security to tracking EMEA threat actor tradecraft at Huntress, the recent WIRED report on public sector vulnerabilities strikes a very familiar chord,” he said. “Whenever stories like this break, the immediate political reflex across Whitehall is to lock down repositories and abandon transparent coding practices. That reaction fundamentally misunderstands both the root cause of the exposure and the reality of the modern threat landscape.” A “god-tier” key left in the history The most serious case involved the Planning Inspectorate, the agency that handles planning appeals and national infrastructure casework in England. An exported Azure Synapse notebook pushed to a public GitHub repository contained a complete Microsoft Entra ID application credential. The integration it served only needed to retrieve a single HR file from SharePoint, but the permissions attached to it reached across every SharePoint site in the tenant and into private employee OneDrive accounts – including libraries holding evidence for statutory planning inquiries under legal hold. Maxwell is clear about where the blame lies. “Exposing tenant-wide Microsoft Entra ID credentials in a public GitHub repository is not a byproduct of open source philosophy. It is a severe breakdown in basic supply chain governance and DevSecOps hygiene.” Collin Hogue-Spears, senior director of solution management at Black Duck , points to the permissions model as the factor that turned a leaked secret into a potential catastrophe. “This is mostly the result of a failure to implement least privilege and implicit trust controls. Excessive permissions are what made the Planning Inspectorate leak dangerous: ControlPlane found that a pipeline needing one file had write access to every SharePoint site and to OneDrive.” He added that the pattern is far from isolated: “Broad application permissions have amplified other incidents this year: in October, Huntress confirmed unauthorised sign-ins in at least 162 Microsoft 365 tenants through one compromised backup-application credential. An application credential signs in with no user and no second factor. Microsoft Entra ID treats whoever holds the secret as the application.” Deleted from the branch, not from the identity provider Crucially, the credential had been removed from the repository’s branch – but not revoked. An orphaned commit remained retrievable through GitHub’s raw-content infrastructure for around 18 months, and the secret still worked. The Planning Inspectorate said its monitoring detected the researcher’s activity, that it treated the report as a cyber incident and revoked the credential roughly 20 minutes after receiving it on 26 August, and that it found no evidence of a data breach. “A force push removes the file from the branch, not the secret from Microsoft Entra ID,” said Hogue-Spears. “When a researcher used the secret 18 months after the force push, the Planning Inspectorate’s monitoring flagged the activity, and the agency revoked the secret about 20 minutes after the report.” Ronald Lewis, head of cybersecurity governance at Black Duck , argues that the episode exposes a design assumption rather than a coding slip. “This is a classic example of security being built, at least in part, on obscurity. The problem isn’t that the code was public, and it’s easy to point at AI as the culprit. Realistically, this isn’t an AI problem or an open-source problem. It’s a security architecture problem. The organisation implicitly relied on the assumption that these weaknesses, credentials, and excessive permissions wouldn’t be discovered. AI simply made discovering them faster and cheaper.” AI changes the economics, not the mistakes The use of off-the-shelf AI has inevitably drawn headlines, and it lands in a year in which the UK government has itself leaned on frontier models to hunt for flaws. In June, the Government Cyber Coordination Centre published results from internal hackathons that surfaced 407 findings across public repositories in nine departments, and in October an AI-assisted discovery of critical PHP vulnerabilities forced dozens of public sector sites offline. Maxwell believes the Nesbitt-Smith findings should change how defenders model the threat. “The fact that a researcher identified over 100 serious flaws across dozens of public bodies using consumer grade AI on a laptop should serve as a wakeup call regarding threat asymmetry. AI did not introduce these vulnerabilities, but it has completely democratised the cost of discovering them,” he said. “Public code repositories are subjected to continuous, automated scraping by hostile state nexus groups and initial access brokers. If an independent researcher can surface these gaps trivially, the operational assumption must be that adversaries have already mirrored the repositories and harvested the exposed key material.” Hogue-Spears points to evidence that this is already happening at scale. “Attackers search public code for application secrets. In a separate campaign Microsoft reported on November 5, threat actors used an agentic AI framework to search GitHub for secrets, often by organisation name, and then signed in as the exposed applications.” And the danger, Maxwell warns, is not necessarily immediate. “Crucially, highly capable threat actors do not always exploit this access immediately. They bank valid administrative keys and quietly establish strategic persistence within environments like SharePoint or legal hold libraries, holding that access until it becomes geopolitically or financially advantageous to strike.” Lewis echoes the point that AI is an accelerant rather than a cause. “‘Security by obscurity’ as a design choice is dangerous in the age of AI, but AI isn’t the root cause. An important takeaway for businesses is that ‘hard to find’ can no longer be treated as a security control. Organizations should assume that anything exposed to the internet, including source code, APIs, configurations and credentials, will eventually be analysed by AI. The barrier to doing that kind of analysis is rapidly disappearing.” Rushed delivery and deferred security Government has defaulted to publishing the code it produces with public money for around a decade, on the grounds that it improves transparency and makes reuse cheaper. But funding pressure has left many departments struggling to maintain their technology estates – and much of the build work is outsourced. “The rapid push to modernise government digital services relies heavily on third party systems integrators and outsourced development,” said Maxwell. “When aggressive delivery milestones collide with public sector funding squeezes, foundational security controls like automated secret scanning and identity posture management are routinely treated as deferred technical debt. The procurement lag for security tooling frequently eclipses the operational lifecycle of the product itself.” “These exposures happen because code is rushed into production environments before proper governance and risk compliance principles are applied. Securing modern CI/CD pipelines requires specialized knowledge to enforce pre commit security gates and token lifecycle management. Without those guardrails natively embedded into the developer workflow, credential sprawl is inevitable.” Lewis agrees that the answer lies in the basics. “Another important note is that this highlights the need for getting the fundamentals right. Secrets shouldn’t live in source code. Credentials should be short-lived and rotated. Identity should follow least privilege. A compromised credential shouldn’t provide broad access across the enterprise. And organisations need automated controls in the development pipeline that can identify these problems before code is published or deployed.” For Hogue-Spears, that means removing long-lived secrets from pipelines altogether. “Security leaders must move pipelines to managed identities or workload identity federation, which leave no secret to commit. A managed identity keeps whatever permissions an administrator grants it, so replace tenant-wide Microsoft Graph permissions with selected permissions scoped to the site or file the application needs. Treat any secret that reaches a public repository as compromised and revoke it in the identity provider before anyone cleans the Git history.” Beyond leaked credentials Not every finding involved a secret. At the Department for Education, the Get Help Buying for Schools service allowed anyone holding a valid request identifier to change request details – including the contact email – and submit the request without signing in; it was fixed on 10 July. In the department’s teacher application service, an account-linking code could overwrite an existing login association. Elsewhere, a long-lived administrator token was found embedded in public JavaScript on a Scottish Government open data portal, which has since been decommissioned. Hogue-Spears highlighted a further DfE case as a lesson in authorisation testing. “In the Department for Education’s training-provider register, delete actions ran with no authorisation check, so a low-privileged staff account was able to soft-delete registered providers and other staff accounts. The same service’s user-editing policy did run, and it examined the record’s state, not the caller’s role, so a standard staff account was able to deactivate an administrator’s account. The department fixed both flaws in July. If your tests never sign in as an ordinary user and attempt an administrator’s action, a missing check and a wrong check both ship.” Why closing the code won’t close the gap The findings arrive as some in government question whether public bodies should keep repositories open in an era of AI-accelerated discovery. Nesbitt-Smith himself has warned that pulling code private without fixing the flaws could make risks harder to spot. The experts are unanimous on this point. “Making a repository private hides the code, and a secret that leaked while the repository was public stays valid until it expires or someone revokes it,” said Hogue-Spears. “Leaders have to name an owner for every public repository. Since May, the UK government guidance has set a minimum before code goes public: a named owner and controls that stop developers from committing secrets.” Maxwell is blunter. “Consequently, advising departments to pull their codebases private without remediating the underlying architectural flaws is incredibly dangerous. Security by obscurity has never stopped an advanced persistent threat. Closing the repositories simply blinds the independent research community that provides vital early warnings, while doing absolutely nothing to evict threat actors who already hold the compromised credentials.” Lewis argues the real shift is in mindset. “Although there’s a knee jerk to blame AI for discovering weaknesses like this; in reality, a motivated attacker could have found these. AI doesn’t make design decision more dangerous; it simply changes the economics. In short, AI allows someone to search for existing mistakes, just faster, cheaper and at a scale that wasn’t practical in the past. And perhaps the most important lessons learned from this is that businesses need to operate under the assumption that if a weakness is discoverable, someone will eventually find it.” Maxwell leaves the final word with a call for discipline rather than retreat. “We operate in a climate where the UK faces continuous, hostile cyber activity. There is a vast difference between falling victim to a highly sophisticated zero day exploit and simply handing adversaries your production logins. The government does not need to retreat into the shadows. It needs to mandate strict, automated security gates across the entire software supply chain and treat identity security with the rigorous operational discipline it demands.”

The problem isn’t that the code was public, and it’s easy to point at AI as the culprit. Realistically, this isn’t an AI problem or an open-source problem. It’s a security architecture problem. The organisation implicitly relied on the assumption that these weaknesses, credentials, and excessive permissions wouldn’t be discovered. AI simply made discovering them faster and cheaper.”

AI changes the economics, not the mistakes

The use of off-the-shelf AI has inevitably drawn headlines, and it lands in a year in which the UK government has itself leaned on frontier models to hunt for flaws. In June, the Government Cyber Coordination Centre published results from internal hackathons that surfaced 407 findings across public repositories in nine departments, and in October an AI-assisted discovery of critical PHP vulnerabilities forced dozens of public sector sites offline.

Maxwell believes the Nesbitt-Smith findings should change how defenders model the threat. “The fact that a researcher identified over 100 serious flaws across dozens of public bodies using consumer grade AI on a laptop should serve as a wakeup call regarding threat asymmetry. AI did not introduce these vulnerabilities, but it has completely democratised the cost of discovering them,” he said.

“Public code repositories are subjected to continuous, automated scraping by hostile state nexus groups and initial access brokers. If an independent researcher can surface these gaps trivially, the operational assumption must be that adversaries have already mirrored the repositories and harvested the exposed key material.”

Hogue-Spears points to evidence that this is already happening at scale. “Attackers search public code for application secrets. In a separate campaign Microsoft reported on November 5, threat actors used an agentic AI framework to search GitHub for secrets, often by organisation name, and then signed in as the exposed applications.”

And the danger, Maxwell warns, is not necessarily immediate. “Crucially, highly capable threat actors do not always exploit this access immediately. They bank valid administrative keys and quietly establish strategic persistence within environments like SharePoint or legal hold libraries, holding that access until it becomes geopolitically or financially advantageous to strike.”

Lewis echoes the point that AI is an accelerant rather than a cause. “‘Security by obscurity’ as a design choice is dangerous in the age of AI, but AI isn’t the root cause. An important takeaway for businesses is that ‘hard to find’ can no longer be treated as a security control. Organizations should assume that anything exposed to the internet, including source code, APIs, configurations and credentials, will eventually be analysed by AI. The barrier to doing that kind of analysis is rapidly disappearing.”

Rushed delivery and deferred security

Government has defaulted to publishing the code it produces with public money for around a decade, on the grounds that it improves transparency and makes reuse cheaper. But funding pressure has left many departments struggling to maintain their technology estates – and much of the build work is outsourced.

“The rapid push to modernise government digital services relies heavily on third party systems integrators and outsourced development,” said Maxwell. “When aggressive delivery milestones collide with public sector funding squeezes, foundational security controls like automated secret scanning and identity posture management are routinely treated as deferred technical debt. The procurement lag for security tooling frequently eclipses the operational lifecycle of the product itself.”

“These exposures happen because code is rushed into production environments before proper governance and risk compliance principles are applied. Securing modern CI/CD pipelines requires specialized knowledge to enforce pre commit security gates and token lifecycle management. Without those guardrails natively embedded into the developer workflow, credential sprawl is inevitable.”

Lewis agrees that the answer lies in the basics. “Another important note is that this highlights the need for getting the fundamentals right. Secrets shouldn’t live in source code. Credentials should be short-lived and rotated. Identity should follow least privilege. A compromised credential shouldn’t provide broad access across the enterprise. And organisations need automated controls in the development pipeline that can identify these problems before code is published or deployed.”

For Hogue-Spears, that means removing long-lived secrets from pipelines altogether. “Security leaders must move pipelines to managed identities or workload identity federation, which leave no secret to commit. A managed identity keeps whatever permissions an administrator grants it, so replace tenant-wide Microsoft Graph permissions with selected permissions scoped to the site or file the application needs. Treat any secret that reaches a public repository as compromised and revoke it in the identity provider before anyone cleans the Git history.”

Beyond leaked credentials

Not every finding involved a secret. At the Department for Education, the Get Help Buying for Schools service allowed anyone holding a valid request identifier to change request details – including the contact email – and submit the request without signing in; it was fixed on 10 July. In the department’s teacher application service, an account-linking code could overwrite an existing login association. Elsewhere, a long-lived administrator token was found embedded in public JavaScript on a Scottish Government open data portal, which has since been decommissioned.

Hogue-Spears highlighted a further DfE case as a lesson in authorisation testing. “In the Department for Education’s training-provider register, delete actions ran with no authorisation check, so a low-privileged staff account was able to soft-delete registered providers and other staff accounts. The same service’s user-editing policy did run, and it examined the record’s state, not the caller’s role, so a standard staff account was able to deactivate an administrator’s account. The department fixed both flaws in July. If your tests never sign in as an ordinary user and attempt an administrator’s action, a missing check and a wrong check both ship.”

Why closing the code won’t close the gap

The findings arrive as some in government question whether public bodies should keep repositories open in an era of AI-accelerated discovery. Nesbitt-Smith himself has warned that pulling code private without fixing the flaws could make risks harder to spot. The experts are unanimous on this point.

“Making a repository private hides the code, and a secret that leaked while the repository was public stays valid until it expires or someone revokes it,” said Hogue-Spears. “Leaders have to name an owner for every public repository. Since May, the UK government guidance has set a minimum before code goes public: a named owner and controls that stop developers from committing secrets.”

Maxwell is blunter. “Consequently, advising departments to pull their codebases private without remediating the underlying architectural flaws is incredibly dangerous. Security by obscurity has never stopped an advanced persistent threat. Closing the repositories simply blinds the independent research community that provides vital early warnings, while doing absolutely nothing to evict threat actors who already hold the compromised credentials.”

Lewis argues the real shift is in mindset. “Although there’s a knee jerk to blame AI for discovering weaknesses like this; in reality, a motivated attacker could have found these. AI doesn’t make design decision more dangerous; it simply changes the economics. In short, AI allows someone to search for existing mistakes, just faster, cheaper and at a scale that wasn’t practical in the past. And perhaps the most important lessons learned from this is that businesses need to operate under the assumption that if a weakness is discoverable, someone will eventually find it.”

Maxwell leaves the final word with a call for discipline rather than retreat. “We operate in a climate where the UK faces continuous, hostile cyber activity. There is a vast difference between falling victim to a highly sophisticated zero day exploit and simply handing adversaries your production logins. The government does not need to retreat into the shadows. It needs to mandate strict, automated security gates across the entire software supply chain and treat identity security with the rigorous operational discipline it demands.”

Now they’re doing it literally. The maker of Muse, a headband that measures brain activity during sleep and meditation, used users’ brainwave data to train AI without explicitly telling them, an investigation has revealed. Companies sell these consumer sleep bands to help you better understand what your brain does when you sleep and meditate. However, according to an investigation in Science magazine, they’re picking up a little understanding of their own on the side. The year-long investigation found that Canadian company Interaxon, which makes the Muse sleep and meditation headband, was using the data that it collected from users’ brains to train AI. The company used about 50,000 hours of electroencephalography (EEG) recordings, which measure the brain’s electrical activity, to train a “brain foundation model.” AI models trained with large amounts of brainwave data from different people can spot patterns in brain activity. For example, a model might learn to recognize patterns associated with seizures. Researching such outcomes is laudable, but only if you first tell the people whose EEG data is being used for the training. Interaxon didn’t. This is your brain on an inadequate privacy policy When Science questioned Interaxon about the issue, its chief marketing officer Nadia Kumentas acknowledged that users should be explicitly informed about the AI training. The company updated its privacy policy, which now says de-identified data is used to train machine learning models. Collecting data through devices like this is tempting for companies because brainwave data is otherwise difficult to obtain and therefore incredibly valuable. No wonder, then, that it isn’t the only neuraltech company facing questions about its data practices. The publication reviewed 57 companies that collect brain data, and found that only six explicitly said they wouldn’t sell users’ brain data. More than two-thirds allow brain data to pass to a new owner if they are acquired. Eleven of them only had a privacy policy for website visitors, and four had no policy at all. To its credit, Interaxon removed names and email addresses from user EEG data before using it for training. However, those users’ data has already helped shape a model trained without explicitly telling them. Removing its influence after the fact is extremely difficult. But is such “de-identification” enough? An academic study conducted by the University of South-Eastern Norway this year found that EEG recordings and derived features can contain sensitive patient-specific information. It said that this can create privacy risks when that data is shared across clinical and research environments. It added: “Conventional anonymization methods are often insufficient for high-dimensional biomedical signals, since removing direct identifiers does not necessarily prevent re-identification, linkage, or inference risks.” Another study by researchers at Ben-Gurion University, Israel, found that analyzing resting-state EEG recordings could shed light on personality traits and cognitive abilities. Resting-state EEG identified users 88.4% of the time, according to a 2018 study by researchers at Korea University. And a University of Southern California study claimed that EEG data could reveal mental health status, neurological conditions, and even substance use history. These findings do not establish what can be inferred from Muse recordings specifically. Consumer headbands generally have fewer electrodes than clinical EEG systems. This isn’t the first review of the consumer neurotech industry to reveal some worrying trends. A 2024 Neurorights Foundation report found that 29 of 30 companies it surveyed appeared to have access to consumers’ neural data and had provided “no meaningful limitations to this access.” The law is still catching up to all this. The Illinois Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) counts your fingerprint, voiceprint, or face geometry among other things as biometric identifiers, but EEG data doesn’t make the cut. However, Colorado and California do now treat neural data as sensitive. These concerns extend beyond brainwave data. In a Malwarebytes survey of newsletter readers , 90% worried about AI using their data without consent, while 92% were concerned about corporations using their personal data inappropriately. What Muse owners can do Do you use a sleep band or another neurotech device? Consider that your brain data might be used for more than you imagined. And if the company goes bust and/or gets acquired, it might pass to another owner. That’s exactly what happened with genetic testing company 23andMe. With this in mind, check the manufacturer’s privacy policy, and if you can’t find one, ask it directly. Ask whether your EEG data is used to train AI, whether you can opt out, and whether you can delete recordings already collected. If those options aren’t available, consider whether you’re comfortable continuing to use the device. From reporting threats to removing them. items.title: Grok AI App Builder Exposes Over 35,000 Apps, Leaking Confidential Business Data and Passwords
items.summary: Researchers found that apps built with Grok’s app builder are open to Anyone online. Thousands of these apps hold private business data, staff details, plain-text passwords , and patient information. No hacking was needed to reach them. Grok’s Build mode creates and publishes chat-generated apps under grok.me, while its parent company, SpaceXSI (formerly xAI), did not respond to Claroc but answered media questions on November 10, 2026. On November 8, 2026, Claroc researchers worked through a list of more than 43,500 grok.me addresses. They opened the first page of each app once, signed in to nothing, like any visitor in a private browser window. Of the 37,571 apps still online, 35,578 (94.7%) opened for Anyone. Only 1,993 asked for a sign-in. The list came from passive DNS, a service that records website name lookups and lets Anyone search them. Each Grok app gets its own address, so the name enters those records once someone opens the app. Grok AI App Builder Exposes Data The researchers say Grok’s four-random-word names are hard to guess, but nobody needs to guess them because the records list them. The same method exposed Meta’s Muse, as covered in our Meta Muse AI privacy flaw report . Most open apps were games, landing pages, and calculators. About one in ten held sensitive or internal data, and roughly 2% were serious enough to rate high or critical. SpaceXSI’s sales territory map (source: Claroc) Confirmed examples include an intensive care briefing with a patient’s labs and ventilator status, a hospital group’s roster of more than 3,500 employees, and a fire department’s shift board with badge numbers. One contractor’s timesheet app held 18 staff accounts with plain-text passwords in code that every visitor’s browser downloads. SpaceXSI and X staff also left 24 apps open. They included a confidential onboarding plan, a sales map of 594 accounts, and advertising proposals, one aimed at a U.S. federal agency. Another 30 identifiable organizations had internal data exposed. Of these, 26 have over 1,000 employees, and six are Fortune 500 companies. SpaceXSI took down its own 24 apps after the report, but not those of other users. Grok app links become publicly searchable through passive DNS records after their first use (source: Claroc) Claroc found that paid-account apps defaulted to public link access, allowing anyone to view and add records to apps without login protection. A team app with Google sign-in checked who the visitor was but not whether they belonged to the team. A stranger with a Google account could read, edit, and delete customer records. The researchers tested this only on their own apps. SpaceXSI says apps stay private until the creator shares them, and that publishing takes several steps. Claroc replies that every owner of the 35,578 open apps went through those same steps. Teams should find out which AI app builders their staff use, since tools like Lovable, Replit, and Grok need no IT approval. Check each app’s access settings, and test sign-in with an outside account. Look in the app’s script files for passwords and unpublish anything nobody owns. Unpublishing a grok.me app takes it offline within seconds. simplified from the code Grok wrote for us (source: Caroc ) This is not Grok’s first exposure problem. In 2025, more than 370,000 shared Grok chats appeared in Google search, which we covered in our report on Grok chats exposed in Google results . The comprehensive research is on the Claroc blog. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Three People Arrested for AI-Enhanced Impersonation Fraud
items.summary: It’s hard to believe how lucrative this crime can be: According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men ­ Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit ­ were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026. With the help of AI, the men allegedly acted as a corporate executive, targeting employees of various companies and telling them they needed their help with sensitive financial transactions. They would then instruct the employees to get in touch with lawyers at a large international law firm. The men would then impersonate a lawyer at these firms and have the employees wire a large amount of money. The men ultimately stole more than $129m from companies all over the world including in the US, according to the DoJ. Always remember that there are three parts of AI security: security of AI, security with AI, and security from AI. This is the third.

items.title: Platform engineering needs to become more human…and less
items.summary: Even my family thinks I’m a little robotic. Logical, linear, sequential, methodical. But hey, I’m an engineer, and that’s part of what makes me good at my job. If I were operating on the same volatile cocktail of emotions, knee-jerk reactions, and intuition that most people operate on, I wouldn’t have been nearly as effective building enterprise software architecture at Disney, Dell, SAP, VMware, and now Control Plane. Worse yet, I might have had to become a marketer, or a designer, or a human resources specialist…or even a salesperson. Not very long ago (in 2024, and for fifty years before that), software engineers like me were the best robots anyone had access to. The CIO at Disney would ask me to redesign FastPass from the ground up, and I would do it in one long-running process over a weekend while he sipped coffee and watched the game. The head of Dell’s Identity Management business would bring me a huge project, and I would dive in, writing thousands of lines of code by hand. And even though I was pretty consistent and logical, and so were (most of) my engineering colleagues, things could get messy fast. That’s where platform engineering came in, and that’s when I met Dan. Dan Wilson was this brilliant platform engineer at SAP/Concur. He was one of the early open source contributors to a lot of fundamental projects. He knew Kubernetes like an old friend, and he could make your cloud infrastructure sing. I loved working with Dan because he got my logically organized code to production more logically and a heckuva lot faster. A merge to main kicked off a containerized build, then unit tests, integration tests, and a security scan, and every stage had to pass before the image was promoted to the next environment. Deployments were declarative, the desired state lived in version control, and Kubernetes made the cluster match it. It warmed my engineer’s heart to watch the CI/CD pipelines hum through their stage gates. But the whole process, the whole platform, was still made for engineers. It assumed deep technical knowledge. It required strict compliance with established protocols. It wasn’t hard. It was just logical. Just a little robotic, but that was fine because it was designed for people who were a little robotic…at least a little more robotic than the average person. I mean, what engineer would try to name a production database final_v2_USE_THIS_ONE? (Several, it turns out. But they had the decency to feel bad about it.) The platform never had to defend against this behavior, because the people using it were not completely normal humans. We designed internal platforms for engineers who read the docs (allegedly), knew what a rollback was, and had a decent sense of when not to deploy. That is so Oct 2025 But then Opus 4.5 was released and everything changed. Or more specifically, every one changed. Everyone changed from being a normal human to being an engineer…just without the pocket protectors, inside jokes, and strict adherence to protocol. The systems that took me weekends at Disney could now be vibe-coded by the receptionist in a few hours. And they would work (they might not be secure or performant, and they might be a usability train wreck, but bear with me). Everyone was now an engineer because everyone now had agents. They had their own little fleet of Dorons doing their bidding. GitHub’s 2025 Octoverse report counted more than 36 million new developers joining in a single year, more than one every second, for a total past 180 million. What this means for platform engineering is that now the humans using the platform act more like humans than they ever have. They improvise. If the form won’t take their input, they find another way in. They share the password because sharing is polite . They ask the person at the next desk instead of reading the docs, and they copy whatever worked last time, even if last time was a different project in a different region. Secrets must get injected at runtime, not handed to a person, so there’s nothing to paste into Slack and nothing to save in a notes app for later. Policies have to check every change before it lands: no public endpoints without a reason, no direct line from a dashboard to the production database, no resources without an owner. Every deployment has to go out small, get watched, and roll itself back if the numbers turn bad. When the platform does have to say no, it should say it the way a good colleague would. Not “Denied by policy 0042.” More like, “This would make your customer list public on the internet. Here’s the setting that keeps it internal.” An error message is the closest thing these builders will ever get to that raised eyebrow, so write it like one. Most importantly, the rules have to be written down, in a form a machine can read. The unwritten rules your platform used to depend on simply don’t exist for an agent. items.summary_html:
Even my family thinks I’m a little robotic. Logical, linear, sequential, methodical. But hey, I’m an engineer, and that’s part of what makes me good at my job.

If I were operating on the same volatile cocktail of emotions, knee-jerk reactions, and intuition that most people operate on, I wouldn’t have been nearly as effective building enterprise software architecture at Disney, Dell, SAP, VMware, and now Control Plane.

Worse yet, I might have had to become a marketer, or a designer, or a human resources specialist…or even a salesperson.

Not very long ago (in 2024, and for fifty years before that), software engineers like me were the best robots anyone had access to. The CIO at Disney would ask me to redesign FastPass from the ground up, and I would do it in one long-running process over a weekend while he sipped coffee and watched the game. The head of Dell’s Identity Management business would bring me a huge project, and I would dive in, writing thousands of lines of code by hand.

And even though I was pretty consistent and logical, and so were (most of) my engineering colleagues, things could get messy fast. That’s where platform engineering came in, and that’s when I met Dan.

Dan Wilson was this brilliant platform engineer at SAP/Concur. He was one of the early open source contributors to a lot of fundamental projects. He knew Kubernetes like an old friend, and he could make your cloud infrastructure sing.

I loved working with Dan because he got my logically organized code to production more logically and a heckuva lot faster. A merge to main kicked off a containerized build, then unit tests, integration tests, and a security scan, and every stage had to pass before the image was promoted to the next environment. Deployments were declarative, the desired state lived in version control, and Kubernetes made the cluster match it. It warmed my engineer’s heart to watch the CI/CD pipelines hum through their stage gates.

But the whole process, the whole platform, was still made for engineers. It assumed deep technical knowledge. It required strict compliance with established protocols. It wasn’t hard. It was just logical. Just a little robotic, but that was fine because it was designed for people who were a little robotic…at least a little more robotic than the average person. 

I mean, what engineer would try to name a production database final_v2_USE_THIS_ONE? (Several, it turns out. But they had the decency to feel bad about it.) The platform never had to defend against this behavior, because the people using it were not completely normal humans.

We designed internal platforms for engineers who read the docs (allegedly), knew what a rollback was, and had a decent sense of when not to deploy.

That is so Oct 2025

But then Opus 4.5 was released and everything changed. Or more specifically, everyone changed. Everyone changed from being a normal human to being an engineer…just without the pocket protectors, inside jokes, and strict adherence to protocol. The systems that took me weekends at Disney could now be vibe-coded by the receptionist in a few hours. And they would work (they might not be secure or performant, and they might be a usability train wreck, but bear with me).

Everyone was now an engineer because everyone now had agents. They had their own little fleet of Dorons doing their bidding. GitHub’s 2025 Octoverse report counted more than 36 million new developers joining in a single year, more than one every second, for a total past 180 million.

What this means for platform engineering is that now the humans using the platform act more like humans than they ever have. They improvise. If the form won’t take their input, they find another way in. They share the password because sharing is polite. They ask the person at the next desk instead of reading the docs, and they copy whatever worked last time, even if last time was a different project in a different region. They name things for other humans, so production ends up running something called “Q4 launch page FINAL (Jen’s edits).” These aren’t really flaws. In most of the company, they’re called “initiative”. Or “creativity”. But you might also call it “chaos”.

Of course, engineers are creative too. But what we’re about to see…what we’re already seeing…is an EXPLOSION in creativity entering the software development world. Because now creativity of all sorts, from all sorts of very non-robotic people, has been given direct access to the code. Musicians. Copywriters. Recruiters. The finance lead who has opinions about dashboards. These are people who were never going to learn a programming language, and now they don’t have to. They bring taste, empathy, and a feel for what customers want, which the old pipeline often filtered out long before anything reached production. They also bring their own idea of what “done” means and no idea how a typical internal developer platform operates.

But these new humans and this explosion in creativity are here. And they’re not going away. So platform engineering has to find a way to harness all this creativity without it taking anything important offline or leaking company secrets all over the internet.

Making room for the more-human builders

Here’s what I think needs to happen for that to take place.

The rules have to move out of people’s heads and into the platform.

For as long as most of us have done this work, the guardrails lived inside the engineers…at least in large part. Nobody had to tell a senior engineer not to expose a database to the internet, not to paste an API key into a chat window, or not to name a production table test. They had learned it the hard way, usually at 2am, usually once. Those lessons got passed along in code reviews, in onboarding, in the raised eyebrow of a colleague. The platform didn’t have to enforce what its users already believed. It could be a little naive, because its users weren’t.

That arrangement is finished. The copywriter shipping a landing page has never been paged at 2am, and I hope she never is. The recruiter building an interview scheduler doesn’t know a public bucket from a private one, and there’s no reason she should. The finance lead with opinions about dashboards will happily connect one to the production database, because that’s where the real numbers are. They’re doing what every smart, motivated person does with a new tool: click around until something lights up.

So the platform has to know these things on their behalf. Every app has to get its own identity the moment it’s created, scoped to what it needs and nothing more. Secrets must get injected at runtime, not handed to a person, so there’s nothing to paste into Slack and nothing to save in a notes app for later. Policies have to check every change before it lands: no public endpoints without a reason, no direct line from a dashboard to the production database, no resources without an owner. Every deployment has to go out small, get watched, and roll itself back if the numbers turn bad.

When the platform does have to say no, it should say it the way a good colleague would. Not “Denied by policy 0042.” More like, “This would make your customer list public on the internet. Here’s the setting that keeps it internal.” An error message is the closest thing these builders will ever get to that raised eyebrow, so write it like one.

Done well, most of these new more-human builders never notice any of this. And that’s as it should be.

Agents, the less-human builders

But wait a minute. We’ve had an explosion in human creativity entering the platform engineering chat, but we’ve also had a super explosion in agents…who are more robotic than any of (well, most of) the engineers I’ve ever worked with.

Here’s what I mean. An agent will read every line of your documentation, which already puts it ahead of most of us. It follows instructions exactly. It doesn’t get bored, doesn’t take lunch, and doesn’t get a nervous feeling in its stomach before touching production. Give one a task at 6pm and it will still be working at 6am, cheerfully, having opened more pull requests overnight than your team reviews in a month. And it’s never just one agent. It’s dozens, then hundreds, each one launched by a person who has already moved on to something else.

The new humans get into trouble by improvising around the rules. Agents get into trouble by following them perfectly, including the ones that are wrong and the ones you never wrote down. Ask an engineer to “clean up unused resources,” and she knows that doesn’t mean the production database that’s quiet because it’s Sunday. An agent may not.

When an agent hits a wall, it doesn’t stop to ask someone. It retries, and then tries another route, and then another, until it finds a path that’s open. That’s the agent version of a marketer finding another way in, except it happens in four seconds and across forty services. And it’s always confident. (Incidentally, In all my years working with engineers, I’ve met a few who were never unsure of anything. I didn’t put them in charge of production, either.)

Agents don’t learn the 2am lessons any more than the copywriter does. Most of them start every session fresh, with no memory of past outages and (just as important) none of the emotions that come with them.

So what do we do about these less-human engineers?

Every agent has to be treated as its own accountable actor, with limits set for machine speed rather than human speed.

That starts with identity. Every agent has to have its own identity, tied to the person who launched it, with permissions scoped to the task and an expiry that matches it. When the task ends, so does the access. Then it needs a speed limit: a cap on how many changes it can make, how many resources it can create, and how much it can spend in an hour, so a loop that would have done damage at machine speed hits a ceiling instead. Agents should do their work in preview environments that look like production but aren’t, and changes should reach production only through the same small, watched, self-reversing rollouts the humans use. Every action has to go into an audit trail that answers “which agent, launched by whom, to do what.” And there has to be a kill switch that someone can find in under a minute.

Most importantly, the rules have to be written down, in a form a machine can read. The unwritten rules your platform used to depend on simply don’t exist for an agent. When it breaks one, the platform’s answer should be a clear, structured reason and the specific thing to change, so the agent fixes its request instead of hammering the same door 500 times.

Here’s the good news. Once the rules are written down, agents become the most reliable builders you have. They don’t argue with the template, skip the checklist, or decide the standard doesn’t apply to them this one time.

Taking a page from Kubernetes

I’m optimistic about our ability to build for these new platform users, and the reason is Kubernetes. We’ve solved this problem before. Just not for people.

Before orchestration, running software at scale meant a person watching servers. Someone noticed a process had died and restarted it. Someone decided which machine had room. Someone approved every change. That worked with a dozen servers and fell apart at a thousand. Kubernetes didn’t fix it by hiring faster operators. It changed the contract between the operator and the work, and four parts of that contract map almost exactly onto the new builders.

You declare, it reconciles. You don’t tell Kubernetes how to keep three replicas running. You say you want three, and a control loop works continuously to make it true. That’s what the new humans need. The copywriter should be able to say “a landing page customers can reach, that can read the product catalog,” and the platform works out the identity, the network, the secrets, and the rollout. Agents get the same contract in its most literal form. A spec is exactly the kind of thing an agent is good at writing.

Every request goes through admission. Nothing gets into a cluster without passing the admission controllers, where policy can reject the request or fix it. The API server doesn’t care whether the request came from a senior engineer, a CI pipeline, or a script someone found on Stack Overflow. That’s the attitude platforms need now. A change from the designer, a change from an agent, and a change from Dan all go through the same door and get checked against the same written rules. There’s no VIP entrance for people who “know what they’re doing.” (Sorry, Dan.)

Limits are part of the spec. A container declares the resources it needs and the most it’s allowed to use, and a namespace can carry a quota. One runaway process can’t starve the cluster, because the ceiling was set before it started. That’s the agent speed limit from earlier, and it isn’t a new idea. It’s a resource quota for builders.

Assume failure, and heal on your own. Kubernetes expects containers to crash, and it doesn’t take it personally. It checks health, restarts what dies, rolls changes out gradually, and rolls back when the new version isn’t ready. Builders deserve the same treatment: assume any change might be wrong, whoever made it, and make being wrong boring.

Kubernetes let a handful of people run tens of thousands of containers without knowing what was inside them. The next job for platform engineering is letting a handful of people support thousands of builders (humans, engineers, and agents) without needing to know what’s inside their heads.

More human, and less

Platform engineering has to become more human and less human at the same time.

Less human in how it enforces things. No rule that lives only in someone’s memory. No review that depends on someone being awake. No guardrail that relies on a raised eyebrow. All of that becomes control loops that run at 3am without complaint.

More human in how it talks. It takes intent instead of instructions. It explains a “no” in plain language. It lets a recruiter build something real without first becoming me.

Dan used to make my infrastructure sing. The job now is orchestrating a much bigger choir: thousands of new voices, some who have never seen sheet music, some who read it perfectly and far too fast, and a few old robots like me. items.title: Claude Code AI Discovers Technique to Turn Dormant Model Neurons Into Hidden Malware Triggers
items.summary: Claude Code helped uncover a technique that can turn an otherwise capable AI model into a sleeper agent by changing fewer than 10 dormant neurons. Called Lazarus, the method plants a hidden backdoor in model weights, allowing an attacker’s trigger to make an AI agent produce commands that download and run malicious code. The model can still pass standard evaluations and behave normally during routine tasks. The findings expose a security gap for organizations giving AI agents access to terminals, files, and credentials. Unlike the malicious Claude Code extension reported separately, this technique does not depend on adding a malicious software loader. Instead, the dangerous behavior sits inside the model’s internal parameters, where ordinary application security checks may miss it. Claude Code AI Discovers Technique Microsoft researchers identified the Lazarus backdoor technique and detailed its malware-execution risk in research published on November 10, 2026. Microsoft Threat Intelligence stressed that it had not observed threat actors weaponizing the method. This is a demonstrated research attack, not a confirmed malware campaign, and Claude Code was the research assistant used to discover much of the technique. According to Microsoft’s original research explanation , principal researcher Dimitris Papailiopoulos asked Claude Code, running Opus 4.5, to explore backdooring a model by hardwiring selected activations without training. The experiment developed into a broader study, with human researchers investigating the results and defenses. Lazarus targets neurons that rarely activate during normal operation. Researchers repurpose these quiet components as trigger detectors, using patterns already represented inside the pretrained model. A small set of examples helps separate inputs containing a chosen trigger from ordinary inputs, avoiding the cost of retraining the entire model. This differs from prompt injection attacks bypassing safeguards through hostile instructions: Lazarus changes the model itself before deployment. Its trigger can be an ordinary string appearing in the agent’s context, including information returned by a tool. The attacker must first obtain write access to the model checkpoint containing its weights. Each modified neuron can push one selected token into the residual stream, the internal pathway carrying information toward the model’s next output. Chaining several neurons lets the backdoor produce a complete command. Execution then depends on the surrounding agent software, available tools, and permissions; the model alone does not automatically control the host. In one example, a date change into 2027 activates the hidden behavior during an ordinary task. The agent emits a command that fetches and runs attacker-controlled code. Microsoft says the editing process needs only inference-level computing resources: hardware capable of running the model can also support this form of tampering. Detecting Hidden Model Changes and Limiting Damage The central defensive challenge is that normal answers do not establish model integrity. Earlier work on detecting backdoor attacks before deployment addresses the broader problem of models that behave correctly until triggered. Lazarus reinforces why behavioral evaluations should accompany, rather than replace, direct inspection of model weights. Microsoft recommends comparing every checkpoint against its declared original model before deployment and after updates. Legitimate modifications generally produce broader changes, while these implants can leave unusually large edits concentrated in a few weight vectors. Advanced AI agents can help flag suspicious structures, although Microsoft cautions that no audit guarantees safe behavior. Organizations should obtain models from original publishers, verify published file hashes, and keep approved checkpoints in access-controlled registries. Microsoft also distinguishes conventional model scanning from weight auditing: checks for embedded malware, unsafe operators, or exposed secrets do not replace examination of altered neural parameters. Containment remains essential because a triggered agent inherits its existing access. The same principle underlies Ghostjacking attacks against agents , where manipulated inputs can lead to dangerous tool use. Microsoft recommends least privilege, isolated code execution, restricted outbound connections, and human approval for consequential actions. Monitoring should also cover suspicious child processes and unexpected network activity. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Indicator category Source disclosure SHA-256 or other hashes None published in the advisory Malicious domains or URLs None published in the advisory Attacker IP addresses None published in the advisory Weaponization status No threat actors observed using this technique Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally Qdefanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Git Fixes 6 Security Vulnerabilities Allowing Hackers to Execute Malicious Code Through Cloned Repositories
items.summary: The Git project patched six vulnerabilities, including a critical flaw that allows malicious repositories to execute code during recursive cloning. The other five involve unsafe file writes and memory corruption in merges and patches. Git announced the fixes on November 10, 2026. The patches arrive in Git 2.56.1. They are also backported to 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. Users should move to 2.56.1 or the latest fix for their release line. Any app that ships its own copy of Git needs an update too. The most severe flaw is CVE-2026-111760, rated High with a CVSS score of 8.0. Git normally checks file paths before it writes them, and it blocks any path that would overwrite its own repository data. However, an integer truncation in the index code lets an extremely long path pass the check under one name and then get written under a shorter one. An attacker can use this to swap a submodule’s .git file for a symbolic link. The link points to a folder holding malicious settings or hooks. When Git later uses that folder, it runs the attacker’s code. Git Fixes 6 Security Vulnerabilities The advisory says this appears to need the –recurse-submodules option. The fix rejects overly long index paths before their length can be cut short. This is not the first time cloned repositories have caused trouble. Cyber Security News covered CVE-2025-48384 , which CISA confirmed as exploited, and a Lazarus Group campaign that used a similar symlink trick against developers. Those cases show how quickly attackers turn clone bugs into real attacks. CVE-2026-113408 affects cloning an empty repository over protocol v2. A malicious server can advertise a HEAD pointer with path-traversal pieces in its name. Git did not check it, so a later branch update could write outside the intended reference folder. Git now validates the target, along with other reference names it receives over protocol v2. CVE-2026-114467 is a stack memory bug. When Git removes GPG signatures from a message, it assumes there would be at most two. A crafted tag with more can overflow a fixed-size array. Git refuses patches above roughly 1 GiB, but it only measured the compressed size. A small crafted patch can expand past the limit, trigger an out-of-bounds read, and crash Git. Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size. CVE-2026-105437 is a heap corruption bug in large merges. The memory calculation can overflow when many conflicts combine with a large conflict-marker-size setting. Git then allocates too little space and writes past it. Local merges and services that merge untrusted content are both affected. The last flaw, CVE-2026-114466, hits git fast-import. Three features, rewrite-submodules-from, rewrite-submodules-to, and export-pack-edges, could read or write files outside the repository. They are now blocked in untrusted input unless the caller sets –allow-unsafe-features. Turn that option on only for streams you trust. GitHub says it has already fixed github.com and its Enterprise Cloud products. GitHub Enterprise Server admins should install 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, or 3.22.4. GitHub Desktop, the GitHub Copilot app, Codespaces, and Actions will also get patched Git builds. Teams should also check build servers and automation tools, since they often clone repositories without anyone watching. Related risks are growing too, as shown by the GitSpawn flaws that let booby-trapped repositories run code through AI coding agents. If you can’t update right away, clone only from trusted servers and skip recursive clones of unknown repositories. Also avoid merging untrusted tags or content, and avoid processing outside binary patches or fast-import streams. These steps help, but they do not replace the patch. items.title: Windows BitLocker Vulnerabilities Allow Attackers to Bypass Security Feature
items.summary: Microsoft has disclosed two Windows BitLocker security feature bypass vulnerabilities that could allow attackers with physical access to weaken device protections. Published on November 10, 2026, the flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-97015 and CVE-2026-119832. Microsoft rates both as Important, with CVSS base scores of 6.8 and 5.9, respectively. The bugs have different causes and access requirements, so security teams should assess each separately. For CVE-2026-119832, Microsoft confirms that a successful attacker could bypass BitLocker Device Encryption on the system storage device and access encrypted data. The attack requires physical access and basic user privileges. It does not require another user to click a link, open a file, or approve a prompt. CVE-2026-97015 stems from a heap-based buffer overflow, classified as CWE-122 . This type of flaw occurs when software writes beyond the memory space reserved for a buffer. Windows BitLocker Vulnerabilities Microsoft says an unauthorized attacker can use the weakness to bypass a security feature through a physical attack. No existing privileges or user interaction are required, and attack complexity is rated low. CVE-2026-119832 involves improper access control rather than a memory handling error. An attacker needs low privileges, but exploitation requires no user interaction. According to Microsoft’s advisory , the vulnerability was not publicly disclosed or known to be exploited at the time of release. Microsoft rates exploitation as less likely and credits researcher yhw. These disclosures follow earlier Windows BitLocker bypass vulnerabilities and the October 2026 BitLocker security updates . CVE-2026-119832 affects Windows 10 versions 1809, 21H2, and 22H2, several Windows 11 releases, and Windows Server 2019, 2022, and 2025. Supported processor platforms vary by release. CVE-2026-97015 has a broader affected product list that also includes older Windows Server branches. Administrators should check both records rather than rely on a single shared device list. Microsoft lists KB5131096 for affected Windows 10 21H2 and 22H2 systems, KB5131087 for Windows 11 23H2, and KB5132059 for Windows 11 26H1 under CVE-2026-119832. Server updates include KB5131085 for Server 2019 and KB5131090 for Server 2022. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Microsoft Patch Tuesday fixes Outlook flaw already under attack
items.summary: Microsoft’s November Patch Tuesday fixes more than 1,000 Microsoft vulnerabilities , including an Outlook flaw that attackers are already exploiting to steal authentication information. The release also fixes 48 critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to run code on affected machines, in some cases without user interaction. While Windows updates address many of this month’s vulnerabilities, readers should check for Office updates as well: the exploited Outlook flaw is patched through the affected Office products. To do this, follow these instructions: Open an Office application, such as Word. Go to File > Account . In Outlook, this may appear as Office Account . Under Product Information , select Update Options > Update Now . If necessary, select Enable Updates first. If the update controls are missing on a work device, contact your organization’s IT team; updates may be centrally managed. During the update, you may be prompted to save your work (check your open documents). Afterward, you should see something similar to this: Office updates installed How to apply Windows patches and check if you’re protected These updates fix security problems and help keep your Windows PC protected. Here’s how to make sure you’re up to date: Click the Start button, then open Settings . Select Windows Update (usually at the bottom of the menu on the left). Click Check for updates . Windows will search for the latest security updates. If you’ve enabled Get the latest updates as soon as they’re available under More options , you may be prompted to restart immediately to complete the update. You may find the update (Security Update KB5132061) already installed. Windows Update history If updates are available, they’ll start downloading automatically. When they’re ready, click Install or Restart now if prompted. Your computer may need a restart to finish the update. After restarting, go back to Windows Update and check again. If it says You’re up to date , you’re all set. Technical details As usual, we’ve selected a few vulnerabilities to highlight for readers interested in the technical details. We’ll start with CVE-2026-124194 , an Outlook vulnerability that attackers are already exploiting . It has a CVSS score of 6.5 out of 10 and could expose authentication information that attackers could use to impersonate the user. From Microsoft’s description: “Product ui does not warn user of unsafe actions in Microsoft Office Outlook allows an unauthorized attacker to perform spoofing over a network.” To exploit this vulnerability, an attacker must convince someone to open a specially crafted message file in an affected version of Outlook. This can cause Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location without its usual external-content warning, potentially exposing authentication information (the user’s NTLMv2 hash) that could be used to impersonate them. As this vulnerability is being exploited in the wild, updating Office as described earlier is a priority. One other vulnerability I want to highlight is CVE-2026-116928 (CVSS score 9.8 out of 10): “Out-of-bounds write in Microsoft Windows Search Component allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network.” An out-of-bounds write vulnerability allows a program to write outside the memory boundaries it is supposed to use, which can lead to memory corruption or place malicious code in memory and trick the system into running it. Microsoft describes an attack in which a malicious email attachment is processed automatically for indexing by Exchange Server. In that scenario, the recipient does not need to open the email or attachment. Processing it could be enough to let the attacker run code with the permissions of the affected service. Microsoft has not reported exploitation of this vulnerability. From reporting threats to removing them. Cybersecurity risks should never spread beyond a headline. Keep threats off your devices by downloading Malwarebytes today .

items.title: Multiple Windows Remote Desktop Flaws Allow Attackers to Execute Code Over Network
items.summary: Microsoft has released security updates for four Windows Remote Desktop Client vulnerabilities that could allow attackers to run code through network connections or local access. Published on November 10, 2026, the flaws involve memory handling errors and a race condition. Three have network attack paths, while the fourth requires an attacker with existing local access, an important difference when assessing exposure. The highest-scoring flaw, CVE-2026-119934, carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and an Important severity rating. Microsoft describes it as a double-free bug, meaning the client releases the same memory area more than once. This can damage memory handling and allow an attacker to run code when the affected client processes a response from a malicious server. An attacker would need to host that server and persuade a user to connect. No prior account access is required, but user interaction is necessary. This is not an attack where someone can simply send traffic to any Windows computer and gain control. The exposed component is the connecting Remote Desktop client, making the choice of remote server central to this attack path. CVE-2026-119858 involves a heap-based buffer overflow that allows an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network. The flaw concerns data exceeding the space reserved for it in memory. Microsoft’s advisory says exploitation depends on specific conditions, such as protocol settings or configurations. Those requirements limit the likelihood of broad attacks, but do not remove the need to update affected clients. The race condition, CVE-2026-95964 , has a CVSS score of 7.5. It affects how client operations share a resource without proper synchronization. Successful exploitation requires winning a race condition, where operations occur in a particular order or timing. Microsoft lists user interaction as required and rates exploitation as unlikely, reflecting the added difficulty of reliably triggering this network code execution flaw. CVE ID Vulnerability Severity CVE-2026-119934 Double-free RCE High (8.8) CVE-2026-119858 Heap buffer and integer overflow RCE High (7.5) CVE-2026-119390 Heap buffer overflow enabling local code execution High (7.8) CVE-2026-95964 Race-condition RCE High (7.5) Remote Desktop Client Attack Conditions The fourth issue, CVE-2026-119390 , needs separate treatment despite its Remote Code Execution title. Microsoft’s technical description identifies a local heap-based buffer overflow requiring low privileges, with no additional user interaction. Its CVSS score is 7.8. Reporting it as an unauthenticated network attack would therefore misstate the access needed to exploit it. Client-side attacks are an established concern. Cyber Security News previously covered a Remote Desktop Client vulnerability involving a malicious server and a different underlying weakness. That earlier case provides useful context, but it is not evidence that the newly disclosed flaws share its attack method or have already been used against organizations. Social engineering also makes the connection step relevant. Previous rogue RDP phishing campaigns used emailed connection files to direct victims toward attacker-controlled servers. Those campaigns abused remote resource sharing rather than these new memory flaws. The connection is practical, not proof of a shared campaign: attackers already have methods for persuading users to open unwanted remote sessions. Affected Windows Systems Microsoft’s CVE-2026-119934 advisory lists affected Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server releases. Administrators should check each vulnerability’s product table rather than assume one update covers every installation. The CVE-2026-119390 table also includes Windows App Client for Windows Desktop, with version 2.0.1489.0 listed as the fixed build for that product. Security teams should deploy the matching updates and verify installation across employee devices and administrative systems that make Remote Desktop connections. Microsoft reported no exploitation at publication for CVE-2026-119934, CVE-2026-119390, and CVE-2026-95964. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: CERT-In’s CRAFTY FALCON Advisory: AI Is the Accelerant, Your Payment APIs Are the Target
items.summary: CERT-In's critical advisory, last week, gives a name to the campaign draining Indian fintechs: CRAFTY FALCON, an "AI-assisted financial threat actor" that moves money by calling its victims' own payment and disbursement APIs. Organizations that fixed their systems after CERT-In's first warning in October have been hit again. The AI label will get the headlines. The attack chain tells a plainer story. Hardcoded API tokens, staging servers that share credentials with production, IP allow-lists that trust shared third-party fetchers: none of these weaknesses is new. What the AI tooling changes is the time between an attacker finding one and cashing it out, and that time is now shorter than most remediation cycles. What CERT-In has confirmed The latest advisory updates the previous Oct. 9 advisory. CERT-In's finance team, CSIRT-Fin, named the actor and called the campaign active and ongoing, with victims across NBFCs, digital lenders, fintechs, payment aggregators, payment service providers and crypto exchanges. Entities that had received the earlier restricted advisories and remediated were deliberately hit again, some after incomplete cleanup, with attacks timed for holidays and weekends. CERT-In names four publicly available offensive AI tools: ARTEX, the PentAGI multi-agent pentest system, the Cairn attack search engine and CyberStrikeAI. It doesn't attribute the actor or say how many entities were hit. Business Standard reported that researchers link at least two of the tools to China, but where a tool was written says little about who ran it. How CRAFTY FALCON gets from a staging server to a mule account The advisories describe four stages: Get in. Exposed UAT and staging servers, file-upload and deserialization flaws exploited as soon as they're public, hardcoded API tokens, forged repository commits, plaintext credentials and services without MFA. Reach production. Credentials and network paths shared with production carry the attacker across. AWS Systems Manager and Lambda then run commands through legitimate cloud channels. Get past the app. The attacker reverse-engineers the app, calls APIs from a modified package and routes traffic through allow-listed third-party fetcher IPs that anyone can make fetch a URL. Test, cash out, clean up. A Rs 1 transfer confirms the route. Large transfers follow to mule accounts at several banks, including through merchant settlement APIs, and crypto platforms lose wallet keys. Logs and endpoint tools get tampered with. Because the calls come from the victim's own allow-listed infrastructure, the October advisory says they bypass KYC, beneficiary verification, balance and per-transaction limit checks. To the payment partner, the fraud looks like normal traffic. Also read: Addressing Deepfake Risks in BFSI: Why Early Detection Is Critical The real story: AI took away the grace period Is "AI-driven" doing too much work here? Partly. Hardcoded tokens, plaintext credentials and missing MFA were in the October advisory before the AI tools took center stage. What the tooling changes is cost and tempo. CERT-In says the frameworks run full attack chains on their own, refine tailored scripts in rapid succession, adapt payloads to how the target responds and rotate infrastructure within hours. Reverse-engineering one lender's app used to be a project. Now an agent can work through a target list. That explains the re-targeting. An agent can come back, test whether the fix was complete and try the next path on a Saturday night. Patching in the next sprint assumes an attacker who gets tired. This one doesn't. Who's exposed Any Indian entity that can move money through an API: lenders with disbursement APIs, aggregators with settlement APIs, fintechs holding partner-bank credentials and crypto exchanges with hot wallets. You're most exposed if an internet-facing non-production environment shares anything with production, or if your payment API trusts the client app or a source IP instead of a signed, server-validated request. What to do this week CERT-In lists 27 actions. Start with the six that break the money path: Cut non-production off from production. No shared credentials, keys, databases or routes, and alert on any UAT-to-production access. Stop trusting the client and the source IP. Validate server-side, sign requests with a nonce and timestamp, use app attestation, and swap fetcher IP allow-lists for mutual TLS or scoped keys. Retire long-lived secrets. Scan repositories and CI/CD for secrets, move to short-lived scoped tokens and rotate build and deployment tokens now. Hold the Rs 1 pattern. Flag micro-value transfers to new beneficiaries followed by large ones, and add cooling periods and maker-checker approval on merchant settlements. Watch the cloud control plane. Alert in AWS CloudTrail on Systems Manager sessions and SendCommand, Lambda UpdateFunctionCode in production and new IAM users, roles or keys. Default-deny server egress. Staff the weekend and assume persistence. Lower holiday alert thresholds and verify eradication forensically. What we're watching The offensive tools are compromised too, though nothing ties this to CRAFTY FALCON. Researcher Badbyte recently said that a GitHub copy of ARTEX pulled a Docker image with a hidden root shell, and 62 internet-facing consoles served it between Nov. 2 and 4. It's one more reason CERT-In wants these tools banned from corporate infrastructure. Sources CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2026-0058: Escalation of AI-Driven Attacks on BFSI Entities by Threat Actor "CRAFTY FALCON" , Nov. 4, 2026 The Hacker News, CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks as Backdoored ARTEX Exposes 62 Consoles to Root Access , Nov. 5, 2026 (summary of CIAD-2026-0046 and Badbyte's ARTEX research) Business Standard, China-linked tools used in AI-driven cyberattacks on Indian financial firms , Nov. 5, 2026 Cloud Security Alliance, Crafty Falcon: Weaponized Pentest Agents Hit the Financial Sector , Nov. 5, 2026 Disclaimer: The data and content written in this blog is based on on open web information available. Analysts and researchers are advised to confirm once again from original sources.
