The AI label will get the headlines. The attack chain tells a plainer story. Hardcoded API tokens, staging servers that share credentials with production, IP allow-lists that trust shared third-party fetchers: none of these weaknesses is new. What the AI tooling changes is the time between an attacker finding one and cashing it out, and that time is now shorter than most remediation cycles.

What CERT-In has confirmed

The latest advisory updates the previous Oct. 9 advisory. CERT-In's finance team, CSIRT-Fin, named the actor and called the campaign active and ongoing, with victims across NBFCs, digital lenders, fintechs, payment aggregators, payment service providers and crypto exchanges.

Entities that had received the earlier restricted advisories and remediated were deliberately hit again, some after incomplete cleanup, with attacks timed for holidays and weekends.

CERT-In names four publicly available offensive AI tools: ARTEX, the PentAGI multi-agent pentest system, the Cairn attack search engine and CyberStrikeAI. It doesn't attribute the actor or say how many entities were hit. Business Standard reported that researchers link at least two of the tools to China, but where a tool was written says little about who ran it.

How CRAFTY FALCON gets from a staging server to a mule account

The advisories describe four stages:

  • Get in. Exposed UAT and staging servers, file-upload and deserialization flaws exploited as soon as they're public, hardcoded API tokens, forged repository commits, plaintext credentials and services without MFA.

  • Reach production. Credentials and network paths shared with production carry the attacker across. AWS Systems Manager and Lambda then run commands through legitimate cloud channels.

  • Get past the app. The attacker reverse-engineers the app, calls APIs from a modified package and routes traffic through allow-listed third-party fetcher IPs that anyone can make fetch a URL.

  • Test, cash out, clean up. A Rs 1 transfer confirms the route. Large transfers follow to mule accounts at several banks, including through merchant settlement APIs, and crypto platforms lose wallet keys. Logs and endpoint tools get tampered with.

Because the calls come from the victim's own allow-listed infrastructure, the October advisory says they bypass KYC, beneficiary verification, balance and per-transaction limit checks. To the payment partner, the fraud looks like normal traffic.

Also read: Addressing Deepfake Risks in BFSI: Why Early Detection Is Critical

The real story: AI took away the grace period

Is "AI-driven" doing too much work here? Partly. Hardcoded tokens, plaintext credentials and missing MFA were in the October advisory before the AI tools took center stage.

What the tooling changes is cost and tempo. CERT-In says the frameworks run full attack chains on their own, refine tailored scripts in rapid succession, adapt payloads to how the target responds and rotate infrastructure within hours. Reverse-engineering one lender's app used to be a project. Now an agent can work through a target list.

That explains the re-targeting. An agent can come back, test whether the fix was complete and try the next path on a Saturday night. Patching in the next sprint assumes an attacker who gets tired. This one doesn't.

Who's exposed

Any Indian entity that can move money through an API: lenders with disbursement APIs, aggregators with settlement APIs, fintechs holding partner-bank credentials and crypto exchanges with hot wallets. You're most exposed if an internet-facing non-production environment shares anything with production, or if your payment API trusts the client app or a source IP instead of a signed, server-validated request.

What to do this week

CERT-In lists 27 actions. Start with the six that break the money path:

  1. Cut non-production off from production. No shared credentials, keys, databases or routes, and alert on any UAT-to-production access.

  2. Stop trusting the client and the source IP. Validate server-side, sign requests with a nonce and timestamp, use app attestation, and swap fetcher IP allow-lists for mutual TLS or scoped keys.

  3. Retire long-lived secrets. Scan repositories and CI/CD for secrets, move to short-lived scoped tokens and rotate build and deployment tokens now.

  4. Hold the Rs 1 pattern. Flag micro-value transfers to new beneficiaries followed by large ones, and add cooling periods and maker-checker approval on merchant settlements.

  5. Watch the cloud control plane. Alert in AWS CloudTrail on Systems Manager sessions and SendCommand, Lambda UpdateFunctionCode in production and new IAM users, roles or keys. Default-deny server egress.

  6. Staff the weekend and assume persistence. Lower holiday alert thresholds and verify eradication forensically.

What we're watching

The offensive tools are compromised too, though nothing ties this to CRAFTY FALCON. Researcher Badbyte recently said that a GitHub copy of ARTEX pulled a Docker image with a hidden root shell, and 62 internet-facing consoles served it between Nov. 2 and 4. It's one more reason CERT-In wants these tools banned from corporate infrastructure.

Sources

CERT-In, Advisory CIAD-2026-0058: Escalation of AI-Driven Attacks on BFSI Entities by Threat Actor "CRAFTY FALCON", Nov. 4, 2026

The Hacker News, CERT-In Flags AI-Driven Attacks as Backdoored ARTEX Exposes 62 Consoles to Root Access, Nov. 5, 2026 (summary of CIAD-2026-0046 and Badbyte's ARTEX research)

Business Standard, China-linked tools used in AI-driven cyberattacks on Indian financial firms, Nov. 5, 2026 Cloud Security Alliance, Crafty Falcon: Weaponized Pentest Agents Hit the Financial Sector, Nov. 5, 2026

items.title: AI Agents Promise Convenience, But Are We Giving Them Too Much Control?
items.summary: AI agents are quickly becoming part of everyday life, moving beyond answering questions and generating content to carrying out tasks on users’ behalf. From booking holidays and managing diaries to making purchases and accessing personal accounts, the technology promises to make our lives easier than ever before. However, as AI agents become increasingly autonomous, questions are emerging about how much control people are willing to hand over and whether adequate safeguards are in place. Research commissioned by cybersecurity PR agency Eskenzi PR and conducted by Censuswide among 2,000 UK adults found that 84% would give AI agents only moderate or low control over their daily lives, or none at all . More than a third (34%) wouldn’t feel comfortable giving AI agents any control whatsoever, suggesting that while consumers recognise the potential benefits of AI, many remain hesitant about allowing it to act independently. Security concerns are holding back trust As AI agents gain greater access to sensitive information and personal accounts, the potential consequences of security failures become increasingly significant. Eskenzi’s research found that 36% of Brits are concerned about their personal data being hacked or stolen when using AI agents. Almost a third (31%) worry an AI agent could make a mistake, while 30% are concerned about it having access to too much personal information. Financial security is another major concern, with 28% worried that an AI agent could spend their money or make purchases they never intended to authorise. Perhaps most surprisingly, one in seven (14%) fear an AI agent could implicate them in something illegal, rising to 21% among 18 to 24-year-olds. These concerns highlight the security challenges associated with giving autonomous systems access to personal information and the ability to perform actions on behalf of users. Unlike traditional AI chatbots, which primarily generate responses to user prompts, AI agents may be connected to external applications and granted permissions to interact with accounts and services. This introduces potential risks around compromised credentials, excessive permissions and malicious instructions designed to manipulate an agent’s behaviour. For cybersecurity professionals, ensuring these systems operate within clearly defined boundaries will be essential to reducing the risks associated with wider adoption. People want assistance, not complete autonomy Despite concerns about security, the findings suggest that consumers are not rejecting AI entirely. Instead, they appear more comfortable using it as an assistant than allowing it to make important decisions independently. More than a quarter (27%) of respondents would allow an AI agent to prepare tasks for them but would want to approve every action. A further 23% would allow AI to handle routine tasks independently while requiring permission for more significant decisions. There are also clear generational differences. Almost half of over-55s (47%) would not give AI agents any control over their daily lives, compared with 21% of 18 to 24-year-olds. The findings suggest that organisations developing AI agents need to consider how much autonomy users are comfortable granting, rather than assuming greater independence will always be welcomed. Introducing meaningful human approval checkpoints, limiting agent permissions and ensuring users can review actions before they are completed could help organisations address some of these concerns. Who takes responsibility when AI goes wrong? Beyond security and privacy, the research raises important questions about accountability. When asked who should bear primary responsibility if an AI agent with access to their accounts was hacked, tricked or carried out an unauthorised action, 40% of respondents pointed to the company that developed the AI. A further 25% believed responsibility should sit with the company or service the agent was accessing, while only 18% thought the individual using the AI should be primarily responsible. While these findings reflect public expectations rather than legal liability, they demonstrate the importance of establishing clear accountability as autonomous systems become more widespread. The implications extend to businesses deploying AI agents in customer-facing and decision-making processes. When asked how they would react if a company they relied on used an AI agent to advise its board on important decisions, 37% wanted reassurance that a human would always have the final say. Meanwhile, 20% said they would consider switching provider, suggesting that concerns around AI oversight could also have reputational and commercial consequences. Building confidence through security and transparency AI agents have the potential to deliver significant improvements in convenience and productivity, but their growing autonomy creates new responsibilities for developers and organisations deploying the technology. Clear permission controls, secure authentication, monitoring, audit trails and human oversight can all play an important role in reducing risks and improving accountability. Equally important is ensuring that users understand what an AI agent can access, what actions it can perform and how they can intervene if something goes wrong. The research suggests that consumers are willing to embrace the benefits of AI, provided they can retain control over decisions that matter. As AI agents become more integrated into everyday life, the challenge for the cybersecurity industry will be ensuring that innovation is accompanied by the security, transparency and safeguards needed to earn public trust. The research was conducted by Censuswide among a nationally representative sample of 2,000 UK adults between 16 and 18 September 2026, on behalf of Eskenzi PR. Read the full Eskenzi PR research .

items.title: Finding it a day later isn’t protecting it
items.summary: In September, Delinea published new research on how AI behaves inside companies. Of the 2,254 IT and security leaders it surveyed, 87% said an AI tool or agent had accessed sensitive data beyond what its task needed in the past year. And 55% of organizations said it takes a full day or longer to catch an agent that steps outside its scope. The report also shows where the gap sits. 99.7% of organizations have a formal policy on what data AI tools and agents can access, but only 51% check access against that policy in real time. In a separate survey of 2,250 non-IT employees, 76% said they have bypassed the required approval to use AI, and 60% said they felt pressured to use AI on sensitive or confidential data when they weren’t sure it was allowed. Source: Delinea, 2026 Identity Security Report: The AI Enforcement Gap , Sept. 2026. Policies and approvals say what is allowed. They don’t change what is in the file when someone, or something, gets there anyway. PK Protect protects the file itself. What a data security platform does PK Protect finds sensitive data on endpoints, in the cloud, in Microsoft 365, and on z/OS and IBM i mainframes. It classifies what it finds under one classification policy, so the fix matches the data. Then it acts: encrypt it, mask it, or redact it. Part 2 compares this with DLP and DSPM. What changes about the day-long gap A late alert tells you what an agent reached. When PK Protect encrypts a file, the protection stays on the file after it moves. An agent that hasn’t been given access to the key can reach the file and still can’t read it. An agent working on a person’s behalf can open what that person can open, which is why controls on the agent still matter. This covers the file types PK Protect can protect. If someone keeps an unprotected original, that copy isn’t covered. On supported databases, warehouses, and cloud storage, sensitive values are masked instead, so there is no key. A late alert tells you what an agent reached. When PK Protect encrypts a file, the protection stays on the file after it moves. items.title: The SASE “Trilemma”: How Regulated Enterprises are Navigating Digital Sovereignty, Resilience, and Global Cyber Threat Intelligence
items.summary: Modern enterprise architecture faces a critical tension: architecting a Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) deployment where data sovereignty, operational resilience, and global cybersecurity are perceived to be fundamentally at odds. To address this, we first must look at what modern SASE truly requires. It is not merely the basic convergence of cloud security and SD-WAN. Rather, Prisma SASE converges networking and security into a cloud-native architecture that delivers continuous Zero Trust access—unifying continuous trust verification, security inspection, and data protection for any user, device, or branch accessing apps across data centers, clouds, and SaaS. Built on a foundation of unified data and runtime security and resilient, always-on infrastructure, it advances this architecture to secure the future of work. It protects with AI to close every security gap before attackers have a chance to exploit it, secures AI by enforcing visibility and governance across GenAI and agentic workflows, and operates with AI to automate lifecycle management and reduce total cost of ownership. However, when mapping this advanced architecture to the strict compliance, data protection, and infrastructure mandates of European governments, healthcare, and critical infrastructure, a "trilemma" emerges: The Digital Sovereignty vs. Threat Intelligence Trap Regulated entities demand in-country data processing and zero cross-border data leakage. Yet, defending against zero-day exploits requires inspecting telemetry at a global scale. Some vendors attempt to solve this by simply dropping their global software into a single, regional cloud provider's data center. This often forces a compromise: either telemetry is still sent abroad, violating true digital sovereignty, or the deployment is entirely cut off, resulting in a localized, air-gapped security posture that is blind to global threat actor infrastructure. The Resilience vs. Jurisdictional Hard Walls Dilemma For critical infrastructure, a network outage is existential. Recent market attempts to address sovereignty involve security vendors partnering with a single, regional cloud infrastructure provider to host their services locally. While this may check a data residency box, it introduces a massive single point of failure. If that specific local cloud experiences an outage or a routing issue, the enterprise network goes dark. Organizations are forced to trade architectural resilience for jurisdictional compliance. Cryptographic Control vs. Network Performance Deep packet inspection requires TLS decryption. Mandating Customer-Managed Keys (CMK) via local Hardware Security Modules (HSMs) often forces traffic hairpinning, introducing latency that destroys the end-user experience. Solving the Trilemma: Sovereign Prisma SASE by Palo Alto Networks For years, organizations faced an unresolvable trade-off: world-class global protection, strict local regulatory adherence, or cobbled-together single-cloud infrastructure partnerships. Following the launch of Sovereign Cortex , Palo Alto Networks is introducing Sovereign Prisma SASE , which extends the same comprehensive SASE solution with specific sovereignty controls. Designed for specific, highly regulated organizations requiring EU digital sovereignty controls, it maintains consistent features and functionality with Prisma SASE Commercial. Instead of bolting a security platform onto a single third-party regional cloud, Sovereign Prisma SASE allows enterprises to leverage purpose-built architectural innovations: A Multi-Cloud Approach to True Resilience To solve the clash between failover and jurisdiction without introducing single points of failure, Sovereign Prisma SASE is built upon a highly resilient, multi-cloud backbone. Rather than relying on a single local cloud provider, all cloud components leverage Sovereign CSP solutions. This multi-cloud redundancy ensures that if one underlying infrastructure fails, traffic dynamically routes to an alternate provider within the same jurisdiction, preserving both operational uptime and strict data residency. Advanced Hybrid Architecture Relying entirely on a regional public cloud for digital sovereignty also ignores the reality of highly sensitive environments. Sovereign Prisma SASE offers a deeply integrated hybrid architecture. Organizations can also deploy a SASE Private Location to process sensitive traffic and hold encryption keys for core OT, patient records, or state databases. Crucially, this localized processing securely feeds anonymized telemetry into global threat lakes, ensuring that strict data residency does not forfeit machine-speed threat prevention. Uncompromising Sovereign Controls Alongside our AI-driven security, multi-cloud resilience, and hybrid flexibility, Sovereign Prisma SASE is compliant with local regulations and delivers the strict technical controls required by European boards: EU Data Residency & Access: Establishes an EU-region data boundary. Administrative access is restricted to EU-only admin personnel, and the solution performs in-jurisdiction break and inspect. Encryption & Key Control: Empowers organizations with a "Hold Your Own Key" model. Provider Transparency: Provides readily available audit trail logs, which include user geo-location data for compliance teams. Local Operations: All operations rely on EU-based Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) and Support. The Bottom Line Sovereign Prisma SASE bridges the gap between regulatory compliance and real-world defense. Digital sovereignty without global threat intelligence is an isolated vulnerability, and relying on a single regional cloud provider for resilience is an outage waiting to happen. The future of enterprise architecture isn't settling for disjointed infrastructure partnerships—it’s adopting a cohesive, cloud-native, AI-powered SASE platform designed from the ground up to deliver security, resilience, and sovereignty simultaneously. items.title: New GhostFrame Malware Lets Hackers Hijack VMware ESXi VMs and Steal Windows Credentials
items.summary: A new hacking toolkit called GhostFrame gives criminals a single control panel for taking over VMware ESXi servers and the virtual machines that run on them. Researchers at Recorded Future’s Insikt Group found the framework while tracking a group named TAG-218, whose activity overlaps with Settra ransomware. The tool can also pull Windows passwords out of hosted machines without ever running a program inside them. The key point is where GhostFrame works. ESXi is a hypervisor, the layer that runs many virtual machines on one physical server. If a criminal controls that layer, they can reach every system on it. Security tools inside each virtual machine often cannot see what is happening below them. Insikt Group’s report says the framework does not exploit a bug to get in. The operator must already have root access to the ESXi host. GhostFrame Stays on the Server The framework has a web panel with two sections, “Sessions” and “Builder.” The builder creates an ESXi implant named vmhostd-core. Once it runs, it copies itself to /opt/vmhostd-core and edits the boot script /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh so it starts again after every reboot. The script also turns off the ESXi firewall and the execInstalledOnly setting, which normally blocks unsigned programs. It repeats this about every five seconds, so an administrator who turns the protections back on loses them again almost at once. The implant calls /sbin/auto-backup.sh to save its changes across restarts. It also renames itself vmhostd, which looks like VMware’s real vmware-hostd service, to hide in plain sight. The implant tries six network ports at the same time to reach its command server: 53, 2222, 3389, 4444, 8443 and 9443. It keeps the first connection that works and drops the rest. If nothing connects within thirty seconds, it waits between five and twelve seconds and tries again. That pattern can show up as six nearly simultaneous connection requests from one ESXi host to one address, which gives defenders a useful clue to hunt for. After connecting, the implant loads code straight into memory and runs it, so nothing is written to disk. If it cannot get memory for that, it falls back to a plain /bin/sh reverse shell. GhostFrame lets an operator list virtual machines, change their power state, and create or delete snapshots. It can switch on VNC remote screen access and send the screen view through its own servers to the panel. It can also expose the ESXi HTML Host Client, which is the management website for the hypervisor. A SOCKS5 proxy tool named gfsox lets operators send traffic through the host to reach internal systems that are hidden from the internet. The credential theft features matter most. A component called sdkmon changes the ESXi service setup and captures the usernames and passwords of later ESXi logins. GhostFrame also includes VMkatz, an open-source tool. It pulls secrets from VM memory snapshots, virtual disk images, or a scan of every VM on a datastore. The data it can recover includes NTLM hashes, WDigest credentials, Kerberos tickets, SAM and LSA secrets, and NTDS.dit data. In short, a criminal can steal Windows passwords from the outside, with no malware installed in the guest. Link to Settra Ransomware and VPN Break-Ins Insikt Group watched TAG-218 servers go after VPN devices in the US and Europe from late August to October 2026. The targets were mostly SonicWall, Palo Alto Networks, and Fortinet products. Four of those victims later appeared on the Settra leak site. The same servers connected to two GhostFrame command servers and a MeshCentral server used to maintain access. On October 12, 2026, a Fortinet VPN device was seen contacting both GhostFrame and MeshCentral. Huntress had already tied MeshCentral to Settra. Its report shows the group installing MeshAgent for lasting access, using a vulnerable driver, clearing Windows logs, and blocking recovery. Our earlier coverage of the Settra ransomware and its MeshAgent tricks covers those steps in more detail. The timing matches the recent abuse of CVE-2026-0257, a flaw in Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect that lets someone open a VPN session without valid credentials or MFA. Unit 42’s updated guidance says intruders moved from the VPN to the virtualization layer in one case. They turned off execInstalledOnly and used a custom tool to dump domain controller credentials straight from a virtual disk. That skips security software inside the guest. We reported on how hackers used this Palo Alto VPN flaw to steal credentials from VMware disks , and the GhostFrame findings fit the same pattern. Fixes for the Palo Alto flaw have been out since May 2026. Start by locking down who can reach ESXi. Allow management access only from trusted systems and look into any unexpected root logins or setting changes. Watch for edits to /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh, new files under /opt, and the repeated firewall and execInstalledOnly changes. Look at network logs for the burst of six connection attempts to one address. Patch VPN devices quickly and review the earlier reporting on ransomware groups targeting VMware ESXi for more hardening ideas. Insikt Group does not know if GhostFrame is limited to Settra or how it is shared. Still, it says it is highly likely that other money-driven criminals will use GhostFrame or similar ESXi tools. Treat your hypervisors as high-value systems and give them the same close watch you give domain controllers. Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: Critical Fortinet Flaws Expose FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer to Remote Code Execution Without Login
items.summary: Fortinet has disclosed critical security flaws affecting FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer, and FortiOS, including weaknesses that could let attackers execute code without logging in. Published on November 10, 2026, the disclosures cover management APIs, device communication services, routing, and specific high availability setups. Attack requirements differ, making enabled features and network access central to assessing exposure. Critical Fortinet Flaws Patched The highest-rated issue, CVE-2026-126170, carries a CVSS score of 9.8. Tracked as FG-IR-26-219 , it involves JSON injection in the JSON-RPC API used by FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer. When the JSON API is enabled, crafted requests could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code or commands. Systems using the API for automation need close review. Another critical flaw, CVE-2026-126261, affects FortiManager’s FGFM service. Rated 9.0 and tracked as FG-IR-26-275 , the authorization weakness allows attackers who can reach the FGFM port to send crafted packets and potentially execute code. The problem occurs before the registration password is verified, placing the service itself within the attack path. CVE-2026-126262, tracked as FG-IR-26-276 and rated 9.3, exposes FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager systems with FortiAnalyzer features enabled to SQL injection through OFTP. An attacker does not need to log in, and successful exploitation could lead to code execution. This makes access to the log transfer service an important part of exposure checks. The disclosures follow the October security releases previously covered in Cyber Security News’ Fortinet patch warning . Fortinet released updates before publishing the detailed advisories, giving customers time to upgrade. However, administrators should not assume that installing one October build resolves every November finding, because fixes vary by vulnerability and software branch. Fortinet’s FGFM advisory lists FortiManager 8.0.0, 7.6.0 through 7.6.7, 7.4.0 through 7.4.5, and 7.2.0 through 7.2.8 as affected by CVE-2026-126261. Fixed releases are 8.0.1, 7.6.8, 7.4.6, and 7.2.9, respectively. Fortinet marks this issue as not known to have been exploited when published. CVE-2026-126260, tracked as FG-IR-26-274, adds a separate OFTP risk. Rated 9.0, this pre-authentication server-side request forgery flaw affects FortiAnalyzer and FortiManager with FortiAnalyzer features enabled. It should not be confused with confirmed remote code execution. Its impact involves causing the server to make requests, while the SQL injection issue provides a different attack path. These weaknesses also show why protecting the browser login page is not enough. FGFM uses TCP port 541, while OFTP uses TCP port 514. Administrative login restrictions do not directly protect those services. Earlier FortiManager compromise reporting showed how access to a central management appliance could expose sensitive information linked to hundreds of managed firewalls. Routing and Access Controls Also Affected The broader release includes CVE-2026-126254, a 9.6-rated numeric truncation flaw in FortiOS BGP handling that requires traffic from a configured iBGP neighbor. CVE-2026-126253, rated 9.3, concerns an OSPF authentication bypass that could permit forged routing advertisements. These are routing risks, not interchangeable examples of management server code execution. CVE-2026-126229, rated 9.1, could allow an authenticated administrator to access other virtual domains, or VDOMs, outside their permitted scope. Separately, CVE-2026-126259 carries a 9.0 rating and allows command execution with super-admin privileges in specific FortiOS setups involving FGSP with standalone configuration synchronization, or affected autoscale configurations. Neither issue should be described as affecting every deployment equally. Fortinet’s security release guidance urges customers to prioritize exposed systems, back up configurations, and monitor unauthorized changes. For CVE-2026-126170, the 8.0 branch requires particular attention because 8.0.3 was listed as forthcoming. Disabling unused JSON API access with set rpc-permit none reduces exposure while administrators verify the latest advisory and plan the appropriate update.

items.title: Microsoft Confirms Hackers Are Exploiting Outlook 0-Day to Steal Windows Authentication Hashes
items.summary: Microsoft has confirmed that hackers are exploiting an Outlook zero-day that can expose Windows authentication information when a user opens a malicious file. Tracked as CVE-2026-124194, the spoofing vulnerability was patched on November 10, 2026. Microsoft marks it “Exploitation Detected” and says it was not publicly disclosed before the update. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 6.5 and a Moderate severity rating. However, confirmed attacks make it a patching priority. Microsoft’s Exploitability Index states that “Exploitation Detected” means the company knows of actual exploitation, not just that attackers could develop a working exploit. Outlook 0-Day Vulnerability An attacker does not need an account or prior access to the target’s system. Instead, they send a specially crafted message file and convince the recipient to open it in an affected Outlook version. Successful exploitation requires both user interaction and network connectivity. Opening the file can cause Outlook to connect to a network location controlled by the attacker without showing its usual external-content warning. Microsoft classifies the underlying weakness as CWE-356, where a product’s interface fails to warn users about unsafe actions. The missing warning removes an important chance to stop the connection. Microsoft explicitly states that the Preview Pane is not an attack vector. Simply previewing a message does not meet the documented exploitation requirements. That separates this flaw from earlier Outlook attacks covered in Cybersecuritynews.com’s report on Russian hackers exploiting Outlook , which involved a different vulnerability requiring no user action. According to Microsoft’s advisory , successful exploitation discloses the user’s NTLMv2 hash, potentially allowing an attacker to authenticate as that user. This is authentication-data theft, not evidence that the flaw directly runs malicious code. Microsoft rates confidentiality impact as High, with no direct integrity or availability impact. NTLM-related leaks can support follow-on attacks, depending on the receiving service’s protections. Microsoft’s earlier Outlook investigation documented authentication relay and offline password cracking as possible uses of captured Net-NTLMv2 data. Cybersecuritynews.com’s coverage of compromised Ubiquiti routers shows how attackers previously used external infrastructure for credential theft. Those historical details do not establish attribution for this new campaign. Affected Versions Affected products include Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise and Office LTSC 2021 and 2024, across 32-bit and 64-bit editions. Microsoft lists fixed builds 16.0.14334.21048 for LTSC 2021 and 16.0.17932.21140 for LTSC 2024. Administrators should deploy the applicable Office security updates promptly. As added protection, Microsoft recommends blocking unnecessary outbound SMB traffic on TCP port 445 to the internet. This limits external SMB exposure but does not replace installing the Outlook fix. Affected product Architecture Fixed build / security update Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise 32-bit Install the applicable November 2026 security update for the deployed update channel. Microsoft does not list a single fixed build in the advisory. Microsoft 365 Apps for Enterprise 64-bit Install the applicable November 2026 security update for the deployed update channel. Microsoft does not list a single fixed build in the advisory. Microsoft Office LTSC 2024 32-bit 16.0.17932.21140 Microsoft Office LTSC 2024 64-bit 16.0.17932.21140 Microsoft Office LTSC 2021 32-bit 16.0.14334.21048 Microsoft Office LTSC 2021 64-bit 16.0.14334.21048 Give your SOC the alert context to stops incidents quickly. items.title: The SIEM Zombie Apocalypse: Why Every SIEM Killer Becomes the Corpse
items.summary: Warning : this blog is another experiment. The idea for a blog came from a real conversation I had with somebody. The content is researched, debated, refined, “hardened” by a Gemini skill I created (using Gemini 4 Argon). Then Claude Fable 5.2 performed a peer review, and tore some parts to shreds. Then rewrote them. Then Gemini 4 Carbon made fun of Claude’s dry style and restyled it. And then I very lightly edited it, and tuned a few jokes. I removed a metaphor involving a taximeter (wut?) Let me know if this sucks, and I will stop. Promise! I met my first SIM appliance in January 2002. Roughly eighteen months later, somebody at a conference told me the category was a dead end, and possibly even dead. So began the story of “SIEM is dead.” Since then, I have attended at least five formal industry funerals for SIEM: first when Log Management arrived around 2006, then when UEBA promised “math instead of rules” around 2014, then when XDR promised “endpoint-first nirvana” around 2020, and most recently when the Security Data Lake and Agentic AI crowds showed up holding shovels (some: pitchforks) in 2024 and 2026. Funny thing about all those funerals: the corpse keeps eating the pallbearers! (BTW, I am a constructive cynic, not a SIEM museum curator .) Look at the 2026 SANS SOC Survey (surveying 513 practitioners and security leaders). EDR earns the highest tool satisfaction in the SOC ( not surprising ), yet SIEM remains the number-one most sought-after skill in hiring, at nearly double the demand of EDR. People love complaining about their SIEM on Tuesday, try to replace it on Wednesday, and then hire two new SIEM engineers on Friday. Why does every “SIEM killer” end up quietly rebuilding a SIEM two years into production — and occasionally dying while trying? The short version fits on a sticker: you can fire your SIEM vendor, you can unbundle your SIEM storage, and you can ban the word “SIEM” from your architecture slides, but you cannot fire the SIEM job. Five Funerals and the Same Six Missing Parts Back in March 2023, in Debating SIEM in 2023, Part 2 , I proposed a simple sanity check: stop arguing about the four-letter acronym and list the actual problems you solved with it. If you refuse to buy a SIEM, those problems do not politely excuse themselves from your building. Every replacement wave starts with one genuinely superior wedge and an unspoken assumption that the other five parts of security operations are trivial plumbing! Here is The “Accidental SIEM Gravity Well” : what happens between Day 1 and Month 18 of every “SIEM-less” revolution (the four most recent are shown): SIEM killers list (2010–2026+) None of these waves failed because their core invention was bad. They won their narrow argument, walked into the SOC, and slammed straight into the Six Irreducible Jobs of SecOps Gravity (is this cool or what?): Hostile-World Ingestion & Drift Survival: Collecting from 80+ sources whose vendors change JSON schemas on Friday afternoons without telling you. Semantic Normalization & Identity Resolution: Knowing that achuvaki, anton@corp.local, and uid=2342 on an AWS role assumption are the same human, not just three strings in a column. Stateful, Cross-Source Correlation : Joining ten failed IdP logins, one new MFA device registration, and a SharePoint bulk download within a 10-minute sliding window. Alert Deduplication, Grouping & Queue State: Turning 47 firing rules from one intrusion into one work item with an owner, SLA timer, and status, instead of 47 Slack webhooks. Warning: this blog is another experiment. The idea for a blog came from a real conversation I had with somebody. The content is researched, debated, refined, “hardened” by a Gemini skill I created (using Gemini 4 Argon). Then Claude Fable 5.2 performed a peer review, and tore some parts to shreds. Then rewrote them. Then Gemini 4 Carbon made fun of Claude’s dry style and restyled it. And then I very lightly edited it, and tuned a few jokes. I removed a metaphor involving a taximeter (wut?) Let me know if this sucks, and I will stop. Promise!

I met my first SIM appliance in January 2002. Roughly eighteen months later, somebody at a conference told me the category was a dead end, and possibly even dead. So began the story of “SIEM is dead.”

Since then, I have attended at least five formal industry funerals for SIEM: first when Log Management arrived around 2006, then when UEBA promised “math instead of rules” around 2014, then when XDR promised “endpoint-first nirvana” around 2020, and most recently when the Security Data Lake and Agentic AI crowds showed up holding shovels (some: pitchforks) in 2024 and 2026.

Funny thing about all those funerals: the corpse keeps eating the pallbearers! (BTW, I am a constructive cynic, not a SIEM museum curator.)

Look at the 2026 SANS SOC Survey (surveying 513 practitioners and security leaders). EDR earns the highest tool satisfaction in the SOC (not surprising), yet SIEM remains the number-one most sought-after skill in hiring, at nearly double the demand of EDR. People love complaining about their SIEM on Tuesday, try to replace it on Wednesday, and then hire two new SIEM engineers on Friday.

Why does every “SIEM killer” end up quietly rebuilding a SIEM two years into production — and occasionally dying while trying?

The short version fits on a sticker: you can fire your SIEM vendor, you can unbundle your SIEM storage, and you can ban the word “SIEM” from your architecture slides, but you cannot fire the SIEM job.

Five Funerals and the Same Six Missing Parts

Back in March 2023, in Debating SIEM in 2023, Part 2, I proposed a simple sanity check: stop arguing about the four-letter acronym and list the actual problems you solved with it. If you refuse to buy a SIEM, those problems do not politely excuse themselves from your building.

Every replacement wave starts with one genuinely superior wedge and an unspoken assumption that the other five parts of security operations are trivial plumbing!

Here is The “Accidental SIEM Gravity Well”: what happens between Day 1 and Month 18 of every “SIEM-less” revolution (the four most recent are shown):

SIEM killers list (2010–2026+)

None of these waves failed because their core invention was bad. They won their narrow argument, walked into the SOC, and slammed straight into the Six Irreducible Jobs of SecOps Gravity (is this cool or what?):

  1. Hostile-World Ingestion & Drift Survival: Collecting from 80+ sources whose vendors change JSON schemas on Friday afternoons without telling you.
  2. Semantic Normalization & Identity Resolution: Knowing that achuvaki, anton@corp.local, and uid=2342 on an AWS role assumption are the same human, not just three strings in a column.
  3. Stateful, Cross-Source Correlation: Joining ten failed IdP logins, one new MFA device registration, and a SharePoint bulk download within a 10-minute sliding window.
  4. Alert Deduplication, Grouping & Queue State: Turning 47 firing rules from one intrusion into one work item with an owner, SLA timer, and status, instead of 47 Slack webhooks.
  5. Local Environment Memory (“Context as Code”): Remembering that svc_backup_02 is supposed to touch every file share at 2 AM on Sundays, and who approved that exception.
  6. The Tamper-Evident Time Machine: Proving to an auditor — or an incident responder nine months later — exactly what happened, with role-based access controls so junior analysts can’t read the CEO’s workstation logs where he mistyped his password.
“Its alive!!!” by Gemini

Skip any one of those six jobs in your shiny “not SIEM” replacement, and your own teams will quietly start writing Python scripts and gluing Jira tickets together to rebuild a SIEM organically. Not organically as in “tasty and healthy,” but as microbes decomposing a dead body kinda organic … [A.C. — this joke is me, not AI, obviously]

Let’s test today’s favorite boardroom sacred cow: “We will dump all our logs into S3/Athena or Snowflake, write SQL queries as detections, and fire our SIEM vendor!” (I picked this fight in 2017 and again in 2022.)

Take a mid-size enterprise generating 2 TB per day of raw security telemetry (AD, Okta, EDR, VPC flow, proxy, SaaS audit logs):

  • Naive Pay-Per-Scan Polling: Suppose your SOC runs 250 SQL (gasp!) correlation rules every 5 minutes (72,000 query runs per day). If your data lands as semi-structured JSON or tables partitioned by day rather than minute (or joining across a 30-minute lookback window), where each rule scans a 50 GB slice of recent multi-source logs, 72,000 queries × 0.05 TB = 3,600 TB scanned per day. The ghost of SIEM curses you from the great beyond.
  • “Wait, Anton, Nobody Does Unpruned JSON Scans!” Fair enough! A sharp data engineer will object: “Convert everything to OCSF in Apache Parquet/Iceberg, partition by eventDay and eventHour, buffer writes with Firehose, compact small files on a schedule, and push down predicates so each rule scans 50 MB instead of 50 GB!” [Ok, fine, AI made this up, but this is plausible! — A.C.]
  • Now Add Up the Engineering Bill: Congratulations, your scan bill just dropped by 99.9%, and your people and pipeline bill just arrived! To keep that running without dropping events, you now own: (a) a streaming ingestion and compaction tier; (b) OCSF mappers across 50+ messy sources where — as practitioner deployments keep rediscovering — mapping an IP to src_addr vs. proxy_addr takes security judgment, not just regex; (c) a stateful engine for sliding-window joins across partition boundaries; and (d) an alerting and case-management UI. Staffing that “free” architecture reliably takes 2 to 3 dedicated security data engineers ($200,000 to $500,000+ a year in loaded comp) before you write a single detection rule or hire an analyst to read the output (agents would do it?). You haven’t killed the SIEM — you have just entered the unregulated, artisanal SIEM software business, with one customer (yourself) and zero vendor support when it breaks, or any other time frankly.

Where the “SIEM Killers” Were Actually Right

Why do ambitious CISOs and brilliant detection engineers keep trying to kill SIEM every five years? Because the monolithic 2010-era SIEM bundle need evolution, if not a revolution!

For fifteen years, traditional SIEMs tightly coupled storage, data management, and detection. Worse, per the 2025 SANS SOC Survey, 42% of SOCs dumped all incoming data into their SIEM without a retrieval plan — paying hot-index rates for debug noise and compliance wallpaper nobody ever queried. SIEM is not log management.

Still, over the years, the “SIEM killers” got three big things right [this point alone is worth the price of reading this blog — A.C.]:

  1. Decoupling storage from compute became credible. (I asked in 2023 whether decoupled SIEM was brilliant or stupid before softening my stance on this). This is how several modern security platforms work in 2026, and even some legacy SIEM vendors spent the last few years replatforming onto lakehouse backends.
  2. Data pipelines broke log lock-in. Putting a routing and transformation layer in front of your detection engine means switching SIEMs no longer requires re-plumbing 10K servers and 220 log source types from scratch.
  3. Detection-as-Code beat click-ops. Engineering teams were right to demand Git-versioned detections, CI/CD testing, and open schemas like OCSF instead of clicking around brittle GUI wizards.

So the twist isn’t that data lakes, UEBA, XDR, or AI SOC failed. They succeeded at evolving the monolithic SIEM, and SIEM survived by eating their architecture. Calling a platform built on Iceberg + streaming correlation + OCSF + case management + AI triage “Not-a-SIEM” doesn’t prove SIEM is dead. It proves SIEM is alive!

As I wrote in The Ancient Art of SIEM: Why 2003 Problems Look So Familiar in 2026, the cost currency keeps changing (from RAID arrays to EPS to GB/day to warehouse credits and LLM tokens) while the underlying operational physics refuses to budge.

The Secret of SIEM’s Staying Power: It Owns the Messy Seams

SIEM survives because it is the only place in security forced to reconcile cross-domain state with local human reality under adversarial pressure.

In Can AI Let You Jump SOC Maturity Levels? (Spoiler: Only the Boring Half), I separated time cost from learning cost. AI and modern data lakess slash SecOps time cost — generating parsers, translating SPL to SQL, or scanning ten billion rows in three seconds. Take that win immediately.

What neither a Parquet file nor an out-of-the-box XDR sensor possesses is your security learning cost:

  • Which third-party vendor VPN is allowed to touch the claims database during month-end close?
  • Which subsidiary still runs a legacy AS/400 or custom billing app whose logs look like hieroglyphics?
  • When an alert spans Okta, AWS, and CrowdStrike, where does a human (or agent) record why it was benign — with an owner and expiration date — as I detailed in Stop Building a 2003 SOC with AI (Part 3: Local Context)?

Sit strictly below that seam (pure object storage) and you build a data swamp; sit strictly inside one silo (pure EDR) and you go blind the moment attackers log in instead of break in. Reach across the seam to correlate state and hold local context, and — whoosh welcome back to the Accidental SIEM Gravity Well.

The Lean Team Reality

Now let’s leave Silicon Valley hyperscaler land for five minutes. Suppose you run security for smaller enterprise with four security engineers, an MDR contract, compliance auditors breathing down your neck, and a SIEM renewal bill that just jumped 30%.

When a vendor or ambitious consultant pitches “Let’s ditch our SIEM and build a SIEM-agnostic AWS/Snowflake Security Data Lake!”, run away from the “replace the SIEM” half of that sentence. In advisory conversations I have had with smaller teams attempting this exact move, homebrew SIEM projects suffer a brutal failure rate.

What actually works for a lean team is the two-tier split I first argued for in 2009 and updated in SIEM: Centralize Like You Mean It, Federate Like You Have To:

  • Keep real-time detection, stateful correlation, and case triage in a commercial SIEM (or MDR-managed SIEM/XDR), shrink its hot retention window (say, from 90 days to 30), and strip out high-volume, low-signal compliance and network noise.
  • Put a commercial data pipeline in front of it (this mostly works, I swear, though YMMV on exotic legacy sources) to fork raw archival logs — plus daily structured exports from your SIEM — into cheap S3 or Snowflake storage for 1-year+ compliance, retro-hunting, and future migration leverage.

Same reason as in 2006: store only raw logs, and pivoting from a live SIEM alert into 9-month-old lake history is painful; store only SIEM-parsed exports, and anything your old SIEM failed to parse is lost forever while locking you into its schema!

You get most of the CFO cost relief and close to none of the broken homegrown correlation engine misery.

Potentially Useful Actions Based on This

Four usable ideas here:

  1. Audit your “SIEM Tax” by job, not by vendor invoice. Take your top 15 log sources and apply the Output-Driven SIEM test: which sources feed active, multi-source detections versus sitting there for annual audit comfort? Evict the compliance wallpaper instead of throwing out your correlation and case engine. (If an MDR runs your SIEM, ask at renewal which ingested feeds fired zero reviewed detections in the past 180 days, and stop paying hot-tier rates for logs their analysts never touch.)
  2. Run the “Six Irreducible Jobs” checklist on every “SIEM-less” pitch. Whenever an internal architect or startup proposes replacing your SIEM with Snowflake/Iceberg, XDR, or an AI agent mesh, score them against the Six Jobs above — and demand the 24x7 computer/storage cost estimates for your intended SIEM use.
  3. Unbundle your pipeline before you touch your platform. If your real pain is renewal extortion, use that vendor-neutral pipeline and 12-month S3 archive as commercial leverage. Owning routing and historical copies in your own bucket lets you swap SIEMs — or renegotiate your current one — without a 14-month re-plumbing nightmare.
  4. Use lakes and LLMs to kill toil. Point compute at petabyte-scale IOC sweeps and cold retro-hunts where SIEM hot tiers choke on cost. Point LLMs at writing parsers, translating detection logic, and drafting investigation summaries, while keeping deterministic engines in charge of streaming correlation, state, and gating. Do not point LLM at raw logs, unless you hate money.
So, Why Won’t SIEM Just Die Already?

Every few years, our industry confuses a clumsy product generation with an optional operational problem. Monolithic appliance SIEMs deserved to die. Blindly stuffing firewall debug garbage into premium-priced hot storage deserved to die. Swivel-chair L1 human triage is in the middle of dying right now.

What refuses to die is the messy, unglamorous center of gravity where half-broken logs from eighty vendors, stateful attacker timelines, compliance receipts, and quirky local business reality all collide at 3 AM. Call that box a Next-Gen SIEM, an Open Security Lakehouse, a Unified SecOps Platform, or “Bob.” [A.C. — which AI came with Bob?]. It is still a SIEM. And it is alive!
